title: Tenant Protection Act sunsets January 1, 2030
bodyText: Both halves of California's Tenant Protection Act carry an identical sunset: Civil Code sections 1946.2(n) and 1947.12(o) each provide that the section remains in effect only until January 1, 2030, and is repealed as of that date. Both became operative in their current form on April 1, 2024.

title: No pre-lease notice-of-default disclosure duty (repealed 2018)
bodyText: California no longer requires a landlord to disclose a recorded notice of default to a prospective tenant before signing a lease. Civil Code section 2924.85 imposed that duty on owners of single-family and 1-4 unit properties from January 1, 2013, but the section repealed itself on January 1, 2018 by its own terms and was not extended. A separate provision, Civil Code section 2924.8, governs notice to tenants after a notice of sale is posted and has not been examined here.

title: Security deposit photograph duties (2025)
bodyText: California requires landlords to photograph the unit in connection with security deposit deductions. For tenancies beginning on or after July 1, 2025, the landlord must take photographs immediately before or at the inception of the tenancy. Beginning April 1, 2025, the landlord must photograph the unit within a reasonable time after possession is returned and before any repairs or cleaning that will be deducted, and again after that work is completed. Photographs must be provided to the tenant with the itemized statement wherever a deduction for repairs or cleaning is made, unless repair and cleaning deductions together are $125 or less or the tenant has validly waived the supporting documents. Even then, provide them if the tenant asks within 14 days of receiving the statement.

title: California municipal rent and eviction ordinances (out of scope)
bodyText: Many California cities and counties impose their own rent stabilization and just-cause eviction rules that operate alongside or instead of state law. Civil Code section 1947.12(d)(3) yields to a local cap that is stricter than the state limit, and section 1946.2(i) provides that a local just-cause ordinance adopted on or before September 1, 2019, applies instead of the state scheme, as does a later ordinance that is more protective and contains a binding local finding to that effect. A property is never subject to both a local just-cause ordinance and section 1946.2.

title: Bed bug duties beyond the move-in disclosure
bodyText: California imposes three bed bug duties on landlords beyond the written disclosure given before a new tenancy. A landlord may not show, rent or lease a vacant unit the landlord knows has a current bed bug infestation. There is no duty to inspect for bed bugs absent notice of a suspected or actual infestation, but an infestation evident on visual inspection counts as notice. And where a pest control operator inspects units, the landlord must notify the tenants of those units of the operator's findings in writing within two business days of receiving them; for a confirmed infestation in a common area, all tenants must be notified. The information-about-bed-bugs notice is owed to prospective tenants before a new tenancy begins (Civ. Code 1954.603); the lease's optional clause carries the text and the reporting procedure, but give it before signing.

title: California mold: a habitability duty, and a booklet disclosure duty since 2022
bodyText: California treats mold primarily as a habitability matter, but it does also carry one live disclosure duty. Visible mold growth is listed as a substandard condition under Health and Safety Code section 17920.3(a)(13), and Civil Code section 1941.1(a) makes a dwelling untenantable if it is a residential unit described in section 17920.3. Two limits apply: the visible mold growth must be determined by a health officer or a code enforcement officer, and mold that is minor and found on surfaces that accumulate moisture as part of their properly functioning and intended use is excluded. The mold article contains two separate disclosure sections with different triggers, and only one of them operates. The general mold disclosure at Health and Safety Code section 26147 is suspended by section 26147(e) until six months after the department adopts permissible exposure limits and health guidelines and develops remediation guidelines, and it has never adopted them. But section 26148 requires a residential landlord to give prospective tenants a consumer-oriented booklet on the health risks of mold before entering the rental agreement, and section 26148(c) makes that duty operative six months after the department approves a booklet rather than after any standards are adopted. The department published its renters' booklet and states that landlords have been required to provide it since January 1, 2022. A landlord is never required to conduct air or surface testing for mold. The Department of Public Health's dampness-and-mold booklet must be given before the lease is signed; the lease's optional clause records that it was, and the tenant's duty to report dampness or mold.

title: Returned-check service charge and treble damages are alternatives
bodyText: California gives the payee of a bad check two separate remedies, and a landlord cannot have both. The service charge is capped at $25 for a first check and $35 for each subsequent one. Alternatively, the landlord may pursue treble damages, but only after mailing a written demand by certified mail that states the provisions of the statute, the amount of the check, and the amount of the service charge, and then waiting 30 days for payment. Treble damages are not less than $100 and not more than $1,500. Once a tenant becomes liable for treble damages on a check, the tenant is no longer liable for the service charge or the mailing costs on that check. A tenant is liable only once per check. No service charge is owed if the tenant stopped payment to resolve a good-faith dispute with you, or shows written confirmation from their bank that the instrument was returned because of the bank's error, or that the account was short because a regularly scheduled social security or government benefit deposit was delayed (Civ. Code 1719(a)).

title: Methamphetamine or fentanyl remediation order: disclosure mechanics
bodyText: Where a local health officer has issued a methamphetamine or fentanyl remediation order affecting a property, the owner's disclosure duty to prospective tenants continues until the owner receives written notice from the health officer that the property requires no further action. During that period the owner must give written notice of the order to every prospective tenant who has completed a rental application, provide a copy of the order, obtain the tenant's written acknowledgment of receipt before the rental agreement is signed, and attach the notice to the rental agreement. A prospective tenant may void the rental agreement if the owner does not do all of this. The lease's optional clause records the notice and acknowledgment; the duty itself is owed before the rental agreement is signed.

title: Assistance animals: what a landlord may ask and require
bodyText: California limits how a housing provider may verify an assistance animal. For a service animal, only two questions may be asked: whether the person is an individual with a disability, and what disability-related task the animal has been trained to perform. The person may not be asked to demonstrate the task. Service animals need not be professionally trained or certified. Animal vests, identification cards and certificates are not by themselves documentation of a disability or of the need for an accommodation. A support animal certification bought from an online service, without an individualized assessment by a medical professional, is presumptively not reliable third-party information - but before denying the request the housing provider must give the individual an opportunity to supply information that does meet the standard. A denial for direct threat must rest on an individualized assessment of objective evidence about that specific animal's actual conduct, not on speculation, fear, or what other animals have done.

title: Lease translation duty (five languages)
bodyText: California requires a landlord who negotiates a lease primarily in Spanish, Chinese, Tagalog, Vietnamese or Korean to deliver the tenant a full translation of the lease, including every term and condition, before the lease is signed, and to provide a notice in that language at the time and place of signing. The duty applies only to a tenancy for a period longer than one month. It does not apply where the tenant negotiated through the tenant's own interpreter, meaning an adult fluent in both languages who is not employed by or supplied through the landlord. House rules and furnishing inventories ordinarily incorporated by reference do not have to be translated, but a later document making substantial changes to the parties' rights does. The English lease governs the parties' rights; the translation is admissible only to show that no contract was formed because of a substantial difference in material terms. A tenant may rescind the lease if the landlord does not comply, and any waiver of these requirements is void.

title: Lease provisions void as contrary to public policy, and the before-possession rule
bodyText: California voids two categories of lease provision outright. First, any provision by which a tenant agrees to modify or waive rights or remedies under the security deposit statute or the landlord entry statute, the right to assert a future cause of action against the landlord, the right to a notice or hearing required by law, procedural rights in litigation over the tenancy, or the right to have the landlord exercise a duty of care imposed by law to prevent personal injury or personal property damage. Second, any provision modifying or waiving any other statutory right is void unless the lease was presented to the tenant before the tenant took actual possession of the premises. That second rule does not apply to a renewal that carries forward the same provision from the agreement being renewed. Both rules apply to leases executed on or after January 1, 1976.

title: Disability accommodations: the interactive process and inquiry limits
bodyText: When a landlord cannot immediately grant a requested accommodation or modification, California requires the landlord to engage in a timely, good-faith interactive process with the tenant. A request may not be denied for lack of information without first asking for the missing information and giving the tenant a reasonable opportunity to supply it, and undue delay in responding can itself amount to a denial. What the landlord may ask depends on what is already apparent: if the disability and the need are apparent or known, no further information may be requested at all; if only the need is unclear, the landlord may ask only for a description of the accommodation and how it relates to the disability. A landlord may never ask about the tenant's diagnosis, the severity of the disability, medical records, or medical history. A tenant can often establish disability by self-certification, such as proof of receipt of disability benefits or a credible statement. All information about a disability or a request must be kept confidential. Where the need for an accommodation arises from the landlord's own failure to maintain or repair the property as required by law, the undue-burden and fundamental-alteration defenses do not apply. A tenant, a family member or anyone the tenant authorizes may request a reasonable accommodation or modification at any time, orally or in writing, without particular words, forms or procedures; you may not charge any fee, deposit or other financial contribution for receiving, processing or granting one, and a lease can't make the tenant give up the right to ask in future (2 CCR 12176(f)(1)). Reasonable modifications: a tenant may make reasonable modifications at their own expense where a disability makes them necessary. You may ask for a reasonable description of the work and reasonable assurances it will be done competently with any required permits, but not require a particular contractor; you may not raise a customary security deposit, require a liability waiver or insurance, or require a move to another unit as a condition. Where reasonable, you may require the interior restored at the end of the tenancy, reasonable wear and tear excepted, but not exterior or common-area modifications (2 CCR 12181).

title: Retaliation: the 180-day window and what counts
bodyText: California bars a landlord from recovering possession, causing a tenant to quit involuntarily, increasing rent, or decreasing services within 180 days of a tenant exercising rights relating to tenantability, where the tenant is not in default on rent. The triggering events include the tenant giving repair notice, giving notice of a suspected bed bug infestation, making an oral complaint about tenantability, filing a complaint with an agency, an inspection or citation resulting from such a complaint, commencing a proceeding involving tenantability, and a judgment on tenantability against the landlord; where more than one applies, the 180 days run from the latest. A tenant may invoke this protection only once in any 12-month period. Separately, and without that time limit, it is unlawful to retaliate because a tenant organized or participated in a tenants' association or lawfully exercised any legal right. Threatening to report a tenant, or anyone the landlord knows to be associated with the tenant, to immigration authorities is retaliatory conduct under both rules. A landlord may still act within the 180 days for a lawful reason if the notice states the good-faith ground relied on, and must prove that ground if it is challenged. A landlord who violates the section is liable for actual damages plus punitive damages of $100 to $2,000 for each retaliatory act involving fraud, oppression or malice, and the court awards attorney's fees to the prevailing party if either party requests them when the action begins. Any waiver of these protections is void.

title: Application screening fees
bodyText: A landlord may charge an application screening fee only to cover the actual cost of screening, capped at a statutory amount that is adjusted annually for inflation, and may not charge one at all when the landlord knows or should know that no unit is or will soon be available. The landlord must also operate one of two processes: either consider completed applications in the order received against written screening criteria given to the applicant with the application form and approve the first applicant who meets them, or return the entire fee to every applicant not selected within seven days of selecting a tenant or thirty days of the application, whichever comes first. The landlord must give the applicant an itemized receipt, refund any part of the fee not actually used, and give the applicant a copy of any consumer credit report obtained within seven days of receiving it. A different kind of report, an investigative consumer report on the applicant's character, general reputation, personal characteristics or mode of living, carries its own duties. You must notify the applicant in writing within three days after first requesting one, and offer a box to tick for a copy. If you deny the application or raise the charge because of one, you must tell the applicant and name the agency. The tenant-records guidance covers these in full.

title: Three-day notice content and service
bodyText: California's three-day notices are governed by statute rather than by the lease. For the notices to pay rent or quit and to perform or quit, the three days exclude Saturdays, Sundays and judicial holidays. The notice to quit for nuisance, waste, unlawful use or unlawful assignment says only three days, so count it the same way to be safe. A notice demanding rent must state the amount due and the name, telephone number and address of the person to whom rent is to be paid, with the usual days and hours that person is available if payment may be made personally; alternatively it may give a financial institution account number with the institution's name and street address, provided the institution is within five miles of the rental property, or refer to an electronic funds transfer procedure already established. It must be served on the tenant and on any subtenant in actual occupation, and may be served at any time within one year after the rent becomes due. A notice to perform other covenants gives the tenant, a subtenant, a mortgagee or another interested person three days to perform and save the lease from forfeiture, and no such notice is required where the violated covenant can no longer be performed. Assigning or subletting contrary to the lease, committing waste, maintaining a nuisance or using the premises for an unlawful purpose terminates the lease and supports a three-day notice to quit with no opportunity to cure. Notices may be served by personal delivery; by leaving a copy with a person of suitable age and discretion at the tenant's residence or usual place of business and mailing a copy to the residence; or, where neither can be ascertained and no suitable person is found, by posting conspicuously on the property, delivering to a person residing there if one can be found, and mailing to the property. A landlord may not charge any fee for serving, posting or delivering these notices. You also may not charge the tenant any fee for serving, posting or otherwise delivering any notice about the tenancy, including a notice ending a periodic tenancy or a three-day notice (Civ. Code 1946.1(i); CCP 1161(6)). One more rule governs how these notices travel: California's electronic transactions law says outright that an electronic record may not be substituted for any notice required to be served under Code of Civil Procedure section 1162, which is the section that governs service of these notices. So a three-day notice, or a notice terminating a tenancy, cannot be emailed or texted in place of the statutory service methods, whatever the lease says about electronic delivery.

title: Who counts as a tenant, and which occupancies fall outside the chapter
bodyText: California's residential landlord-tenant chapter applies to everyone who hires a dwelling unit in the state, including tenants, lessees, boarders and lodgers, however they are described in the agreement. A dwelling unit means a structure or part of a structure used as a home, residence or sleeping place by one person maintaining a household or by two or more people maintaining a common household. Two occupancies are outside the chapter: transient occupancy in a hotel, motel, residence club or similar facility where the stay is subject to transient occupancy tax, and occupancy at a hotel or motel where the innkeeper keeps a right of access to and control of the unit and the establishment offers all of five services to every resident - personal property safekeeping, central telephone service under filed tariffs, maid, mail and room services, occupancy for periods of less than seven days, and food service from an establishment on or next to the premises connected to the innkeeper. Unless a particular provision says otherwise by its own terms, the chapter's provisions apply to a tenancy in a dwelling unit.

title: Reusable tenant screening reports
bodyText: California lets a rental applicant supply a reusable tenant screening report - a consumer report prepared within the previous 30 days at the applicant's own request and expense, made available to the landlord at no cost either directly or through a third-party service. Such a report must include the applicant's name and contact information, verification of employment, last known address, and the results of an eviction history check, and must state prominently the date through which its information is current. A landlord is not required to accept these reports. A landlord who does accept them may ask the applicant to confirm that nothing in the report has materially changed, but may not charge that applicant any fee to access the report and may not charge an application screening fee at all. Where a local ordinance conflicts with these rules, whichever gives applicants greater protection applies.

title: Nuisance-based eviction and the city-prosecutor assignment
bodyText: California deems certain conduct a nuisance for the purpose of a three-day notice to quit, but the provisions are narrower than they appear. Using a building or property for dogfighting or cockfighting is a public nuisance statewide. A separate controlled-substance eviction procedure lets a city prosecutor or city attorney bring an unlawful detainer action, but it operates only in the City of Los Angeles. Under that procedure the prosecutor must first give the owner 30 calendar days' written notice requiring the owner to act, and the owner must within 30 days either supply all relevant information or give a written safety-related explanation together with an assignment of the right to bring the action. Accepting the assignment can cost the owner up to $600 in investigation, discovery and attorney's fees. If the owner does not act, or does not prosecute the action diligently and in good faith, the prosecutor may file and join the owner as a defendant, and on a finding of unlawful detainer the prosecutor's costs may be assessed against the owner and recorded as a lien on the property. The court may order a partial eviction removing only the person involved and barring their return, rather than ending the whole tenancy.

title: Forfeiture election and the five-day redemption window
bodyText: In California a judgment in an unlawful detainer action declares the lease forfeited only if the three-day notice stated the landlord's election to declare a forfeiture. If the notice did not say so, the lease is not forfeited. Separately, where the action is for nonpayment of rent, the lease has not expired by its own terms and the notice did not elect forfeiture, the court may delay the writ for five days after judgment so that the tenant, a subtenant, a mortgagee or another interested party can pay the rent, damages and costs and be restored to the tenancy. That five-day delay is mandatory rather than discretionary where the lease is in writing, is for a term of more than one year, and contains no forfeiture clause.

title: No general right of periodic inspection
bodyText: California limits landlord entry to the purposes listed in Civil Code section 1954. A general right to conduct periodic inspections of an occupied dwelling is not among them. The inspections the statute provides for are narrow: the initial inspection a tenant may request before the end of the tenancy under Civil Code section 1950.5(f); entry for water submetering purposes under Civil Code section 1954.201 and following; and entry to comply with the exterior elevated element (balcony and deck) inspection law in Health and Safety Code section 17973 and following. Entry to make necessary or agreed repairs, to supply agreed services, or to show the unit is permitted, but a lease term reserving periodic inspections has no statutory basis and any waiver of section 1954 rights is void under Civil Code section 1953(a)(1).

title: Damages when a tenant breaches and abandons
bodyText: When a tenant breaches the lease and abandons, or the landlord ends the tenant's right to possession for breach, California lets the landlord recover unpaid rent earned before termination, the rent that would have been earned between termination and the award less whatever loss the tenant proves could reasonably have been avoided, and any other detriment proximately caused by the breach. Recovering rent for the balance of the term after the award is different: it is available only if the lease expressly provides for it, or if the landlord re-rented the property before the award and proves the re-rental was reasonable and in good faith. Interest on the pre-award amounts runs at the rate stated in the lease if lawful, otherwise at the legal rate. Making efforts to re-rent does not waive the landlord's right to damages.

title: Abuse and violence: eviction bar, lock changes, confidentiality
bodyText: A landlord may not terminate or refuse to renew a tenancy based on an act of abuse or violence against the tenant, the tenant's immediate family member, or a household member once the landlord has received qualifying documentation. There are two exceptions: where the perpetrator is a tenant in residence of the same unit, and where the perpetrator's words or actions have threatened the physical safety of other tenants, guests or invitees and the tenant continues to permit the perpetrator on the premises after a three-day notice requiring them not to. Where a person restrained by court order is a tenant of the same unit, the landlord must change the locks at the landlord's own expense within 24 hours of a written request accompanied by the order, and give the protected tenant a key; if the landlord does not, the tenant may change the locks and the landlord must reimburse the cost within 21 days. Information a tenant provides under these protections may not be disclosed to third parties without written consent or a court order. A landlord is not liable to other tenants for complying. Ending the lease (Civ. Code 1946.7): a tenant may terminate if the tenant, a household member or an immediate family member was the victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, stalking, human trafficking, elder or dependent-adult abuse, a crime that caused bodily injury or death, a crime involving a firearm or other deadly weapon, or a crime involving force or its threat. The tenant gives you written notice, within 180 days of the order, report or act, attaching a qualifying restraining or protective order, a peace officer's written report that a report was filed, qualified third-party documentation in the statutory form, or other documentation reasonably verifying the act. The tenant owes rent for no more than 14 days after the notice (prorated if you re-rent sooner), is released without penalty, forfeits no deposit or advance rent, and isn't in breach; any other tenant stays bound. Keep the tenant's information confidential. Where the person who committed or allegedly committed the abuse or violence is not a tenant of the same unit, change the locks at your own expense within 24 hours of the tenant's written request with any documentation listed in Civ. Code 1941.5(d), and give the tenant a key. If you don't, the tenant may change the locks without your permission and you must reimburse them within 21 days, provided they use locks of similar or better quality, tell you within 24 hours and give you a key.

title: Protected classes and source-of-income rules
bodyText: California prohibits housing discrimination on the basis of race, color, religion, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation, marital status, national origin, ancestry, familial status, source of income, disability, veteran or military status, or genetic information, including a perception that a person has any of those characteristics or is associated with someone who does. Source of income includes federal, state and local public assistance and housing subsidies, expressly including Section 8 vouchers and HUD-VASH vouchers, so refusing to rent because an applicant holds a voucher is unlawful. Where there is a government rent subsidy, any financial or income standard must be based only on the portion of rent the tenant actually pays, and an applicant must be offered the option of supplying alternative evidence of ability to pay instead of a credit history. A landlord must also count the aggregate income of people residing together on the same basis as it would for married people.

title: Tenant harassment and immigration-status disclosure
bodyText: California makes it unlawful for a landlord, for the purpose of influencing a tenant to vacate, to engage in conduct amounting to theft or extortion, to use or threaten force or menacing conduct interfering with the tenant's quiet enjoyment, to commit a significant and intentional violation of the entry statute, or to threaten to disclose information about the immigration or citizenship status of a tenant, occupant or anyone associated with them. A tenant who prevails may recover a civil penalty of up to $2,000 for each violation. Separately, it is unlawful to disclose such immigration or citizenship information to any immigration authority, law enforcement agency or government agency for the purpose of harassing or retaliating against a tenant, influencing them to vacate, or recovering possession. A court that finds such a disclosure must order statutory damages of between 6 and 12 times the monthly rent for each person whose status was disclosed, issue injunctive relief, and notify the district attorney. Separately, you may not ask about the immigration or citizenship status of a tenant, prospective tenant, occupant or prospective occupant, or require them to disclose or certify it (Civ. Code 1940.3(b)). You may still request information or documentation needed to verify financial qualifications or identity, and comply with federal law, a subpoena, warrant or court order.

title: Disposing of personal property left after a tenancy
bodyText: California provides an optional procedure for personal property a tenant leaves behind after the tenancy ends and the premises are vacated. The landlord gives written notice to the former tenant and anyone else reasonably believed to own the property, describing it well enough to be identified, stating where it may be claimed, that reasonable storage costs may be charged, and a claim deadline at least 15 days after personal delivery or 18 days after mailing. The statute supplies notice forms that satisfy the requirement. Property must be left on the premises or stored safely with reasonable care. If it is not claimed, it must be sold at public sale after published notice, unless the landlord reasonably believes the total resale value is under $700, in which case the landlord may keep or dispose of it. Sale proceeds left over go to the county within 30 days and may be claimed by the former tenant for a year. A landlord who follows the procedure is protected from liability. No storage cost may be charged if the tenant reclaims property within two days of vacating.

title: Death on the premises: the three-year rule
bodyText: California law occupies the field on disclosing deaths that occurred on a property. An owner or agent is not required to disclose the occurrence of an occupant's death, or the manner of death, where the death occurred more than three years before the prospective tenant offers to rent, and is never required to disclose that an occupant was living with HIV or died of AIDS-related complications. The implication is that a death within the previous three years is treated as a material fact. An owner or agent is also not immunized for an intentional misrepresentation made in response to a direct question about deaths on the property.

title: Eviction court records are masked for 60 days
bodyText: An unlawful detainer court file in California is not publicly accessible for the first 60 days after the complaint is filed. During that period the clerk may release records only to a party or their attorney, to someone who supplies the names of a plaintiff and a defendant plus the address including any unit number, to a resident of the premises who identifies a party or the case number and proves residency, or by court order on a showing of good cause. After 60 days the file opens if judgment has been entered for the plaintiff, and in a residential case based on a post-foreclosure claim only if judgment was entered for the plaintiff after a trial. The parties may also stipulate to bar access entirely. The clerk mails every named defendant a notice within 24 to 48 hours of filing, with legal-aid and lawyer-referral information.

title: Balcony and exterior elevated element inspections
bodyText: Buildings with three or more multifamily dwelling units must have their exterior elevated elements - balconies, decks, porches, stairways, walkways and entry structures more than six feet above ground that rely on wood for support - inspected by a licensed architect, engineer, qualified contractor or certified building inspector hired by the owner. At least 15 percent of each type must be examined. The inspector delivers a written report within 45 days. Inspections were due by January 1, 2026 and are required every six years after that. Elements needing repair must be corrected by the owner under permit, within 120 days of permit approval, and anything posing an immediate threat requires immediate action including blocking access. An owner who does not comply within 180 days faces a civil penalty of $100 to $500 per day and a recordable building safety lien.

title: Criminal history in tenant screening
bodyText: California regulates how criminal history may be used in tenant screening. Blanket bans are unlawful: a policy excluding everyone with a criminal record, or with any prior conviction, misdemeanor or felony, is prohibited outright. A landlord may not seek, consider, use, or take adverse action based on an arrest that did not lead to conviction, on being questioned or detained, on participation in a diversion or deferred entry of judgment program, on an infraction, on a conviction that has been sealed, dismissed, vacated, expunged, pardoned or otherwise rendered inoperative, on a conviction for which a certificate of rehabilitation was granted, or on juvenile adjudications. Only convictions directly related to a substantial, legitimate, nondiscriminatory interest may be considered, judged by the nature and severity of the offense and how much time has passed. Whether a screening practice is defensible turns partly on whether it gives the applicant written notice of an opportunity to present mitigating information and actually considers it, checks the accuracy of the record, and delays the criminal history inquiry until after financial and other qualifications are verified. Mitigating information includes youth at the time of the offense, time elapsed, good tenant history, rehabilitation, and conduct arising from the applicant's status as a survivor of abuse or from a disability. A third rule, in statute, limits what an investigative screening report may contain. It may not report an arrest or conviction more than seven years old, counted from disposition, release or parole, or one later pardoned or that did not lead to conviction. Nor may it report an eviction case the tenant won or that settled. If a vendor's report includes such items, do not act on them.

title: When a landlord may not demand or collect rent at all
bodyText: California bars a landlord from demanding rent, collecting rent, issuing a notice of rent increase, or issuing a three-day notice to pay rent or quit where four conditions all exist. The dwelling substantially lacks one of the standard habitability characteristics, violates Health and Safety Code section 17920.10, or is substandard under section 17920.3 to an extent that endangers life, limb, health, property, safety or welfare. A public officer responsible for enforcing housing law has inspected the premises and notified the landlord in writing of the obligation to abate or repair. The conditions have gone unabated for 35 days beyond service of that notice without good cause. And the conditions were not caused by the tenant. A landlord who violates this is liable for actual damages plus special damages of between $100 and $5,000, and the prevailing party recovers attorney's fees and costs. The court may also order the conditions abated and retain jurisdiction until they are.

title: Attorney-fee clauses are reciprocal by operation of law
bodyText: In California, if a lease provides that attorney's fees incurred to enforce it will be awarded to one party or to the prevailing party, the party who actually prevails is entitled to reasonable fees whether or not the lease names them. A one-sided fee clause therefore operates in both directions, and any provision waiving that rule is void. The fee provision is read as applying to the whole contract unless both parties were represented by counsel in negotiating and executing it and the lease says so. The court decides who prevailed, may find that nobody did, and there is no prevailing party at all where the action was voluntarily dismissed or dismissed under a settlement.

title: Unconscionable lease clauses
bodyText: A California court that finds a contract or any clause of it was unconscionable when it was made may refuse to enforce the contract, enforce the rest of it without the unconscionable clause, or limit the clause's application to avoid an unconscionable result. Where unconscionability is claimed or appears, the parties must be given a reasonable opportunity to present evidence about the clause's commercial setting, purpose and effect.

title: Criminal penalty for faking a service dog
bodyText: In California it is a misdemeanor to knowingly and fraudulently represent yourself, verbally or in writing, as the owner or trainer of a dog licensed, qualified or identified as a guide, signal or service dog. The penalty is up to six months in county jail, a fine of up to $1,000, or both.

title: Relocation benefits during habitability repairs
bodyText: Where a California enforcement agency has cited a building and the court finds conditions substantially endangering health and safety, and the owner's repairs or the conditions themselves significantly affect safe and sanitary use so that a tenant cannot safely remain, the owner must provide or pay relocation benefits. These cover actual reasonable moving and storage costs, including transporting, packing and insuring the tenant's property, replacing property lost or damaged in the move, and reconnecting utilities and equipment. On top of that, relocation compensation equals the difference between the contract rent and the HUD fair market rent for a comparable unit in the area, for the period of repair, up to 120 days. A tenant substantially responsible for causing the conditions receives nothing. The owner must also offer each relocated tenant the first right to occupancy in writing by certified mail before renting to anyone else. If a receiver is appointed, the owner is enjoined from collecting rent at all.

title: Double letting of a room suspends all rent in the building
bodyText: California provides that a person who hires part of a room as a dwelling is entitled to the whole room, regardless of any agreement to the contrary. If a landlord lets a room as a dwelling to more than one family, the first person to whom any part of it was let is entitled to possession of the whole room for the agreed term, and every tenant in the building under the same landlord is relieved of all obligation to pay rent for as long as the double letting continues.

title: Screening: four things a landlord may not hold against an applicant
bodyText: California bars a landlord from taking adverse action in tenant screening based on any of four things: an alleged breach of a prior lease that stemmed from an act of abuse or violence, where the applicant is not alleged to have committed it; the applicant having previously requested a lock change after abuse or violence, whether or not the request was granted; the applicant, or an immediate family or household member, having been a victim of abuse or violence; or the applicant or a guest having previously summoned law enforcement or emergency assistance for a victim of abuse, a victim of crime, or a person in an emergency. Adverse action includes both denying the application and approving it on terms less favourable than those advertised. A landlord who violates this is liable for actual damages plus statutory damages of $100 to $5,000.

title: Mandatory offer of positive rent reporting
bodyText: California requires most residential landlords to offer each tenant the option of having positive rental payment information reported to a consumer reporting agency. For leases entered into on or after April 1, 2025, the offer must be made at the time of the lease and at least once annually after that. The written election must state that reporting is optional, identify each agency, state any fee, explain how to opt in and out, note that a tenant who opts out cannot resume for six months, and include a signature block. A landlord may charge no more than the actual cost or $10 per month, whichever is less, and nothing if there is no actual cost. Non-payment of that fee cannot be reported, cannot be cause for termination, and cannot be deducted from the security deposit. The duty does not apply to a landlord of a building with 15 or fewer units unless the landlord owns more than one building and is a REIT, a corporation, or an LLC with a corporate member.

title: Notice of belief of abandonment
bodyText: Where rent has been due and unpaid for at least 14 consecutive days and the landlord reasonably believes the tenant has abandoned the property, the landlord may serve a notice of belief of abandonment. The statute supplies the form. The notice must specify a termination date at least 15 days after personal service or 18 days after mailing, and the lease terminates on that date unless the tenant gives written notice before then stating an intent not to abandon and an address for service by certified mail. The property is not deemed abandoned if the rent was not in fact 14 days overdue, if the landlord's belief was not reasonable, if the tenant gave the required notice, or if the tenant paid all or part of the overdue rent in the relevant window. Knowing that the tenant left personal property behind does not by itself make the belief unreasonable.

title: Social Security hardship defence to eviction
bodyText: Until January 20, 2029, a California tenant facing an unlawful detainer for nonpayment of rent may assert a Social Security hardship defence by showing that the household's usual Social Security benefits were terminated, delayed or reduced through no fault of the tenant because of federal government action or inaction, and that the interruption prevented payment of the rent claimed. If the tenant proves both, the court must stay the action until 14 days after benefits are restored or six months after the stay, whichever is earlier. The tenant must then pay all past-due rent or agree a payment plan within 14 days of restoration, and if they do, the court must restore the tenancy and dismiss the action or set aside the judgment.

title: When a habitability breach is presumed in an eviction
bodyText: In an unlawful detainer action, California presumes that the landlord has breached the habitability requirements where the dwelling substantially lacks a standard habitability characteristic, is substandard under the Health and Safety Code, or contains lead hazards; a housing enforcement officer has inspected and notified the landlord in writing to repair; the conditions remain unabated 60 days after that notice without good cause; and the tenant did not cause them. The presumption shifts the burden of producing evidence to the landlord. A tenant who cannot establish all four conditions may still raise any other habitability defence.

title: Disaster-displaced hotel and short-stay guests
bodyText: Until January 1, 2031, a guest staying in a hotel, motel or compliant short-term lodging because a declared disaster substantially damaged, destroyed or made uninhabitable their home is not treated as a tenant, and their stay does not become a tenancy for eviction purposes, until they have stayed 270 days. Before or at check-in for a stay exceeding 30 consecutive days, the operator must give the statutory notice in at least 12-point type and a confirmation form on which the guest indicates whether they are disaster-displaced. Once such a guest has stayed more than 30 days, the operator must give 72 hours' written notice before requiring them to leave, unless the guest has failed to pay, interfered with other guests, damaged or threatened to damage property, or poses a risk of harm.

title: Further landlord-supplied facilities
bodyText: Beyond the standard habitability list, a California landlord must keep floors, stairways and railings in good repair; provide a locking mail receptacle for each unit in a residential hotel; and install at least one usable telephone jack and keep the inside telephone wiring in good working order, meeting current electrical code, without restricting the telephone utility's access to its network facilities.

title: Lead hazards as a habitability violation
bodyText: California treats lead hazards as a habitability violation, separately from and in addition to the federal lead-based paint disclosure rule. Any dwelling unit, or any portion of a building or its premises, that contains lead hazards is deemed in violation of the state housing law. Lead hazards means deteriorated lead-based paint, lead-contaminated dust, lead-contaminated soil, or disturbing lead-based paint without containment, at levels likely to endanger the health of occupants or the public. Deteriorated paint and paint disturbed without containment count only where the affected area reaches at least two square feet in any one interior room, twenty square feet on exterior surfaces, or ten percent of the surface of a small component such as a window sill, baseboard or trim - unless a smaller area is associated with a person whose blood lead level is 10 micrograms per deciliter or higher, in which case the smaller area counts. Because a unit containing lead hazards is untenantable, the tenant's habitability remedies apply, and repair or renovation work that disturbs lead-based paint without containment can itself create a violation. Paid lead inspections and risk assessments, abatement plans, and permanent lead-hazard reduction work must be done by certified people. From July 1, 2027, a firm you pay for renovation, repair or painting that disturbs lead-based paint must be certified too. Routine maintenance and repairs outside those activities need no certificate.

title: The consumer all-in pricing rule does not reach rent
bodyText: California's general all-in pricing rule under the Consumers Legal Remedies Act, which makes it unlawful to advertise or offer a price that omits mandatory fees, applies to transactions for the sale or lease of goods or services to a consumer. A residential tenancy is neither: the Act defines goods as tangible chattels and services as work, labor and services, and a lease of real property is the hiring of land, not a chattel or a service. On the statute's text, that rule does not govern how rent is advertised. California instead regulates specific rental charges directly - screening fees, check-payment fees, notice-service fees, accommodation fees and separately listed rent concessions - and those rules apply regardless.

title: Exculpatory clauses in residential leases: the case law
bodyText: The California Supreme Court has held that a residential lease affects the public interest, so a clause exempting a landlord from liability for its own future negligence is invalid. More recently, the Court held that no contract may release a party from liability for violating a statutory duty: the older public-interest test applies only to releases of ordinary common-law negligence. Because most of a California landlord's duties to tenants are statutory - habitability, locks, smoke alarms, building conditions, balcony inspections - a lease release cannot reach a claim that one of those duties was breached. A narrow exception recognised by a court of appeal, for injuries from using an on-site recreational amenity such as an exercise facility, survives only for ordinary negligence claims, not for claims that a statutory duty was violated.

title: Jury trial waivers in a lease are unenforceable
bodyText: In California a contractual waiver of the right to a jury trial made before any dispute arises is unenforceable unless a statute expressly authorizes it, and no statute authorizes one in a residential lease. A jury waiver clause in a California lease therefore has no effect. Separately, a residential lease provision waiving a tenant's procedural rights in litigation is void by statute.

title: Accepting rent can waive a breach or renew the tenancy
bodyText: In California, a landlord who accepts rent with full knowledge of a tenant's breach waives the right to declare a forfeiture for that breach and for any earlier breach, and is estopped from relying on it. A landlord may avoid that waiver by giving the tenant notice at the time rent is accepted that acceptance is not consent to the breach or a waiver of the right to forfeit. A separate and harder rule applies after a notice terminating the tenancy has expired: accepting rent then creates a presumption that the tenancy was renewed, and a court of appeal has held that a non-waiver clause did not overcome that presumption where the tenant was not yet in breach when the rent was accepted. A non-waiver clause is more likely to hold where the landlord accepts rent after an actual breach, such as unpaid rent following a three-day notice. As a practical matter, rent tendered after a three-day or termination notice expires should be returned rather than accepted if the landlord intends to proceed.

title: No lockouts, utility shutoffs or removal of belongings
bodyText: A California landlord may not, with intent to end a residential tenancy, willfully cause any utility service to the tenant to be interrupted or terminated - including water, heat, light, electricity, gas, telephone, elevator or refrigeration - whether or not the landlord controls the utility. Nor may the landlord change the locks or use a bootlock or similar device to keep the tenant out, remove outside doors or windows, or remove the tenant's belongings or furnishings without the tenant's prior written consent, except under the statutory procedure for property left after a tenancy ends. The only lawful way to remove a tenant is through a court eviction carried out by the appropriate authorities. A landlord who violates this is liable for the tenant's actual damages plus up to $100 for each day or part of a day the violation continues, with a minimum of $250 for each separate violation, and the prevailing party recovers attorney's fees. A repeat violation on a later occasion counts as a new violation with its own award.

title: Military tenants: no chain-of-command contact, no waivers
bodyText: In collecting any debt or payment from a member of the active California militia or an active or reserve member of the Armed Forces, including unpaid rent, a California landlord may not contact the member's military unit or chain of command without the member's written consent, and that consent counts only if it is given after the obligation has become due and payable. A lease clause consenting in advance to contact with a commanding officer is therefore ineffective, and any waiver of these protections is void. A landlord may not condition a military or veteran discount on the tenant waiving any legal right. A service member's application for or receipt of a stay or postponement of an obligation under California's military protections may not by itself be treated as showing that the member cannot pay. A landlord may not electronically access a service member's Common Access Card, place it in a card reader, or ask for its PIN. Violations carry actual damages, attorney's fees and costs, and are a misdemeanor. Lease termination (Mil. & Vet. Code 409): a tenant may end the lease after entering military service during the term, or, if already in service when signing, after receiving orders for a permanent change of station or to deploy for at least 90 days. The tenant delivers written notice and a copy of the orders by hand, private business carrier or return-receipt mail. For monthly rent, termination takes effect 30 days after the next rent due date following delivery; earlier rent is prorated, you may not charge an early termination fee (other amounts due, such as reasonable excess-wear charges, still apply), you must refund rent paid in advance for after termination within 30 days, the dependents' obligations end too, and you may not hold belongings or the deposit for rent accruing after termination. If you think a request is incomplete, say what is missing in writing within 30 days.

title: Military tenants in eviction: declaration, stays and dependents
bodyText: Before a California court will enter a default judgment - which is how most eviction cases end - the landlord must file a declaration under penalty of perjury stating facts showing the tenant is not in military service, or else declaring that the tenant is in service or that the landlord cannot determine whether they are. A tenant counts as in military service if they are currently serving or served within the preceding 120 days. Without a declaration showing the tenant is not in service, judgment cannot be entered without a court order, and if the tenant is in service the court must first appoint an attorney to represent them; the court may also require the landlord to post a bond. Where a defense may exist that cannot be presented without the tenant, the court must stay the case for at least 90 days. A judgment entered against a service member during service or within 30 days after may be reopened on application within 90 days after service ends. Knowingly making a false declaration is a misdemeanor, and carries liability for damages and attorney's fees. Separately, at any stage of any case involving a service member during service or within 120 days after, the court must stay the case on the service member's application unless their military service does not materially affect their ability to take part, and on the same test may stay execution of any judgment - including an eviction order - and vacate or stay any attachment or garnishment. A stay can run for the period of service plus three months, on terms the court sets, which may include payment in installments. No fine or penalty accrues during a stay of an action to enforce a contract, and a court may relieve a service member from a penalty - such as a late fee - incurred while in service if service materially impaired their ability to pay. Where the service member is one of several co-tenants, the landlord may, with the court's leave, proceed against the others. Where the unit is occupied primarily as a home by a service member's spouse, children or other dependents, no eviction may be carried out during the period of military service or until 120 days after release except with the court's permission, and the court must stay the case or order partial payments on application unless the tenant's ability to pay is unaffected. Knowingly taking part in such an eviction is a misdemeanor.

title: Megan's Law website data may not be used in housing decisions
bodyText: California prohibits using information from the Megan's Law sex-offender website for purposes relating to housing or accommodations. The only authorized use of that information is to protect a person at risk of becoming a victim of a sex offense committed by the registrant. A landlord who uses it otherwise - for example, to screen out an applicant - is liable for actual damages, up to three times actual damages with a minimum of $250, attorney's fees, and exemplary damages or a civil penalty of up to $25,000, and prosecutors or an aggrieved person may sue to stop a pattern or practice of misuse. Every California lease must still tell tenants that the website exists; the landlord may point tenants to it, but may not use it to decide who to rent to.

title: Unreturned deposits escheat to the state after three years
bodyText: An amount a landlord owes a former tenant - most often an unreturned security deposit refund - that the tenant has not claimed is unclaimed property under California law. If it remains unclaimed for more than three years after it became payable, it escheats to the state, and the landlord, as the holder, must report and remit it to the State Controller. Holders file an annual report before November 1 covering property escheated as of the preceding June 30.

title: After judgment: the writ of possession and occupant claims
bodyText: In California a judgment for possession is enforced by a writ of possession executed by the sheriff or marshal. The officer serves the writ on an occupant, or posts it and serves the tenant, and the occupants then have five days to leave; that period cannot be extended. If the officer does not execute the writ within three court days, a registered process server may. An occupant not named in the judgment who was living there when the case was filed may file a claim of right to possession, which stops the eviction pending a hearing, unless a prejudgment claim form was served on all occupants with the summons. Personal property left behind after the landlord takes possession must be stored and may be reclaimed within 15 days on payment of reasonable storage costs, after which it is sold or disposed of under the abandoned-property procedure. A tenant's bankruptcy filing does not delay execution of the possession writ, and a forfeiture judgment does not end the tenant's liability for damages.

title: Choosing a subletting consent standard
bodyText: A California landlord can require its consent to any sublease or assignment, and must choose how that consent works. Under the reasonable-consent standard, the landlord may refuse only for a reasonable reason - a prospective subtenant's poor credit or rental history, for example - and must be prepared to justify a refusal. In exchange, if the tenant later breaks the lease and moves out, the landlord may keep the lease in force and collect rent as it comes due for the rest of the term. Under the sole-discretion standard, the landlord may refuse for any lawful reason and keeps full control over who lives in the property, but gives up that remedy: if the tenant breaks the lease and moves out, the landlord must end the lease and sue for its losses, and the tenant can reduce what they owe by showing the landlord could have re-rented the unit. Either way, a sublease cannot charge more than the lawful rent, a refusal can never be based on a protected characteristic, and an unauthorized sublease is grounds for eviction.

title: No state duty to pay interest on deposits
bodyText: California imposes no statewide requirement to pay interest on a security deposit or to hold it in a separate interest-bearing account. Some California cities do require deposit interest by ordinance, so a landlord should check local rules for the city where the property is located.

title: No joint move-in inventory requirement
bodyText: California does not require a joint, signed move-in condition inventory. It substitutes two different mechanisms: the tenant may request an initial inspection during the final two weeks of the tenancy, and for tenancies beginning on or after July 1, 2025 the landlord must photograph the unit at the start of the tenancy.

title: No right to pay the deposit in installments
bodyText: California gives tenants no statutory right to pay a security deposit in installments. The statutory cap reduces the need for one: since July 1, 2024 security may not exceed one month's rent for most landlords.

title: No radon disclosure requirement
bodyText: California has no statute requiring a residential landlord to test for radon or to disclose radon to tenants. The state's radon provision addresses construction standards for new buildings rather than landlord duties, and California's Proposition 65 warning requirement does not reach radon, because radon is not on the state's list of chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive toxicity. A known radon problem can still matter: conditions severe enough to affect habitability run through the ordinary habitability rules, and a landlord who conceals a known hazard can face liability on other grounds.

title: Proposition 65 Rental Property Warnings
bodyText: A California landlord with ten or more employees must give tenants a Proposition 65 warning before knowingly exposing them to a chemical the state lists as causing cancer or reproductive harm. In rental housing these are typically tobacco smoke, engine exhaust, carbon monoxide, lead or asbestos. The warning goes to each known adult occupant when the property is rented and again every year after that. It may be delivered by letter addressed to each known adult occupant, by email to the addresses the landlord otherwise uses to reach them, or in the lease itself - but a warning given in the lease covers only the adults who sign it or are named in it, so other occupants still need a letter or email. If the lease or any other required notice is given in another language, the warning must be given in that language too. The regulation prescribes the wording, which names the exposure source and the chemical, tells the tenant to talk to the landlord about how and when exposure could occur, and directs them to www.P65Warnings.ca.gov/apartments. Properties with an enclosed parking facility or a designated smoking area need separate warnings for those areas. Violations carry civil penalties of up to $2,500 per day, and private parties may sue after giving 60 days' notice.

title: No special rule for postdated checks
bodyText: California's bad-check statute contains no exception or special rule for postdated checks. What it does contain is a certified-mail demand procedure that raises a landlord's recovery from a service charge to treble the amount of the check, subject to a good-faith-dispute defence where the tenant stopped payment.

title: Billing tenants for water through a submeter
bodyText: If you submeter water and bill tenants separately from rent, California regulates the bill itself, not just the disclosure. You may bill only for the volume measured by the submeter at allowable rates, a share of the fixed charge the water purveyor bills the property, a fee for your own or your billing agent's costs, and a late fee. Submeters must be read within three days of the same point in each billing cycle, payments must be due at the same point in each cycle, and the bill must separately set out the beginning and ending readings and dates, the consumption in gallons, the rates, any amounts carried over, any late fee, the total, the due date and how to reach you with questions. A tenant cannot be required to pay electronically. A late fee may not be imposed until 25 days after the bill is sent, and is capped at seven dollars on the first bill and ten dollars on each later bill, with all late fees in any twelve-month period limited to ten percent of the unpaid amount; partial payments go against the oldest outstanding bill. Two rules matter most. Water service charges are not rent, so unpaid water is never a pay-or-quit matter: once a bill is 180 days overdue or the unpaid amount reaches two hundred dollars, the route is a three-day notice to perform conditions or covenants or quit. And you may not shut off or interfere with water service for any reason, including nonpayment. Fix reported leaks quickly, because slow repairs cost you billing. If a leak or other problem causing high usage is fixed more than 21 days after you learn of it, usage for the months from 21 days after the investigation to the repair is deemed $15 or actual usage, whichever is less. Where readings before and after exist, you may instead use 50 cents a day or actual usage, whichever is less. If the problem stays unfixed 180 days after investigation, you may charge no further usage until it is repaired. Neither rule applies if you gave proper entry notice and the tenant failed to give access. If a monthly reading is unavailable and the tenant gave access to the submeter, you may charge 75 percent of the average usage billed over the last three complete months, disclosed on the bill, or 50 cents a day if there are no such months. After six months without readings, usage is deemed zero. The submeter disclosure must be given, in at least 10-point type, before the lease is signed; the lease's optional clause carries it.

title: Towing a vehicle from the property
bodyText: A lease clause saying you may tow is not enough in California. Unless the parcel is improved with a single-family dwelling, you may only have a vehicle removed without the vehicle owner's consent if a sign at least 17 by 22 inches, with lettering at least one inch high, is displayed in plain view at ALL entrances to the property, prohibiting public parking, stating that vehicles will be removed at the owner's expense, and giving the telephone number of the local traffic law enforcement agency together with the name and telephone number of every towing company you have a written general towing authorization agreement with. Two other routes exist: 96 hours after a parking-violation notice has been issued, or, for a vehicle missing a major part needed to operate safely, 24 hours after you notify local traffic law enforcement. If you have a vehicle removed without meeting one of those conditions, you are liable for DOUBLE the towing or storage charges. Once you authorize a tow, you must phone the local traffic law enforcement agency within one hour, or use the fastest means available if a call is impractical. If the vehicle's owner asks, you must state the grounds for the removal. Separately, the towing company may not start a tow without your written authorization, and whoever authorizes it must normally be present and verify the violation. There is one exception built for small landlords: if the property has 15 or fewer units with no onsite owner, agent or employee, the tenant may verify the violation and request the tow from that tenant's own assigned space, giving you a signed request or email either up front or within 24 hours of calling, which you pass to the towing company within 48 hours.

title: Selling the property with a tenant in place
bodyText: Selling a tenanted California property triggers four separate duties. First, showings: entry to exhibit the unit to prospective or actual purchasers needs the ordinary written notice, but if you have given the tenant written notice within the previous 120 days that the property is for sale and that you or your agent may contact the tenant to arrange showings, you may then give ORAL notice a reasonable period before entry, and you must leave written evidence of the entry inside the unit. Second, the deposit: on transferring your interest you must either hand the remaining deposit to the buyer and then notify the tenant in writing of the transfer, the claims made against the deposit, the amount held and the successor's name, address and telephone number, or return it to the tenant with a full accounting. Before a voluntary transfer you must also give the buyer a written statement of the deposit remaining, an itemisation of lawful deductions and which of the two routes you chose. Get this wrong and you and the buyer are jointly and severally liable. Third, the identity disclosure must be kept current and runs against the new owner or manager, who has 15 days to comply and may not serve a nonpayment notice for rent that accrued while out of compliance. Fourth, nothing in California law obliges a tenant to sign an estoppel certificate or a certification of lease terms for your lender or buyer; that is a matter of contract only.

title: Holding deposits and money taken before the lease
bodyText: California has no holding-deposit statute, which is exactly why this is a trap. If you take money from an applicant to hold a unit, it is almost certainly security: the deposit statute defines security as any payment, fee, deposit or charge imposed at the beginning of the tenancy to reimburse you for processing a new tenant or as an advance payment of rent, used for any purpose, however denominated. Security counts toward the one-month cap and is refundable, so calling money a non-refundable holding fee does not make it one. The single exception is the application screening fee, which the statute expressly says is not security and not an advance fee, and which has its own cap, receipt and refund rules. Practical consequence: keep the screening fee separate and documented, and treat anything else you collect before move-in as refundable deposit money, or as first month's rent if that is what it is. Whether a true pre-tenancy holding deposit can be forfeited when an applicant backs out is unsettled in the statutes; the safest course is a short written agreement signed before the money changes hands that says what happens if either side walks away.

title: The Tenant's Repair-and-Deduct Remedy
bodyText: If a tenant gives you or your agent written or oral notice of conditions making the premises untenantable that you ought to repair, and you don't repair them within a reasonable time, the tenant may either repair them and deduct the cost from rent, up to one month's rent, or move out and be discharged from further rent and other obligations as of that date (Civ. Code 1942). The tenant may use the remedy no more than twice in any 12-month period, and not for a condition the tenant caused by violating Civ. Code 1929 or 1941.2. A lease can't take the remedy away.

title: Notice Before Raising Rent
bodyText: For a week-to-week, month-to-month or shorter tenancy, you may raise rent only by written notice delivered personally or served by mail under CCP 1013 (Civ. Code 827). If the increase, alone or combined with other increases in the prior 12 months, is 10% or less of the rent charged at any time in those 12 months, give at least 30 days' notice; if more than 10%, at least 90 days. A longer period in another statute, regulation, recorded regulatory agreement or contract controls. The Tenant Protection Act's cap may also apply (see the rent-increase cap note).

title: Tenant Display and Use Rights You Can't Restrict
bodyText: California limits what a lease can restrict. Political signs (Civ. Code 1940.4): a tenant may post signs about an election or legislative vote, an initiative, referendum or recall, or an issue before a public body; in a multifamily building in a window or on the door, and in a single-family home also from the yard, balcony or outside wall. You may prohibit one only if it is over six square feet, violates a law, or violates a lawful common-interest-development governing document, and posting is limited to the period local ordinance sets or, otherwise, a period you set that starts at least 90 days before and ends at least 15 days after the vote. Other rights: a tenant may display a religious item on the entry door or frame, within the limits of Civ. Code 1940.45; own a personal micromobility device and store and recharge up to one per occupant in the unit if it meets the safety standard or is insured, unless you provide secure long-term storage; use a clothesline or drying rack in a private area on the conditions in 1940.20; and, where the property has no more than two units and the tenant has a ground-level private outdoor area, grow personal agriculture in portable containers on the conditions in 1940.10.

title: Never Penalize a Call for Police or Emergency Help
bodyText: A lease can't prohibit or limit a tenant, resident or anyone else from summoning law enforcement or emergency assistance for a victim of abuse or crime or a person in an emergency, and you may not impose or threaten any fee, fine, penalty, termination, non-renewal or worse terms because such help was summoned (Civ. Code 1946.8). You may not demand documentation of the emergency or the belief behind the call, and a waiver of these rights is void (1946.8(d), (e)). Watch the calendar in an eviction. If you file within 30 days of a call for help, on a notice that treats the call as a lease violation or a nuisance, the tenant is presumed to have a defense (1946.8(f)(2)). You can rebut it only by showing another reason was a substantial motivating factor for filing (1946.8(f)(3)). Merely mentioning a call to describe other alleged misconduct does not trigger the presumption.

title: When a Tenant May End the Lease for Your Non-Performance or Destruction
bodyText: A tenant may end the lease early if, within a reasonable time after the tenant asks, you don't put and keep them in quiet possession, put the property in good condition, or repair it; or if the greater part of the property, or the part that was the material inducement to the lease, is destroyed by any cause other than the tenant's want of ordinary care (Civ. Code 1932). If the property is destroyed, the lease ends (Civ. Code 1933). See the disaster note for returning advance rent.

title: Pest Control and Pesticide Notices
bodyText: If you have a contract for periodic pest control service, give each new tenant a copy of the notice the registered pest control company provides (Civ. Code 1940.8). If you or your agent apply pesticide without a licensed operator, give the tenant written notice at least 24 hours in advance naming the pest, the pesticide's name and brand, the approximate date, time and frequency of application, the statutory caution statement, and that the date, time and frequency may change (1940.8.5); for a broadcast application, a total-release fogger or an aerosol spray, give the same notice to adjacent units that could reasonably be affected.

title: After a Declared Disaster
bodyText: If a declared disaster damages the property, remove the disaster debris and mitigate the hazards it causes (mold, smoke, smoke residue and odor, ash, asbestos, water damage) within a reasonable time, following any government cleaning protocols, then tell the tenant in writing that it's done and that they may see and request copies of any environmental studies, tests or reports (Civ. Code 1941.8). Unless the lease is lawfully ended, the tenancy continues and the tenant may return at the same rent once it's safe and practicable. Rent is discharged for any period the tenant can't occupy the unit under a mandatory evacuation order; return rent already paid for that period within 10 days after the order is lifted, or let the tenant deduct it from the next month's rent. If the lease ends because the property was destroyed or the tenant ended it under Civ. Code 1932(2), return advance rent for the period after termination within 21 days.

title: Tenants May Opt Out of Bundled Internet
bodyText: If a tenancy is month-to-month or otherwise periodic and you offer internet service through a bulk-billing arrangement or other subscription with a third-party provider, the tenant may opt out of paying for it, you may not retaliate, and if you don't honor the opt-out the tenant may deduct the subscription's cost from rent (Civ. Code 1942.8).

title: Security Deposit Limits
bodyText: California caps security, however it's labeled, at one month's rent, furnished or not, on top of the first month's rent (Civ. Code 1950.5(c)); deposits collected before July 1, 2024 are grandfathered. Exceptions: a landlord who is a natural person, or an LLC whose members are all natural persons, and who owns no more than two residential rental properties with no more than four units in total may take two months, but not from a service member, and may not refuse to rent to a service member on that account; six or more months' rent may be paid in advance on a lease of six months or more; and you may raise the deposit by half a month's rent for a waterbed (1940.5(g)). A lease may not call any security nonrefundable (1950.5(n)). Use these limits as a guardrail when you enter the deposit amount.

title: Deposit Return Deadline and Itemization
bodyText: Within 21 days after the tenant moves out, give the tenant an itemized statement of any deductions and return the balance (Civ. Code 1950.5). You may deduct only for unpaid rent, damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, cleaning back to the move-in level, and, where the lease authorizes it, replacing personal property or appurtenances. You may not charge for ordinary wear and tear or preexisting conditions, or require professional carpet or other professional cleaning unless it's reasonably necessary. Where repair and cleaning deductions exceed $125, include copies of bills, invoices or receipts and photographs of the unit. The tenant may request an initial inspection during the last two weeks of the tenancy and be present; tell the tenant of that right in writing and give at least 48 hours' written notice of the inspection. See the deposit-photo note.

title: Rent Increase Cap (Tenant Protection Act)
bodyText: Where Civ. Code 1947.12 applies, you may not raise rent over any 12-month period by more than 5% plus the change in the cost of living, or 10%, whichever is lower, measured against the lowest rent charged for the unit in the 12 months before the increase, and you may not impose more than two increases in any 12 months. Discounts, incentives, concessions and credits are left out of the calculation and must be listed separately in the lease (the lease's Rent Discounts and Concessions clause does this). Give notice of any increase as Civ. Code 827 requires (see the rent-increase notice note). The cost-of-living figure is regional and changes each year, and several exemptions apply (see the rent-increase cap row's notes and the TPA notices). Two exemptions change under you rather than staying put. A building is exempt while its certificate of occupancy is less than 15 years old, which means a building that is exempt when you sign becomes covered on its fifteenth anniversary, part way through a tenancy. And the exemption for a separately saleable home depends on who owns it: if the property passes to a corporation, a real estate investment trust or an LLC with a corporate member, the exemption is lost and the exemption statement printed in the lease is no longer true. Re-check both whenever a lease is renewed or the property changes hands.

title: Rent Payment Method Rules
bodyText: California requires you to accept at least one form of rent payment that is neither cash nor electronic funds transfer, so a cash-only or electronic-only policy is unlawful from the start (Civ. Code 1947.3). You must let a third party pay rent on the tenant's behalf, subject to a signed acknowledgment that they aren't a tenant and that accepting payment creates no new tenancy. You may not charge a fee for paying rent or the deposit by check. You may require cash only after a dishonored check or stop-payment, for up to three months, with the written notice the statute requires. A tenant can't waive these rules.

title: Stove and Refrigerator Duty
bodyText: California requires you to provide and maintain in good working order a stove that can safely generate heat for cooking and a refrigerator that can safely store food (Civ. Code 1941.1(a)(10)-(11)). An appliance under a manufacturer or government recall isn't considered safe, and you must repair or replace it within 30 days of notice of the recall. You may not make the tenancy conditional on the tenant supplying a refrigerator; if the tenant asks to bring their own, the lease must carry the statutory acknowledgment and a 30-day route back to one you supply.
