title: Required Locks and Security Devices
bodyText: California requires an operable dead bolt on each main swinging entry door, operable security or locking devices on windows designed to be opened, and code-compliant locking mechanisms on exterior doors that give access to common areas in multifamily buildings (Civ. Code 1941.3). Correct an inoperable device within a reasonable time after the tenant tells you.

title: Unbundled Parking at New Larger Buildings
bodyText: For a qualifying property (certificate of occupancy on or after January 1, 2025, 16 or more units, in one of ten named counties), parking may not be included in the rental agreement; it must sit in a separate parking agreement or an addendum, and it stays unbundled for the life of the property (Civ. Code 1947.1). Tenants have a right of first refusal to spaces built for the property. An unpaid parking fee can't support an eviction; after 45 days you may only revoke the space. Several kinds of unit are excluded (see the unbundled parking row's notes).

title: Ending a Month-to-Month Tenancy
bodyText: A tenant must give notice at least as long as the rental period (30 days for month-to-month), however long they've lived there (Civ. Code 1946.1). You must give at least 60 days' notice, or 30 days if the tenant has lived there less than a year, or if the unit is separately alienable, is being sold to a natural-person bona fide purchaser in escrow, you give notice within 120 days of escrow opening and haven't given notice before, and the buyer intends to live there for at least a year. Your notice must include the statutory abandoned-property statement. Do not rely on a lease term shortening these periods. The general rule (Civ. Code 1946) lets parties agree, when a tenancy begins, on notice as short as seven days. But 1946.1 governs residential periodic tenancies 'notwithstanding' that rule and sets its own periods with no shortening option, so the seven-day option is unavailable for a dwelling. This differs from changing other lease terms (not rent) under Civ. Code 827(a), where a written agreement can allow seven days' notice. Where the Tenant Protection Act (1946.2) applies, notice alone isn't enough: after the qualifying occupancy period you also need, and must state, a just cause.

title: Disclosures Owed Before Signing: Ordnance, Demolition, Shared Meters
bodyText: Before a lease is signed, California requires written disclosure of any former federal or state ordnance location within one mile that you actually know of (Civ. Code 1940.7); if you have applied for a permit to demolish the unit, the earliest approximate demolition date and when you expect to end the tenancy; and if gas or electric service through the tenant's meter also serves areas outside the unit, that fact, with a separate written agreement for paying for it. The lease's optional clause records these disclosures.

title: Just Cause Is Required After 12 Months
bodyText: California has one of the strongest just-cause rules in the country, and it is the single thing most likely to catch out a landlord who has rented elsewhere. Once a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied the home for 12 months, you may not end the tenancy without a just cause, and the cause must be stated in the written notice. If you added another adult to the lease before the original tenant reached 24 months, the rule applies once all tenants have reached 12 months or any one tenant has reached 24. The end of a fixed term is not itself a reason to recover possession: a covered tenancy continues, and a tenant's refusal to sign a renewal on similar terms is itself one of the listed at-fault causes. At-fault causes include nonpayment, breach of a material lease term, nuisance, waste, criminal activity, unlawful subletting and refusing lawful entry. No-fault causes include an owner or close relative moving in, withdrawing the home from the rental market, complying with a government order, and demolition or substantial remodel; a no-fault termination requires relocation assistance or a waiver of the final month's rent, and getting that wrong voids the notice. Several kinds of property are exempt, and a local just-cause ordinance can displace the state scheme entirely.

title: California Has an Algorithmic Pricing Statute
bodyText: California is one of the few states with a statute aimed at algorithmic pricing, and it took effect on January 1, 2026. It is antitrust law rather than landlord-tenant law, and it does not ban revenue-management software. Two things are unlawful: using or distributing a common pricing algorithm as part of an agreement or conspiracy to restrain trade, and using or distributing one to coerce someone else into adopting a price or commercial term the algorithm recommends for the same or similar product or service. A common pricing algorithm is any method, including software, used by two or more people that uses competitor data to recommend, align, stabilise, set or otherwise influence a price or term, and 'price' is defined broadly. The practical reading for a landlord: using pricing software on your own data is not what this targets; feeding or drawing on competitors' non-public rent data through a shared tool, or pressing another owner to follow its numbers, is where the risk sits. Federal and California antitrust and unfair-competition law apply as well.

title: When a Fee Counts as Rent
bodyText: California has no general statute saying whether late fees, utility charges or other fees count as rent for a dwelling, so the lease and the courts decide - with two important exceptions that run in opposite directions. Submetered water is expressly NOT rent: the statute says so, which is why an unpaid water bill can never support a three-day pay-or-quit notice and instead has its own route (180 days overdue or $200 unpaid, then a notice to perform covenants or quit). An unpaid separately-leased parking fee likewise cannot support an eviction on a qualifying property. Practical consequence: do not label fees 'additional rent' in a California lease to make them evictable. A three-day notice that demands rent plus non-rent charges risks being defective for overstating the rent due, and this library's clauses keep fees separate from Rent for that reason. Fees still remain collectible as contract debts, and the deposit may be applied only to the four purposes the deposit statute lists.

title: No Statutory Right to Fix a Breach and Bill It as Rent
bodyText: California gives a landlord no statutory right to step in, fix a tenant's breach and add the cost to rent. What California does give you is better than nothing and differently shaped: a tenant must use ordinary care to keep the home safe and in good condition, and must repair any deterioration or injury caused by the tenant's own want of ordinary care. That is a statutory repair duty you can enforce as a debt or as damages, and the deposit may be applied to repairing damage beyond ordinary wear and tear. The lease may also give you a contractual right to do the work and recover the cost. Two cautions. Do not treat such a charge as rent - see the note on when a fee counts as rent - because a three-day notice that demands repair costs as rent risks being defective. And entry to do the work still needs a lawful entry ground and the required notice.

title: No Rule on Blank Spaces, but You Must Give a Copy
bodyText: California has no statute requiring every blank in a residential lease to be filled in, and no statute making a blank a breach. One related duty is real and often missed: you must give the tenant a copy of the signed lease within 15 days of the tenant signing it, and once each year after that you must give another copy if the tenant asks. If you do not have the lease or a copy, you must instead give a written statement saying so, with the owner and manager details, where rent is paid and the forms of payment you accept. Fill in every blank before signing anyway. California prescribes the exact words for several lease statements and sets minimum type sizes for some of them, and a blank left in a statement whose wording the statute dictates is a compliance problem rather than just an unclear term.

title: California Has a Statutory Covenant of Quiet Possession
bodyText: Unlike most states, where quiet enjoyment is a court-made implied promise, California puts a covenant in the statute: an agreement to let binds the landlord to secure the tenant's quiet possession of the home during the term, against everyone lawfully claiming it. Read it for what it says - it is a promise about superior claims to the property, such as a lender, a co-owner or a prior tenant, rather than a general promise of peace and quiet. The broader protection comes from elsewhere: it is unlawful for a landlord to interfere with a tenant's quiet enjoyment of the home for the purpose of influencing the tenant to vacate, and that provision carries real penalties. The practical point is that you cannot contract out of either one by saying the lease is the whole of your obligations, and a title problem you knew about is your risk, not the tenant's.

title: Wording California Dictates Word for Word
bodyText: California prescribes the exact words for more lease statements and notices than any other state in this library, and in several places the type size too. In the lease itself: the rent-cap and just-cause notice, or instead the exemption statement for an exempt property, both quoted verbatim and the first in at least 12-point type; the tenant acknowledgment where the tenant supplies their own refrigerator; and the owner, manager and rent-payment details. Delivered with or before the lease: the flood-hazard disclosure in at least 8-point type, the bed-bug notice in at least 10-point type, the water-submeter disclosure in at least 10-point type, and the mould booklet the Department of Public Health publishes. In the automatic-renewal clause, the renewal terms must be in at least 8-point boldface. Notices during and after the tenancy have their own prescribed wording: the pesticide caution statement, the abandoned-property statement that must appear in your termination notice, the third-party rent acknowledgment, the abandoned-property claim notice, and the statements a tenant uses to end a tenancy after abuse or violence. Use the statute's words, not a paraphrase.

title: No Rule on Tenant Security Cameras or Video Doorbells
bodyText: No California statute says whether a tenant may install a security camera or a video doorbell, so the lease controls, through its rules on alterations and on attaching things to the building. Two things make this more sensitive in California than almost anywhere else. Privacy is an inalienable right under the state constitution, and California courts apply it to private conduct, not only to the government - so a camera covering a shared hallway, a neighbour's door or a yard is a live issue even between neighbours. And California requires the consent of everyone involved before a confidential conversation is recorded, so a device that captures audio outside the tenant's own space raises a criminal-law question, not just a lease one. A reasonable approach is to allow a device that views only the tenant's own entry and requires no drilling, and to ask for written consent otherwise.

title: Damage the Tenant Causes: What You Can Recover
bodyText: California law already answers most of this, which is why this library offers no separate tenant-caused-damage clause for California. Repair costs: a tenant must use ordinary care and must repair any deterioration or injury caused by the tenant's own want of ordinary care, so the claim is statutory, and the deposit may be applied to repairing damage beyond ordinary wear and tear. Rent while the home is repaired: the tenant's right to end the lease after destruction or serious damage applies only where the damage was not the tenant's fault, the repair-and-deduct remedy is unavailable to a tenant who has breached their own upkeep duties, and the rule barring you from demanding rent for a substandard home does not apply where the tenant caused the condition. So rent generally continues to run where the tenant is at fault. Lost rent if the lease ends: if the tenant breaches and abandons, or you lawfully terminate for breach, the statutory damages measure covers the rent for the balance of the term less what the tenant proves you could reasonably have avoided - the lease's Early Termination clause states it. Adding a no-abatement sentence is not worth the risk here, because the habitability rights it sits next to cannot be waived.

title: You Cannot Pre-Set Cleaning or Repair Charges
bodyText: California does not let you fix cleaning or repair charges in advance, and it singles out carpet cleaning. You may not require a tenant to pay for, or charge the deposit for, professional carpet cleaning or other professional cleaning unless it is reasonably necessary to return the home to the condition it was in when the tenancy began, ordinary wear and tear aside. The same test limits every other claim: work by a contractor, by you, or by your employee is capped at a reasonable amount necessary to restore the home to its condition at the start, and you may not charge at all for conditions that predated the tenancy, for ordinary wear and tear, or for wear and tear built up over several tenancies. So a lease that says “carpet cleaning $250 on move-out” or that attaches a price list is unenforceable, and charging against it in bad faith exposes you to damages of up to twice the deposit. What the law asks for instead is evidence: itemise the actual work, and for your own or an employee's work give the time spent and a reasonable hourly rate.

title: Last Month's Rent Counts Toward the Deposit Cap
bodyText: In California, collecting “last month's rent” at signing does not get you extra money: it is security like anything else. The deposit statute defines security as any payment, fee, deposit or charge imposed at the start of the tenancy, including one imposed as an advance payment of rent, and the cap applies to security “however denominated”. So first month's rent is on top of the cap, but a last-month's-rent payment sits inside it, and a pet deposit, a key deposit or a cleaning fee does too. Calling the payment prepaid rent does not take it outside the return and accounting rules either, and you may not call any of it nonrefundable. There is one real way to hold more rent up front: a tenant may pay six months' rent or more in advance if the lease term is six months or longer. That is a different mechanism with a different test, and it is not a deposit. If you want a cushion against the last month, the lawful route is the one month of security itself, which may be applied to unpaid rent at the end.

title: When the 21-Day Deposit Clock Starts
bodyText: Your 21 days to account for the deposit run from the day the tenant vacates the home, and the statute puts a floor under the start as well: the clock cannot begin before either side gives a termination notice, or a three-day notice is served, or more than 60 days before a fixed term expires. California does not define “vacated”, and it does not require the tenant to give you a forwarding address. It does tell you where to send: mail to the address the tenant provided, and if the tenant provided none, to the unit they left. Two notices sit around the move-out and are easy to miss. Within a reasonable time after either side gives notice, or before the end of the term, you must tell the tenant in writing that they may request an initial inspection and may be present at it, in wording the statute sets out. And if you took the deposit or the rent electronically, you must tell the tenant in writing, in the same window, that they may have the deposit returned electronically to an account they name. Cautious course: count the 21 days from the day possession actually ends, not from when keys come back; ask for a forwarding address in writing at move-out; and diarise both notices at the moment notice is given by either side.

title: No Faster Deposit Route on Request
bodyText: California has one deadline and no fast track. There is no procedure by which a tenant can demand the deposit sooner than 21 days, no shortened route after a mutual move-out, and no fee a tenant can pay to speed it up. The movement runs the other way: two provisions let you take longer. If a repair you or your employee will do cannot reasonably be finished within the 21 days, or an invoice is not in your hands by then, you may deduct a good-faith estimate and give that estimate with the itemised statement, then complete the accounting within 14 days of finishing the work or receiving the document. And where deductions for repairs and cleaning together are $125 or less, or the tenant has signed a valid waiver, you need not send the supporting invoices at all, unless the tenant asks within 14 days of the statement, in which case you have 14 days to comply. Do not treat any of that as extra time for the statement itself or for the money: the 21 days still governs both, and a bad-faith failure costs you the right to claim any of the deposit.

title: No Statute for Deposit Alternatives, and the Fee May Still Be a Deposit
bodyText: California has no statute authorising or regulating a fee charged instead of a security deposit: no insurance-backed deposit-alternative programme, no offer-to-all rule, no right-to-switch rule, and no credit-reporting protections of the kind a few states have enacted. That silence is not permission, and it is the main trap here. The deposit statute defines security as any payment, fee, deposit or charge imposed at the beginning of the tenancy to reimburse you for the costs of processing a new tenant or as an advance payment of rent, and it caps security “however denominated”. A monthly or one-off fee that a tenant pays so as not to pay a deposit is therefore very likely security: it would count against the one-month cap, would have to be accounted for and returned within 21 days, and could not be called nonrefundable. The only fee California carves out of the deposit rules is the application screening fee, and it is capped and tightly conditioned. Cautious course: if you want to offer a no-deposit option, treat anything the tenant pays for it as security, or take no fee at all and rely on a third-party surety the tenant buys directly, where you are not the one charging the tenant.

title: You May Not Call Any Security Nonrefundable
bodyText: California gives you no way to make part of the deposit nonrefundable, and no notice or disclosure unlocks one. The statute is flat: a lease or rental agreement shall not contain a provision characterising any security as nonrefundable. Because security means any payment, fee, deposit or charge imposed at the start of the tenancy, and the cap and return rules reach security however it is denominated, relabelling does not help: a nonrefundable cleaning fee, move-in fee, redecorating fee or pet fee collected at signing is security, so it counts toward the one-month cap and must be accounted for and returned within 21 days like the rest. Two things are genuinely outside the deposit: the application screening fee, which the statute carves out and caps, and a fee for alterations you agree to make at the tenant's request. Everything else you collect at signing should be treated as refundable security, and a nonrefundable label in the lease is not merely unenforceable - claiming or keeping security in bad faith exposes you to damages of up to twice the deposit.

title: No Separate-Document Route for a Nonrefundable Charge
bodyText: Some states let a landlord charge a nonrefundable fee if it is disclosed in a separate signed document. California has no such route, because it has nothing to disclose: the lease may not characterise any security as nonrefundable at all, so there is no separate notice, no separate signature and no acknowledgment that would make such a charge good. The only separate-document rule in this part of California's law runs the opposite way, and concerns parking rather than deposits: on a qualifying property, parking must be kept out of the rental agreement and put in an addendum or its own agreement. Practical effect: do not build a “nonrefundable fee addendum” for California, and do not carry one over from another state's lease.

title: Where the Deposit Sits, and the Trust-Account Trap for Managers
bodyText: California imposes almost no holding rules on an owner and one strict rule on a manager, and the difference catches people out. If you are the owner, you need no escrow, no trust account, no separate bank account and no interest-bearing account; you need not tell the tenant where the money is, and you owe no interest on it. You may keep it in your ordinary operating account. The statute says only that you hold the security for the tenant, and that the tenant's claim to it ranks ahead of any creditor of yours - which is a priority rule, not a trust. If, on the other hand, you collect the deposit as someone else's agent for compensation - a property manager, a leasing agent, a brokerage - you are acting as a real estate broker, and the Real Estate Law requires funds belonging to others to go into a neutral escrow, into the principal's hands, or into a trust fund account at a bank in this state, to stay there until disbursed on the instruction of the person entitled to them, with restrictions on who may sign withdrawals. Two further points: a city may require more, including interest, in rent-controlled jurisdictions; and if you sell, the deposit has its own transfer regime.

title: Deposit Rights Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: Every deposit rule in California is non-waivable, and the statute saying so is blunt: any provision of a residential lease by which the tenant agrees to modify or waive their rights or remedies under the security-deposit section is void as contrary to public policy. The same sentence protects the entry statute, and the same section voids a waiver of the right to sue you later, of a notice or hearing required by law, of procedural rights in litigation, and of your duty of care against personal injury or property damage. So none of these works: a clause making part of the deposit nonrefundable, a clause setting cleaning charges in advance, a clause shortening the 21 days, a clause giving up the itemised statement in advance, or a clause saying the tenant accepts your accounting as final. One narrower rule is worth knowing: a waiver of some other statutory right, not void outright, is void anyway unless the lease was presented to the tenant before they took possession. And there is one lawful, closely conditioned waiver inside the deposit statute itself - of the supporting invoices, signed only at or after a termination notice or a three-day notice, or no earlier than 60 days before a fixed term ends.

title: Selling the Property: What Happens to the Deposit
bodyText: When your interest in the property ends - by sale, assignment, death or a receiver - you must do one of two things within a reasonable time, and either one releases you from further liability for the deposit. You may transfer what is left after lawful deductions to your successor, and then notify the tenant of the transfer, of any claims made against the deposit, of the amount deposited, and of the successor's name, address and telephone number; if you deliver that notice personally, the tenant signs your copy. Or you may return the remainder to the tenant with a full accounting, as at the end of a tenancy. Before a voluntary transfer you owe the buyer a written statement too: what remains, an itemisation of any lawful deductions, and which of the two routes you are taking. Do neither and you and your successor are jointly and severally liable to repay the tenant, and the successor may not ask the tenant for a replacement deposit until it has either refunded the original or given the tenant the accounting. A buyer who, after inquiry and reasonable investigation, has a good-faith belief that the deposit was transferred or returned is protected. Failing to get title right does not void the sale - but it does leave the deposit liability with you.

title: What Getting the Deposit Wrong Costs
bodyText: California's deposit penalties turn on bad faith, and there are two of them. First, if you in bad faith fail to comply with the accounting and return rules, you are not entitled to claim any amount of the deposit at all - the whole of it goes back, whatever the actual damage. Second, a bad-faith claim or retention of the deposit, or a bad-faith demand that the tenant replace a deposit the buyer never received, may be punished with statutory damages of up to twice the deposit, on top of actual damages. Two procedural features make these real rather than theoretical. The court may award bad-faith damages whenever the facts warrant it, even if the tenant never asked for them. And the burden of proof is yours, not the tenant's: you must justify the reasonableness of the amounts claimed, and your authority to demand additional security. The tenant can bring the claim in small claims court, and can prove the deposit existed and its amount by any credible evidence - a cancelled check, a receipt, the lease itself, your own prior statements, or a declaration under penalty of perjury. The practical lesson is documentary: photographs, invoices, hours and rates.

title: Charging a Service Member More Than Your Standard Deposit
bodyText: California sets no general rule requiring you to publish or post how you calculate deposits, and no rule about using different standards for different applicants. It sets one specific rule, for service members, and it has a lease-drafting consequence most landlords miss. Since April 1, 2025, if you charge a service member who will live in the property more than your standard or advertised security because of credit history, credit score, housing history or another tenant-related factor, you must give that tenant a written statement, on or before the day the lease is signed, of the higher amount and why you are charging it. The extra security must come back after no more than six months of residency if the tenant has not been in arrears for rent during that period - and the date for returning it has to be in the lease itself. Note also that the two-month deposit allowance for very small landlords does not apply to a service member, and you may not refuse to rent to one because of that. “Service member” takes its meaning from the Military and Veterans Code.

title: No Landlord-Held Utility Deposit - but Water Bills Can Hit the Deposit
bodyText: California has no statute letting you take or hold a separate utility deposit, and none governing its return. That is not a gap you can fill with a lease term: anything you collect at the start of the tenancy is security “however denominated”, so a “utility deposit” would simply count against the one-month cap and have to be accounted for and returned within 21 days with everything else. A deposit the utility itself requires is a different matter - that is the tenant's arrangement with the utility, held by the utility under its tariff, and not your money or your duty. One real connection between utilities and the deposit does exist, in the submetered-water rules: where water service is submetered, you may deduct an unpaid water bill from the security deposit during or at the end of the tenancy, provided the last bill showing the amount due is attached to the documentation the deposit statute requires. Note that this is an addition to the four purposes the deposit statute itself lists, so a lease that recites only those four is incomplete for a submetered property.

title: Interest on What a Tenant Owes You
bodyText: California gives you interest on unpaid money whether or not the lease mentions it, and lets the lease fix the rate within limits. Where a contract made after January 1, 1986 does not stipulate a rate, the obligation bears interest at 10 percent a year after a breach; where the contract does stipulate a lawful rate, that rate keeps running after the breach until a judgment replaces it. Separately, someone entitled to damages that are certain, or can be made certain by calculation, is entitled to interest from the day the right vested, and the measure for breach of an obligation to pay money is the amount due with interest on it. So unpaid rent accrues interest without any lease term at all. Two cautions. The state constitution's usury article sets 7 percent on the loan or forbearance of money, or on accounts after demand, and allows a written contract rate of up to 10 percent where the money is for personal, family or household purposes - and whether unpaid rent is a “forbearance” or an “account after demand” is not settled by the text. Cautious course: state no more than 10 percent a year in the lease. And interest is not a late fee: a separate charge for lateness is tested as a penalty under the liquidated-damages rule.

title: The Deposit After a Domestic-Violence Termination
bodyText: California does not give the deposit a special clock when a tenant ends the tenancy after domestic violence, sexual assault, stalking, human trafficking, elder or dependent-adult abuse, or another qualifying crime. The ordinary 21 days apply, running from when the tenant has vacated. What the statute does change is who the money goes to. Normally, where several adult tenants live in the home and there is no written agreement about it, you must return the balance by a single check payable to all of the adult tenants on the agreement. That rule would send the money to a household the leaving tenant may be fleeing. So where a tenant has ended the lease under the abuse-and-violence termination section, no written agreement is in place, and that tenant asks you to disburse the deposit some other way, you may return it other than by a check payable to all adult tenants. Note also that a tenant who terminates this way remains liable for no more than 14 days' rent after giving notice, and the remaining tenants' own liability is unaffected. Cautious course: get the leaving tenant's request and their payment details in writing, and account to each adult tenant.

title: The Numbers California Caps
bodyText: California caps more of what a landlord may charge than almost any other state, and the figures are in different statutes, so here they are together. Security: one month's rent on top of the first month, however the payment is labelled; two months for a landlord who is a natural person, or an LLC whose members are all natural persons, owning no more than two residential rental properties with no more than four units between them - but never for a service member. Waterbed: the deposit may go up by half a month's rent. Application screening: $30 per applicant, indexed to the Consumer Price Index since 1998, and capped at your actual out-of-pocket cost plus the reasonable value of your time. Returned payments: a service charge of up to $25 for the first bad check to you and up to $35 for each later one. Rent increases on a covered property: 5 percent plus the change in the cost of living, or 10 percent, whichever is lower, over any 12 months, and no more than two increases in that period. Deposit paperwork: you may skip the supporting invoices where repair and cleaning deductions together are $125 or less. Interest on money a tenant owes: 10 percent a year where the lease sets no rate. And the penalty that matters most: up to twice the deposit for a bad-faith claim. There is no statewide cap on pet rent, late fees or key charges - but an unreasonable charge is tested as a penalty, and a city may cap more.

title: How a California Eviction Actually Runs
bodyText: California evictions run on one statutory track, called unlawful detainer, and the schedule is fast but unforgiving of paperwork errors. You start with a notice, and the notice period for the three-day notices to pay rent or quit and to perform or quit now excludes Saturdays, Sundays and other judicial holidays (count a three-day notice to quit for nuisance or unlawful use the same way to be safe), so a notice served on a Friday does not expire until the following Wednesday or later. Service of the notice is limited to three methods, in order: personal delivery; if the tenant is absent from home and work, leaving a copy with someone of suitable age and discretion at either place plus a mailed copy; and if neither place can be found nor such a person, posting conspicuously, delivering to someone residing there if you can find one, and mailing. You may not charge the tenant a fee for serving, posting or delivering any notice. Then you file a verified complaint that states how you served the notice and attaches the notice and, unless the lease is oral or the case is for unpaid rent alone, the lease; from January 1, 2027 the complaint must also state the date, time and location of service of the notice, and the court must give eviction cases precedence over other civil cases. The tenant has ten days to respond, excluding weekends and judicial holidays, with five extra court days if service went through the Secretary of State's address confidentiality programme. If the tenant answers, trial is set within twenty days of the request; if trial slips, the court can order the tenant to pay rent into court or escrow meanwhile. Either side may demand a jury. If you win, a writ issues, and the occupants get five days from service or posting of the writ before the sheriff removes them. Court records are sealed from the public for the first sixty days. An appeal does not automatically stop the eviction, but the court can stay it on extreme hardship, and must then order the rental value paid into court monthly.

title: The Court Can Give a Tenant More Time
bodyText: Two separate provisions let a California court hold off an eviction for hardship, and both can cost you weeks even after you win. The first is relief against forfeiture. A court may relieve a tenant from forfeiture of the lease and restore the tenancy in case of hardship, whether or not the tenancy has already ended, and it may do so on its own motion. The application can be made at any time before the premises are actually restored to you, by the tenant, a subtenant, a mortgagee of the term, or anyone interested in the tenancy continuing. It is made on a verified petition with five days' notice to you, or orally if the applicant has no lawyer and you are present or have had ex parte notice. The important limit is that relief cannot be granted except on condition that the rent due is paid in full, or the broken covenants performed so far as practicable. The second is a stay pending appeal. An appeal does not automatically stop the eviction, and a stay is granted only where the tenant would suffer extreme hardship without one and you would not be irreparably injured by it - but if a stay is granted, the court must order the reasonable monthly rental value paid into court monthly in advance, which is the contract rent unless the court has modified it. Practical consequence: keep your rent ledger clean, because in both routes the tenant's money has to come to the court, and that is usually where these applications fail.

title: Charging the Tenant for the Eviction
bodyText: California has no statute that bans a lease clause making the tenant pay for an eviction, and none that authorises one either, so three general rules decide what you can collect. First, one charge is banned outright and in three separate places: you may not charge a tenant a fee for serving, posting or otherwise delivering any notice. That covers the three-day notice, the notice ending a periodic tenancy, and the notices for a fixed term. Second, a fixed sum written into the lease as the price of an eviction is a liquidated-damages clause, and in a residential lease a clause fixing damages for a breach is void unless it was impracticable or extremely difficult to fix the actual damage when the lease was made - which it is not, because eviction costs are provable. So state no figure; recover actual, documented costs instead. Third, if your lease has an attorney-fee clause, it runs both ways by operation of law whatever it says, and a voluntarily dismissed or settled case produces no prevailing party and so no award. Two more limits worth knowing: a lease cannot make the tenant give up a notice or hearing the law requires, or procedural rights in litigation; and where a court grants a partial eviction after a domestic-violence defence, only a defendant actually found guilty of unlawful detainer can be made liable for holdover damages, costs, lease-termination fees or attorney's fees.

title: You Cannot Name Someone in the Lease to Take Eviction Papers
bodyText: California does not let the lease nominate a person or address to accept eviction notices or court papers for the tenant. For the statutory notices - the three-day notices and the notice after a sale - the code gives three methods and says the notices may be served by any of those methods, which courts treat as the complete list: personal delivery to the tenant; if the tenant is away from both home and work, a copy left with someone of suitable age and discretion at either place plus a copy posted in the mail; and if neither place can be found and no such person is there, a copy fixed conspicuously on the property, a copy handed to someone residing there if one can be found, and a copy mailed to the property. A subtenant is served the same way. A lease term adding email, text or a nominated agent does not substitute for those methods, and the electronic-transactions act says outright that an electronic record may not be substituted for a notice required to be served under this section. Court papers follow the ordinary civil service rules, not the lease. One point that does turn on the tenant's situation: if service is completed by mail or in person through the Secretary of State's address confidentiality programme, the tenant gets five extra court days to respond, so do not calculate a default off the normal ten days in that case.

title: Evicting for Crime: No Fast Track for You, but the City Has One
bodyText: California gives a landlord no shortened eviction procedure for criminal activity. What it gives you is a ground with no cure right. Assigning or subletting against the lease, committing waste, maintaining or permitting a nuisance, or using the home for an unlawful purpose terminates the lease by operation of law, and you are entitled to possession on three days' notice to quit - a notice to quit, not a notice to perform, so the tenant has no statutory right to fix it and stay. The statute also deems certain conduct to be a nuisance for this purpose, including a controlled-substance offence on the property. The ordinary timetable then applies: the same ten days to respond, the same twenty-day trial window. Separately, and this is unusual, a city prosecutor or city attorney may bring the unlawful detainer itself in the name of the people to abate a drug nuisance, based on a police arrest report. Before filing, the city must give the owner thirty calendar days' written notice requiring the owner to bring the action, and must tell the owner that the action can be assigned to the city; the tenant gets a prescribed warning letter in at least 14-point bold type. So if you receive such a letter, you have a month to act and an option to hand the case over. Note also that the weapons-nuisance eviction section that used to sit alongside the drug one has been repealed.

title: The Two Cure Tracks, and the Breaches With No Cure
bodyText: California runs two different three-day notices, and picking the wrong one loses the case. For unpaid rent, the notice demands payment or possession, and it must state the amount due and tell the tenant exactly how to pay: the name, telephone number and address of the person to be paid, and if payment can be made in person, the usual days and hours that person is available; or a bank account number and the institution's name and street address, provided the institution is within five miles of the property; or, if an electronic transfer procedure was already established, that payment may be made that way. Three days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays and judicial holidays. The notice may be served any time within one year after the rent becomes due. For any other broken condition or covenant - including a covenant not to assign or sublet - the notice demands performance or possession, again three days excluding weekends and holidays, and within that time the tenant, a subtenant, a mortgagee of the term or anyone interested in the tenancy continuing may perform and save the lease from forfeiture. There is an important exception: if the broken covenant cannot afterwards be performed, no notice to perform need be given at all. And the serious grounds - assigning or subletting against the lease, waste, nuisance, unlawful purpose - terminate the lease outright and get a three-day notice to quit with no cure right. The lease cannot set its own cure period or service method in place of these.

title: The Tenant's Last Chance to Pay and Stay
bodyText: After you win a nonpayment judgment, California may still give the tenant five days to pay everything and get the tenancy back - and whether that stay is mandatory or discretionary depends on your lease. Where the eviction is for unpaid rent, the lease has not expired by its own terms, and your three-day notice did not state that you elect to declare the lease forfeited, the court may order that no writ issue for five days after judgment; and it must so order if the lease is in writing, is for a term of more than one year, and contains no forfeiture clause. Within those five days the tenant, a subtenant, a mortgagee of the term or anyone interested in the tenancy continuing may pay into court the rent found due with interest, the damages found, and the costs - and then the judgment is satisfied and the tenant is restored to the tenancy. If the money does not arrive in five days, the judgment is enforced in full. In every other case the judgment may be enforced immediately. Two things follow for drafting. State the forfeiture election in the notice, because without it the judgment cannot declare the lease forfeited at all. And a forfeiture clause in a written lease of more than a year removes the mandatory five-day stay. Separately, relief against forfeiture for hardship can be sought any time before you actually get the property back.

title: No Possession Bond, and No Confessed Judgment
bodyText: California has no end-of-term possession bond: there is no procedure by which you post a bond and take possession at the end of the term without a judgment, and no statute recognising a confessed judgment for possession written into a lease. A clause in which the tenant agrees in advance to a judgment, or gives up procedural rights in the eviction, is void as against public policy. There is one narrow route to possession before trial, and it has nothing to do with the end of the term: where the verified complaint and the evidence satisfy the court that the defendant lives out of state, has left the state, cannot be found after due diligence, or is hiding to avoid service, the court may on motion issue a writ of possession immediately. You must give the defendant written notice of the hearing in a prescribed form telling them they may file affidavits and appear, and you must file an undertaking fixed by the judge, so that if you lose or dismiss you pay the defendant's damages up to that amount. The motion has to say the writ applies to all tenants, subtenants, named claimants and other occupants. Treat it as a tool for an absconding tenant, not a shortcut.

title: When the Tenant Has to Pay Rent Into Court
bodyText: California does not make a tenant deposit rent in order to defend an eviction - there is no general pay-to-play rule, and no mandatory counterclaim. Rent goes into court in three specific situations, and all three favour you. First, delay. If trial is not held within the twenty-day window, the court, on finding a reasonable probability that you will win, must determine your damages from the delay and order the tenant to pay that amount into court or into a court-designated escrow as rent would have fallen due, for as long as the tenant stays. The amount is set from your verified statement of the contract rent, any verified objection, and the evidence at the hearing, and the court weighs any diminution in value or set-off. If the tenant does not pay, trial must be held within fifteen days of the missed payment. The escrow can be ordered into an insured interest-bearing account, with interest split as the funds are, and administration costs are recoverable by the winner. Second, the habitability defence. If the tenant pleads a substantial breach of your repair duties and wins, possession is denied only on condition that the tenant pays the accrued rent, as adjusted to the reasonable rental value, within a period not exceeding five days - and if the tenant does not pay, you get possession. Third, a stay pending appeal must be conditioned on the rental value being paid into court monthly in advance.

title: Who Can Appear for a Company Landlord
bodyText: If you own through a company, trust or partnership, who may stand up in court depends on which court you are in, and getting it wrong can cost you the hearing. In small claims court no attorney may take part in conducting or defending the action, with narrow exceptions for an attorney appearing for themselves or for a firm or professional corporation of which all the principals are attorneys. A corporation may appear in small claims only through a regular employee, or a duly appointed or elected officer or director, who holds that position for purposes other than solely representing the corporation in small claims court - so you cannot appoint someone an officer just to send them to court. Any other non-individual party, a partnership included, appears the same way, through a regular employee, officer, director or partner engaged for some other purpose. A sole proprietor may send a representative without appearing personally only where the claim can be proved by a business record and there is no other factual issue, and the representative is a regular employee qualified to testify about that record. An unlawful detainer is not a small claims case, and California does not have a statute letting a non-attorney appear for an entity there. Cautious course: for the eviction itself, instruct an attorney if the landlord is a company; a property manager, however trusted, should not file or argue it.

title: A Minor Cannot Make a Lease in California
bodyText: This is one of the few places where California is stricter than almost anywhere else, and it is easy to get wrong. A minor is anyone under 18; an adult is 18 or over. A minor may generally make contracts, subject to a power to disaffirm them - but the Family Code then lists three things a minor simply cannot do, and one of them is make a contract relating to real property or any interest in it. A lease is a contract relating to an interest in real property. So a lease signed by a minor alone is not merely voidable at the minor's option: the minor had no capacity to make it. There is a narrow rule elsewhere barring disaffirmance of a contract for things necessary for a minor's support, actually furnished, where the minor was not under the care of a parent or guardian able to provide - but that rule is about disaffirming a contract the minor could make, and it does not obviously cure an incapacity. Practical course: have an adult sign as the tenant, or an adult co-sign and be jointly liable, and never rely on an 18th birthday arriving mid-term. For court, only the tenant and any subtenant in actual occupation when the complaint is filed need be named as defendants, and in small claims a party must be 18 or legally emancipated, though a minor may appear through a guardian ad litem appointed by the court.

title: The Lease Cannot Shorten or Waive a Notice
bodyText: No California lease can shorten, waive or substitute for a notice the law requires. The statute voids, as contrary to public policy, any provision of a residential lease by which the tenant agrees to modify or waive a right to a notice or hearing required by law - and separately voids waivers of the tenant's rights under the security-deposit and entry statutes, of the right to sue you in future, of procedural rights in litigation, and of your duty of care against personal injury and property damage. So none of these works: three days cut to one; a clause saying the tenant accepts email in place of statutory service; a clause waiving the statement of cause a covered tenancy requires; a clause by which the tenant agrees to vacate on demand. There is a second, narrower rule for other statutory rights not void outright: a waiver is void anyway unless the lease was presented to the tenant before they took possession, and that exception does not apply to a renewal containing the same provision. The section reaches leases executed on or after January 1, 1976. Note the direction of travel on notice periods: the three-day notices to pay rent or quit and to perform or quit now exclude Saturdays, Sundays and judicial holidays, so periods have lengthened, and a lease that still recites a flat three days understates the tenant's time.

title: Never Lock Out a Tenant, and Never Cut a Utility
bodyText: California has no opt-in lockout procedure for unpaid rent, and the conduct the question describes is a statutory wrong with its own damages. With intent to terminate the occupancy, you must not wilfully cause, directly or indirectly, the interruption or termination of any utility service furnished to the tenant - water, heat, light, electricity, gas, telephone, elevator or refrigeration are named, and it does not matter whether the utility is under your control. With the same intent you must not wilfully prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access by changing the locks, using a bootlock or any similar method or device, remove outside doors or windows, or remove the tenant's personal property or furnishings without the tenant's prior written consent, except through the abandoned-property procedure. The price is actual damages plus up to $100 for each day or part of a day you remain in violation, with a floor of $250 for each separate cause of action, and later violations not committed at the same time as the first count separately. The court must award reasonable attorney's fees to the prevailing party, the tenant can get an injunction while the case runs, and the remedy is not exclusive. Lawful eviction by the appropriate legal authorities is untouched - which is the point: the writ and the sheriff are the only route.

title: Squatters and Unwanted Occupants: One Narrow Exception
bodyText: California has no squatter-removal procedure outside the eviction process - no sheriff removal on a sworn complaint, no police removal of a transient occupant on an owner's affidavit, no ex parte hearing within 24 hours. Anyone in possession, however they got there, is removed by unlawful detainer and a writ, and taking the property back yourself is forcible entry and exposes you to the lockout damages. There is exactly one exception, and it is narrow. Where you live in the dwelling yourself and have a single lodger - a person renting a room within your home, where you keep a right of access to all areas the lodger occupies and overall control of the home - you may end the hiring by written notice as long as the notice period for a periodic tenancy, served by the statutory methods or by certified or registered mail with restricted delivery and a return receipt. When the notice period expires, the lodger's right to remain ends by operation of law, and a lodger who stays on commits an infraction, may be arrested by you, and may be removed with a peace officer's help - and that removal is expressly not forcible entry. It applies only to an owner-occupied dwelling with one lodger, and the statute says nothing about homes with more than one. On the eviction side, an occupant not named in your judgment can stop the sheriff by filing a claim of right to possession, so serve a prejudgment claim on unknown occupants to close that door early.

title: What the Termination Notice Has to Say
bodyText: For a property covered by California's just-cause rule, the termination notice must state the cause - and the consequence of getting any part of the scheme wrong is severe: the owner's failure to comply with any provision of that section renders the written termination notice void. So the notice is not merely challengeable; it is of no effect, and you start again. Three things therefore have to line up. The notice must state a just cause. If the cause is a no-fault one, the relocation assistance or waiver of the final month's rent must be handled as the statute requires, because that is a provision of the same section. And the tenant must have been given the rent-cap and just-cause notification itself, in no less than 12-point type, in the lease or an addendum or as a signed written notice for a tenancy commenced or renewed on or after July 1, 2020, and that notification is subject to the translation statute. Getting it wrong is expensive beyond losing the case: an owner who attempts to recover possession in material violation is liable for actual damages, attorney's fees and costs at the court's discretion, and up to three times actual damages plus punitive damages on a showing of wilfulness, oppression, fraud or malice - and the Attorney General, a city attorney or county counsel may seek an injunction. Separately, a notice ending a periodic tenancy has to carry the statutory statement about reclaiming abandoned personal property.

title: No Cap on Holdover Charges, and No Statutory Rate Either
bodyText: California sets no holdover rate and caps none: there is no 150-percent-of-per-diem rule, no doubling, and no statutory daily figure for a tenant who stays past the end of the term. What you recover is ordinary damages, proved. A tenant who stays after the term expires without permission is an unlawful detainer, and at trial the court or jury assesses the damages the holding over caused you and finds the rent due. Where malice is shown, statutory damages of up to $600 may be added to actual damages, and the trier of fact decides whether to award actual, statutory or both. If the lease ends because of the tenant's breach, the separate statutory damages measure gives you the unpaid rent plus the rent for the balance of the term, less what the tenant proves you could reasonably have avoided - and a judgment declaring the lease forfeited does not release the tenant from that liability. The drafting trap is the gap this leaves. A lease that fixes holdover rent at a multiple - 150 percent, double, anything - is a liquidated-damages clause, and in a residential lease such a clause is void unless the parties could not practicably or without extreme difficulty have fixed the actual damage when the lease was made. Holdover damages are provable, so state no multiple; charge the rent, and claim your actual loss.

title: How Bad Does a Defect Have to Be?
bodyText: California does not use a "material breach" test for habitability. It uses two different thresholds, and which one applies depends on what the tenant is trying to do. For the repair duty itself, a dwelling is deemed untenantable if it substantially lacks any of the listed standard characteristics - waterproofing and weather protection including unbroken windows and doors, conforming plumbing or gas in good working order, an approved water supply producing hot and cold running water connected to an approved sewage system, conforming heating in good working order, conforming electrical lighting and wiring in good working order, clean and sanitary grounds free of debris and vermin, adequate rubbish receptacles, floors, stairways and railings in good repair, a locking mail receptacle in a residential hotel, and a working stove - or if it is a unit declared substandard, or contains lead hazards, under the Health and Safety Code. "Substantially lacks" is the test, so a chipped tile is not it and a dead furnace in January is. For the tenant's defence to an eviction, the threshold is different and narrower: a substantial breach means a failure to comply with applicable building and housing code standards which materially affect health and safety. So the question is never whether a defect is "material" in the abstract - it is whether the home substantially lacks a listed characteristic, and for the eviction defence whether a code standard affecting health and safety is broken.

title: What the Lease Can and Cannot Change About Habitability
bodyText: California's repair statute opens with words that look like an invitation and are not. The landlord of a building intended for human occupation must, in the absence of an agreement to the contrary, put it into a condition fit for occupation and repair later dilapidations that render it untenantable. A separate section then closes most of that door: any agreement by a tenant of a dwelling waiving or modifying their rights under the repair duty or the repair-and-deduct remedy is void as contrary to public policy with respect to any condition which renders the premises untenantable. Read the two together and the position is clear. You cannot contract out of a condition that makes the home untenantable - not the water supply, not the heating, not the weatherproofing, however the clause is worded and whatever the rent reflects. What the statute does allow is one thing, and it is a reallocation of work rather than a removal of the standard: the landlord and tenant may agree that the tenant will undertake to improve, repair or maintain all or stipulated portions of the dwelling as part of the consideration for rental. Note the condition - it must be part of what the tenant gives for the tenancy, which in practice means reflected in the rent. A bare clause making the tenant responsible for repairs, with nothing given in return, does not meet it.

title: No Habitability Statement Required in the Lease
bodyText: California does not require the lease to say that you will deliver the home fit to live in. The duty exists whatever the lease says, and no statute makes a recital of it part of the required lease content. That is a deliberate contrast with the states that do require such a statement: here the obligation is imposed by statute and protected against waiver, so the Legislature had no need to make you write it down. Two practical consequences. First, leaving the statement out costs you nothing, and putting it in neither adds to nor subtracts from your duty - though a promise that goes further than the statute is enforceable as a contract term like any other, so do not promise more than you mean. Second, and more importantly, the absence of a required statement does not mean there is nothing to put in the lease about condition. California does require several other things in or with the lease, and it does permit one habitability-related agreement: that the tenant will improve, repair or maintain stipulated portions of the home as part of what they give for the tenancy. If you want the tenant doing any of that work, it has to be written and it has to be part of the consideration. There is one reason you might set the statutes out. A written lease that sets out Civil Code sections 1941 to 1942.1 may also provide that either party can send a dispute over an untenantable condition to arbitration, with the arbitrator apportioning the costs. Setting the statutes out is the price of that option; the library does not draft it.

title: Habitability Waivers Are Void - With One Exception
bodyText: A tenant cannot sign away habitability in California. Any agreement by a tenant of a dwelling waiving or modifying their rights under the repair duty or the repair-and-deduct remedy is void as contrary to public policy with respect to any condition which renders the premises untenantable. The exception is single and specific: the parties may agree that the tenant will undertake to improve, repair or maintain all or stipulated portions of the dwelling as part of the consideration for rental. Two features of that exception are easy to miss. It must be part of the consideration - the tenant has to be getting something for the work, which in practice means the rent reflects it - and it covers improving, repairing or maintaining, not accepting a defect. So a clause by which the tenant accepts the home with no working heater, however expressed and however much rent is reduced, is void; a clause by which the tenant maintains the garden or repaints in exchange for lower rent is not. The statute also allows something else worth knowing: if the agreement is in writing and sets out the text of the habitability sections, the parties may agree that any dispute about whether a condition makes the home untenantable goes to arbitration, with the arbitrator apportioning the costs. Separately, the general waiver statute voids any clause waiving a notice or hearing the law requires, the deposit and entry rights, future causes of action, procedural rights, and your duty of care.

title: No Rule About Written Repair Promises
bodyText: California has no statute requiring a promise to clean, repair or improve the home to be in writing, to carry a completion date, or to be given before the lease is signed. Nothing turns on the form of such a promise, and failing to put it in writing is not itself a violation. That does not make a promise harmless. If you promise work and do not do it, three things can follow. A promise in the lease is a contract term, enforceable like any other, and a promise made to get the tenancy signed can support an ordinary claim. If the thing you promised is one of the listed habitability characteristics, your duty exists independently of the promise, and the tenant's remedies - repair and deduct up to one month's rent, no more than twice in any 12-month period, or vacate and stop paying - run from the condition, not from your words. And if an inspector has told you in writing to fix a substandard condition and thirty-five days pass without good cause, you may not demand or collect rent at all, or serve a three-day notice. Practical course: if you agree to do work before move-in, write it into the lease with a date, not because the law requires it but because an undated oral promise is the one you will be arguing about.

title: A Lease Cannot Require Repair Requests in Writing
bodyText: This is a trap carried into California from other states' leases. The repair-and-deduct remedy is triggered by written **or oral** notice to you or your agent - the statute says so in terms - and a lease clause requiring the tenant to report defects in writing cannot change that, because any agreement modifying the tenant's rights under the repair duty or the repair-and-deduct remedy is void as to any condition that renders the home untenantable. So a tenant who telephones you about a dead furnace has given notice, and a clause saying otherwise does not protect you. Two further points sharpen it. The tenant is presumed to have waited a reasonable time if they act after the thirtieth day following notice, but that presumption is rebuttable and does not stop a tenant acting sooner where the circumstances require it - a burst pipe does not wait thirty days. And the two statutes with the heaviest consequences do not depend on the tenant's notice at all: the eviction presumption and the bar on collecting rent both turn on a written notice from a public officer who has inspected the premises. You may of course ask for written requests, and a reporting clause is useful for record-keeping, but write it as a request, not a condition, and never as a waiver.

title: You Cannot End the Tenancy Because a Repair Is Expensive
bodyText: California gives a landlord no right to terminate a tenancy on the ground that a repair would cost too much. There is no uneconomic-to-repair election, no threshold expressed as a share of value or rent, and no procedure for choosing demolition over repair as against a sitting tenant. The termination rights that exist on this subject belong to the tenant: a tenant may end the tenancy before the end of the term where you do not, within a reasonable time after request, fulfil your obligations as to putting the home into good condition or repairing it; and under the repair-and-deduct statute a tenant faced with an unrepaired condition that renders the home untenantable may simply vacate, and is then discharged from further rent and other conditions from the date of vacating. A tenant may also terminate where the greater part of the home, or the part that was the material inducement to rent, perishes other than through the tenant's own want of ordinary care. If a building genuinely cannot be kept in repair, the route is not a termination clause: it is one of the no-fault just causes - withdrawing the home from the rental market, complying with a government order, or demolition or substantial remodel - each with its own notice and its relocation-assistance obligation, and each voided if any part of the scheme is not followed.

title: No Rent Escrow, and No Exemption to Notify
bodyText: California has no rent-escrow scheme. A tenant cannot deposit rent with the court or an escrow agent as a self-help response to disrepair, and there is no administrative repair fund. Because there is no scheme, there is also no exemption from one and nothing for you to notify a tenant about - the question some states' leases answer does not arise here. What California gives a tenant instead is self-executing and does not involve a third party holding money: repair the condition and deduct the cost from the rent, capped at one month's rent and available no more than twice in any twelve-month period; or vacate and be discharged from further rent. Neither is available if the tenant caused the condition by breaching their own care-and-cleanliness duties. Rent does reach the court in an eviction, but only in the three situations the eviction rules set - a delayed trial, the habitability defence, and a stay pending appeal - and in each of those it is the court that orders it, not the tenant who elects it. One more point for completeness: a tenant who has had to pay a utility directly to keep service on, under the utility statutes, may deduct that payment from the rent, which is a true statutory deduction and not an escrow.

title: You Cannot Make the Tenant Use Your Repairer
bodyText: No California statute lets the lease name a contractor the tenant must use, or condition the tenant's repair remedy on using one. The repair-and-deduct remedy belongs to the tenant and the statute says nothing about who does the work: after written or oral notice and a reasonable time, the tenant may repair the condition and deduct the cost, so long as the cost does not exceed one month's rent, and may do so no more than twice in twelve months. A clause requiring your approval of the contractor, or restricting the tenant to a named one, modifies that right, and any agreement modifying the tenant's rights under the repair statutes is void as to any condition that renders the home untenantable. What you can do is practical rather than contractual. Give the tenant a reporting route and respond quickly, because the remedy only arises after a reasonable time has passed - presumed at thirty days, less where the circumstances demand. Keep the one-month cap in mind: the remedy does not reach a large job, so for anything substantial the tenant's realistic options are to vacate and stop paying, or to defend an eviction on habitability. And if the work is the kind you would rather the tenant did routinely, the lawful route is an agreement that the tenant maintains stipulated portions as part of the consideration for the rent.

title: Shifting Maintenance to the Tenant: The Narrow Route
bodyText: California lets you move maintenance work to the tenant, but only through one door and on one condition. The door is the habitability waiver statute's exception: the landlord and tenant may agree that the tenant will undertake to improve, repair or maintain all or stipulated portions of the dwelling **as part of the consideration for rental**. The condition is in those last words. The work has to be part of what the tenant gives for the tenancy, which in practice means the rent reflects it; a clause that simply declares the tenant responsible for repairs, with nothing given in return, does not satisfy the exception and is void as to anything that makes the home untenantable. Note what the statute does not require, because it differs from other states: the portions may be "all or stipulated", so the agreement need not itemise the work, and there is no separate-document rule and no single-family-home limit. Separately, the tenant already owes five statutory duties - keeping their part clean and sanitary, disposing of rubbish properly, using the electrical, gas and plumbing fixtures properly and keeping them clean, not permitting wilful or wanton damage, and using rooms only for their designed purpose. Two of those, the cleanliness and rubbish duties, stop applying if you have expressly agreed in writing to do them yourself - so that provision shifts duty the other way, towards you.

title: What a Tenant Can Do If You Do Not Repair
bodyText: California gives a tenant five routes when a condition rendering the home untenantable goes unrepaired, and they stack rather than compete - the repair statute says its remedy is in addition to any other. First, repair and deduct: after written or oral notice and a reasonable time, the tenant may fix the condition and take the cost out of the rent, up to one month's rent, twice in any twelve months. Second, vacate: the tenant may simply leave and is discharged from further rent and other conditions from the date of vacating. Third, terminate for failure to repair after request, under the general hiring statute. Fourth, defend an eviction: if the tenant pleads a substantial breach and proves it, the court sets the reasonable rental value of the home in its untenantable state, denies you possession on condition the tenant pays the adjusted accrued rent within up to five days, may order you to repair with continuing jurisdiction to make sure you do, must limit the rent to the reasonable rental value until repairs are done, and awards the tenant costs and fees if a statute or the lease provides them. Fifth, and most expensive: if an inspector has given you written notice and thirty-five days pass without good cause, you may not demand or collect rent, raise it, or serve a three-day notice - and the tenant can sue for actual damages plus special damages of between $100 and $5,000, with fees to the prevailing party, in small claims if it fits.

title: When You May Not Collect Rent At All
bodyText: California has a provision that stops the rent entirely, and it is the single most expensive habitability rule to overlook. You may not demand rent, collect rent, issue a notice of a rent increase, or serve a three-day notice to pay rent or quit, if four things are all true before your demand or notice. The home substantially lacks one of the listed habitability characteristics, or violates the lead-hazard section, or has been deemed and declared substandard because conditions exist to an extent that endangers the life, limb, health, property, safety or welfare of the public or the occupants. A public officer responsible for enforcing a housing law has inspected and notified you or your agent in writing of your obligation to abate the nuisance or repair the conditions. Thirty-five days have passed since that notice was served - service being complete on deposit in the mail - without the conditions being abated, and the delay is without good cause. And the conditions were not caused by the tenant breaching their own care duties. Break it and you owe actual damages plus special damages of not less than $100 and not more than $5,000, the prevailing party gets fees and costs, and the court can order you to abate and repair, keeping jurisdiction until you do. The tenant need not try any other remedy first, and can bring it in small claims. So: when an inspection notice arrives, diarise thirty-five days and stop serving rent notices.

title: A Receiver Can Be Put Over Your Building
bodyText: If you let a substandard building stay substandard, California allows a court to take it out of your hands. Where the owner fails to comply within a reasonable time with an enforcement order or notice, the enforcement agency, a tenant, or a tenant association or organisation may petition for the appointment of a receiver over the building - note that a tenant group can do this, not only the agency. The petitioner must prove that notice of the petition was posted prominently on the building and mailed first-class to everyone with a recorded interest in the property at least three days before filing, and must serve the owner by the ordinary summons methods. In appointing a receiver the court must consider whether the owner was given a reasonable opportunity to correct the cited conditions, and must not appoint anyone who has not demonstrated the capacity and expertise to do the work. A receiver appointed under another law does not stop the agency seeking, or the court appointing or replacing, a receiver under this section. The same provision carries other penalties for non-compliance: the statutory penalties, and an order that you not claim state tax deductions for interest, taxes, expenses, depreciation or amortisation on the cited structure for the year of the order, and for the following year if you still do not comply. The lesson is that an enforcement notice is not a negotiation - the clock on it runs toward losing control of the asset.

title: Variances From Housing Standards
bodyText: California's housing standards are state standards, and a landlord cannot get a variance from habitability itself. The one variance power in the State Housing Law is narrow and runs the other way - towards making a home legal rather than excusing a defect. The housing appeals board may, on appeal or on the owner's application, grant variances from local use-zone requirements so that an owner-occupant may build an addition to meet occupancy standards relating the number of persons in a household to the number of rooms or bedrooms. That power is in addition to, and does not affect, other boards' and agencies' powers to allow local use-zone variances. So if the problem is that a household has outgrown the rooms, there is a route; if the problem is that the heating does not work, there is not. Nothing in the habitability statutes admits a variance, and an agreement with the tenant cannot substitute for one: a waiver of the repair duty is void as to any condition that renders the home untenantable. Where a local agency has adopted stricter building standards than the state code, those are the standards your building has to meet, subject to the limits on local modification - see the note on local rental rules.

title: When a City Can Set Stricter Standards Than the State
bodyText: California sets housing standards statewide, and a city or county may depart from them only on narrow grounds - but there is a current change here that matters, because the usual answer stopped being true in October 2025. The ordinary rule is that in adopting its building ordinances a city or county may modify the requirements of the California Building Standards Code, green building standards included, where it determines the changes are reasonably necessary because of local climatic, geological or topographical conditions, with findings. From October 1, 2025 to June 1, 2031, however, a city or county may not make such a change applicable to residential units at all unless one of five conditions is met: the change is substantially equivalent to one the local body had already filed and in effect as of September 30, 2025; the state commission deems it necessary as an emergency standard to protect health and safety; it relates to home hardening; it is a home-hardening standard proposed by a local fire prevention district; or it implements a local amendment aligning with a general plan approved on or before June 10, 2025 permitting mixed-fuel residential construction. So before you assume a local standard applies to your building, check when it was filed. None of this touches the state habitability floor, which no local body and no agreement can lower, and the local just-cause and rent-control layer is a separate matter again.

title: Asbestos: What California Actually Requires of You
bodyText:
California has an asbestos notification law, and it does not apply to the homes you rent. That chapter defines the buildings it covers so as to exclude residential dwellings, and the notice it requires runs to the owner's own employees and to co-owners, never to tenants. It also says in terms that giving or negligently failing to give that notice is not a breach of any covenant in a lease. So there is no asbestos disclosure you owe a residential tenant under state law, and no survey or management plan you are obliged to prepare for a rental.

Three real duties do reach you. First, after a disaster - fire, flood, earthquake, storm and the like - you must mitigate the hazards it caused, and asbestos is named in the list alongside mould, smoke, smoke residue, smoke odour, ash and water damage. Until a local public health agency or official says the debris is not toxic, the unit is presumed untenantable, and once you have done the work you must tell the tenant in writing and let them see any testing or reports. Second, if asbestos turns up during a required balcony and walkway inspection and stops you finishing it, you get up to nine months to abate and three more to complete the inspection, and you must keep the records for three years after it is done. Third, abating asbestos counts towards a substantial remodel if you are ending a tenancy on that ground.

Treat known asbestos as a maintenance and contractor-selection problem rather than a paperwork one: your exposure comes from disturbing it, not from failing to announce it.

title: No Defective Drywall Disclosure in California
bodyText:
California has nothing on defective or imported drywall. The word appears in no California statute, and no California code has a chapter heading on the subject. There is no disclosure to make, no testing obligation, no registry to search and no form to attach to a lease.

What applies instead is the ordinary habitability standard, and it covers the real problem. Corroding wiring and corroding plumbing are each grounds on which a unit is declared substandard, as is defective mechanical equipment including vents, and a dwelling that substantially lacks sound plumbing or sound electrical wiring in good working order is untenantable. So if a building of yours has the sulphur-emitting drywall imported in the mid-2000s, you will meet it as a repair duty - blackened wiring, failed air-conditioner coils, a persistent smell - and not as a disclosure duty.
