The tenant's repair-and-deduct remedy, and the bar on demanding rent once a housing inspector has given you written notice and 35 days have passed, are the exposure to manage.

Two practical points. The written transfer disclosure statement that would catch this on a sale does not reach an ordinary residential lease, so do not reach for that form. And if you do know of a defect of this kind, put it in writing before signing anyway: concealing a known material defect is a fraud problem whatever the disclosure statutes require.

title: Which Construction and Fire Codes Reach Your Rental
bodyText:
California does not leave the model codes to be adopted county by county. One statute requires the state's building standards to impose substantially the same requirements as the most recent editions of seven named model codes - the Uniform Housing Code, the International Building Code, the International Residential Code, the Uniform Plumbing Code, the Uniform Mechanical Code, the National Electrical Code and the International Existing Building Code - published together as the California Building Standards Code. If the state has not adopted a new edition by regulation, the newest edition counts as adopted one year after it is published. Fire and panic safety for apartment houses and dwellings is set separately by the State Fire Marshal, and no local fire inspection of each single-family dwelling before occupancy is required.

Two points decide how any of this lands on a building you already own. Construction standards are not retroactive: the rules on erecting or constructing a building do not reach an existing structure. But standards on use, maintenance and change of occupancy apply to every apartment house and dwelling whenever it was built. So an old building is not required to be rebuilt to today's code, and is required to be maintained to today's maintenance standards.

Local amendment used to be the wild card. From 1 October 2025 to 1 June 2031 a city or county may not change the state's standards as they apply to residential units, with narrow exceptions including emergency health-and-safety standards and home hardening against wildfire. Your building department can still approve an equivalent alternative material or method case by case.

title: Fire Sprinklers: No Retrofit Duty, but Maintain What You Have
bodyText:
No California statute makes you retrofit sprinklers into an existing rental. The statutes that require an approved automatic sprinkler system by name are about round-the-clock care facilities housing more than six guests or patients, not ordinary apartments or houses. Whether sprinklers were required in your building is a question for the construction code in force when it was built or last substantially altered, and construction standards generally do not reach existing buildings. One statute does reach older buildings: an apartment house that existed on January 1, 1975, is more than one storey, and lets sleeping rooms above the ground floor 'shall be conformed' to the State Fire Marshal's rules on structural fire safety and fire-resistant exits (Health & Saf. Code § 13143.2(a), (d)). Those rules are regulations this pass couldn't read, so if your building fits that description, ask your fire authority what they require of it.

The duty that does bite is maintenance. A building is declared substandard if it is not provided with the fire-resistive construction or fire-extinguishing systems the code requires - and the grandfather for a building that complied when built holds only where its fire-resistive integrity and its fire-extinguishing systems have been adequately maintained, and improved to match any increase in occupant load, alteration or addition, or change of occupancy. A substandard building is untenantable, which opens the tenant's repair remedies and, after an inspector's uncured written notice, bars you from demanding rent.

There is also a criminal edge. Willfully or maliciously constructing or maintaining a fire-protection system - sprinklers, standpipe, fixed extinguishing system or fire alarm - that you know to be inoperable, or impairing one, so as to threaten an occupant in a fire, is punishable by two, three or four years in prison, and five to seven if it causes great bodily injury or death. So never take a head out of service or let a riser be shut off without the fire department's say-so, do not promise a tenant the building is sprinklered unless it is, and if you add units, convert a space or change its use, ask your building department before the work whether the fire-protection requirement moves with it.

title: No Sprinkler Disclosure Duty in California
bodyText:
California does not require you to tell a tenant whether the building has a fire sprinkler system, and it has no sprinkler retrofit grant or loan programme a landlord can point a tenant to. There is no statutory wording, no notice, and nothing to attach to a lease.

The one fire-safety-device disclosure California does have proves the point by contrast. It applies to sales, not lettings: a person transferring real property containing a single-family dwelling by sale, exchange or real property sales contract must deliver a written statement that the dwelling has an operable smoke alarm. There is no sprinkler equivalent, and the lease is not the vehicle. The written transfer disclosure statement does not reach an ordinary residential lease either.

The practical risk here runs the other way. Because nothing requires the disclosure, anything you do say about fire protection is a voluntary representation you will be held to. If your marketing or lease describes the building as sprinklered, make sure every area the tenant will use actually is, and that the system is in service. If a sprinkler system exists, say so only in neutral terms, and put the tenant's own duties in the lease - nothing stored on or hung from a sprinkler head, nothing obstructing a riser or a control valve, and a report to you the moment a head is struck or leaking. Those are duties worth stating; a disclosure is not owed.

title: Pools: Your Pool Is a Public Pool
bodyText:
The most important thing to know is that California's public swimming pool rules reach rental housing. A pool on the grounds of an apartment complex, or in any residential setting other than a single-family home, is a public swimming pool, and so is a pool open only to residents of a multiunit building or residential development. A pool at a private single-family home is excluded, and so is a wading pool at a one- or two-unit residence used only by residents and guests. Everything in between is yours to run as a public facility.

What that means in practice: operate and maintain the pool in a sanitary, healthful and safe manner; fit anti-entrapment devices or systems meeting the recognised national standard; a single outlet that is not unblockable needs a listed system such as a safety vacuum release; a pool built from 2010 needs two hydraulically balanced outlets per pump at least three feet apart, and an older one was to have been retrofitted by July 2010; a pool with an outlet anywhere but the bottom must turn its whole volume over within set times, six hours for an ordinary pool and half an hour for a spa; and underwater lights over 15 volts need an approved ground-fault circuit interrupter.

Two things landlords miss. You must file the state compliance form for the pool with your city or county environmental health department within 30 days of finishing the work, and that filing is what your health officer treats as evidence you complied. Fencing and gates sit in a separate statute, the Swimming Pool Safety Act, and it is narrower than its reputation: it bites only when a building permit is issued for a new or remodelled pool at a private single-family home, so it does not reach an apartment pool at all. If you rent out a house and pull a permit, you need two of seven listed drowning-prevention features, and an enclosure has to clear 60 inches with a self-latching gate that opens away from the water. A violation of the pool article is a misdemeanour.

title: Lead Certification Covers Your Contractor, Not Your Building
bodyText:
California has no lead-safe certificate for a dwelling. There is nothing a county issues for a unit, nothing to attach to a lease as an exhibit, and no inspection that buys you a safe-harbour. What California certifies is people and firms doing lead work, and that is where your obligation lies.

A certificate is required now for anyone paid to do a lead hazard evaluation - a lead inspection, risk assessment or clearance inspection - in a residential building; for anyone designing an abatement plan; for anyone doing work meant to reduce or eliminate lead hazards permanently, meaning for twenty years or more; and for anyone doing lead-related construction work that will expose a person to airborne lead at or above the eight-hour permissible exposure limit. From 1 July 2027 the net widens a long way: a firm, and at least one person onsite employed by it, must be certified to do renovation, repair or painting for compensation in a residential building where the work will disturb lead-based paint or presumed lead-based paint. People doing routine maintenance and repairs in housing need no certificate so long as they are not doing any of those things.

The penalties are not nominal: at least five thousand dollars a day per violation for the current requirements and at least ten thousand for the 2027 firm requirement, with up to thirty-seven thousand five hundred a day for repeats. And nobody may do lead-related construction work on a residential building in a way that creates a lead hazard. So before any painting or demolition in a pre-1978 unit, ask your contractor for the certificate and keep a copy.

title: No California Lead Notice Beyond the Federal One
bodyText:
California adds no lead notice, certificate or packet of its own to a residential lease. Its lead chapter creates a certification programme for the people and firms who do lead work and a set of enforcement powers; it says nothing to a landlord about telling a tenant anything. There is no state lead pamphlet you must hand over, no state form, and no state registry to search.

So the lease paperwork is the federal paperwork - the pre-1978 lead warning statement, your own disclosure of known lead-based paint and hazards, the records and reports list, the tenant's acknowledgment and the federally approved pamphlet. Do not add a state layer that does not exist, and do not assume the federal form discharges California's own lead duty, because that duty is not a disclosure duty at all. California treats lead hazards as a habitability violation measured against stated area thresholds, which applies whatever the building's age and routes straight into the tenant's repair remedies.

Two things do generate a California notice in practice, and both come from an agency rather than from the lease. The health department or a local enforcement agency may order you to abate a lead hazard and give you a reasonable opportunity to correct; disobeying is punishable. Once such an order exists, the condition is one you know about, and an order of that kind is the sort of record the federal disclosure requires you to list and give to the tenant. Keep any lead order, report or clearance result in the file for that unit and hand it over at the next letting.

title: No Window Guards, but California Does Regulate Window Bars
bodyText:
California has no window-guard law. There is no duty to install guards, no duty to offer them to a household with young children, no bold-type lease notice and no model wording by regulation. If a tenant asks for a guard, you are free to agree or refuse, and if you do fit one it is an alteration you should document.

California regulates the opposite device. Security bars, or burglar bars, are a fire-escape problem rather than a falling problem, and the rules all point one way: bars must be able to open. No one may install unopenable burglar bars where the building standards require openable ones for emergency escape or rescue. Bars may not be sold in California unless they carry the State Fire Marshal's warning information, and an installer must give the owner a copy of that warning before fitting them. A city or county may set a date by which every rental with security bars on bedroom windows must have a code-compliant safety release mechanism, so check your local ordinance. Where a release mechanism exists, its existence must be disclosed in writing - the statute points to sale documents, but there is no reason not to record it in the lease too.

Separately, every window designed to open must have an operable window security or locking device, except louvered and casement windows and windows more than twelve feet above the ground vertically or six feet horizontally. That is a security duty you do owe, and it is not satisfied by bars that cannot be opened from inside.

title: Water Heater Temperature: Set It, Record It, Check the Code
bodyText:
No California statute tells you what temperature to set a water heater to, or requires you to set it before each new tenancy. The phrase does not appear in the statutes at all, and there is no anti-scald or tempering-valve requirement at statute level. California does have three separate water heater chapters - on strapping and installation, on warning labels and on water heaters generally - and this row does not state what they contain; the detailed temperature requirement, if there is one, sits in the plumbing part of the state building standards, which is a regulation.

What is certain is the duty behind it. A dwelling is untenantable unless it has an approved water supply capable of producing hot and cold running water, furnished to the right fixtures and connected to an approved sewage system. A unit lacking hot and cold running water to its plumbing fixtures is substandard, and serious defects in or lack of adequate water heating is one of the categories that can turn a repeat housing-code offender's penalty into a jail term. So hot water is not optional and cannot be contracted away.

The cautious course, since the figure is in a code and not a statute: at every turnover, confirm the heater is set to the temperature your local plumbing code and the manufacturer's instructions require, confirm the temperature-and-pressure relief valve and its discharge pipe are intact, write the setting and the date on your move-in checklist, and never leave the dial adjustable by a tenant without telling them what it is set to and why. One California duty about water heaters is real, statutory and often missed, though it is about earthquakes rather than scalding: every existing residential water heater must be braced, anchored or strapped against earthquake motion, a violation makes the building a nuisance, and you may not evict anyone in order to do the work.

title: Heat: A Duty You Cannot Contract Out Of
bodyText:
Heating facilities are on California's list of things a home must have. A dwelling is untenantable if it substantially lacks heating facilities that conformed to the law in force when they were installed and are maintained in good working order. Separately, lack of adequate heating makes a building substandard, and serious defects in or lack of adequate space heating is one of the categories that can turn a repeat housing-code offender's sentence into jail time. Because heat is on the untenantability list, no lease term can waive or modify the duty - a clause that tries is void as against public policy.

Three distinctions matter. First, the duty is to the equipment, not to the fuel bill: nothing stops you putting the gas or electricity for the heating on the tenant, so long as the heating facilities themselves work. Second, if the tenant's meter also powers heating outside their unit, you must disclose that before the tenancy and make a written agreement about who pays. Third, your repair duty does not arise where the tenant's own substantial breach of their housekeeping duties caused the problem or is blocking the repair.

No California statute sets a minimum indoor temperature or a date by which heat must be on. The figure, if your building has one, comes from the state building standards and any local ordinance, so do not quote a number in the lease. Say instead that you will maintain the heating equipment, name who pays for the fuel, and ask tenants to report a failure at once - a dead furnace in cold weather is an emergency repair, not a routine one.

title: No Radiator Cover Rule in California
bodyText:
California has nothing on radiator covers. The word radiator appears in no California statute and in no chapter heading in any of the thirty codes. There is no duty to supply a cover on request, no lease rider to attach, no notice to give a household with a small child, and no deadline to meet. Nor is there anything on steam pipes, risers or convectors.

What covers the ground instead is the ordinary heating and equipment duty. The heating facilities must have conformed to the law in force when they were installed and must be maintained in good working order, and defective or badly maintained mechanical equipment, including vents, makes a building substandard. A leaking or venting radiator is therefore a repair matter, and a tenant can use the repair remedies on it.

The exposed-hot-surface risk is a liability question rather than a code one, and California answers it through ordinary negligence law, which this library does not treat as a source. The cautious course is simple and cheap. If a unit has steam or hot-water radiators and the household includes young children or someone with reduced mobility, fit covers when asked and record that you did. Do not put a clause in the lease disclaiming responsibility for burns or for the condition of the heating equipment: an exculpatory clause of that kind is unlikely to hold in a California residential lease, and attempting to waive the heating duty is void outright.

title: Common-Area Lighting: Yours to Keep Lit, and the One Way to Shift the Bill
bodyText:
Lighting in the parts of a building you control is a habitability duty, not a housekeeping one. A dwelling is untenantable if it substantially lacks electrical lighting and wiring maintained in good working order, and all areas under your control must be kept clean, sanitary and clear. A building lacking required electrical lighting is substandard. California singles hallway lighting out: inoperable hallway lighting is one of seven named categories of serious violation that can convert a repeat housing-code offender's penalty into a six-month to one-year jail term with a five-thousand-dollar fine. Treat a dead stairwell light as urgent.

On who pays, California's rule is narrow and procedural. If you do not meter each unit separately and you know that service through a tenant's meter also serves an area outside their unit - a hallway light, a stair light, an exterior fixture, a shared outlet - you must explicitly disclose that to the tenant before the tenancy begins, or as soon as you discover it, and then either make a mutual written agreement for the tenant to pay for it or make other mutually agreed written arrangements, such as becoming the customer of record yourself. Skip the disclosure and a tenant can go to court, have you made the customer of record, and recover everything they paid for outside-the-unit service back to the date your duty arose. The optional lease clause on this topic makes that written agreement. No statute sets a lighting level for an ordinary rental - the one exception is age-restricted senior housing, where walkways and hallways in the common areas must be lit brightly enough to assist people who have difficulty seeing if you want the presumption that the development is designed for senior citizens.

title: Cooling Devices: No Tenant Right Yet, and a 2027 Trap
bodyText:
An ordinary California tenant has no statutory right to install a portable or window cooling device, and you have no statutory duty to provide cooling. Air conditioning is not on the list of things a home must have, there is no maximum indoor temperature you must achieve, and a lease that restricts window units does not have to say so in any particular way.

That is the narrow answer, and the direction of travel is the opposite way. From 2026 it is declared state policy that every dwelling unit should be able to attain and maintain a safe maximum indoor temperature, and from 1 January 2027 state agencies must take that policy into account when they make regulations. The statute says expressly that it does not expand anyone's obligations, so it is a signal rather than a duty - but the regulations it points to are the ones that would create the duty. Mobilehome and RV park residents already have the full right from 2026: no park rule may prohibit or restrict installing, upgrading, replacing or using a cooling system, which is defined to include a portable or window air conditioner, a swamp or evaporative cooler, a cooling fan system and a heat pump.

The trap is for a condominium or planned-development unit. A 2026 act effective 1 January 2027 voids any provision prohibiting or restricting a cooling system, and its wording is not plainly limited to association documents. Until that is settled, do not write a flat ban on window or portable units into a lease. Allow them subject to conditions you can justify - permit, amperage, safe mounting, no damage, removal at the end - and you keep control without betting on the point.

title: Contaminated Land: What California Makes You Disclose, and What Is Still Open
bodyText:
California has no general contamination disclosure for a residential lease. There is no statutory notice about a cleanup site, a hazardous release or a brownfield that you must give a tenant, and nothing of that kind is required to be attached to a lease. The written transfer disclosure statement that would cover it on a sale does not reach an ordinary residential letting.

What California does instead is name specific contaminants and handle each one separately, and the library already has rows for them: methamphetamine or fentanyl contamination after a remediation order; mould, as a habitability condition plus a booklet; lead hazards, measured against area thresholds; bed bugs; and Proposition 65 warnings where they apply. After a declared disaster you must mitigate the hazards it caused - asbestos, smoke residue, ash, water damage - and tell the tenant in writing when you have, and until the public health authority clears the debris the unit is presumed untenantable. Work through that list rather than looking for one omnibus disclosure.

One thing is genuinely unresolved here. California cleans up contaminated land partly through restrictions recorded against the property, and in other states a restriction of that kind must be carried into every later lease. California's statutes make a recorded restriction of this kind bind your tenant directly: a covenant recorded as an "Environmental Restriction" binds anyone holding an interest through the owner, and a cleanup agency's recorded covenant on a hazardous waste site binds the owners' lessees. None of the statutes read says the restriction must be copied into the lease, and the agencies' regulations, which might, couldn't be read. So if the property has any recorded environmental restriction, land use covenant or cleanup agreement, get the recorded document, read what it obliges you to pass on, and attach it to the lease. That is the cautious course. One more thing, because the citation you will find in older forms is dead: California's hazardous-substance release disclosure was renumbered in 2024, and in its current form it binds owners of nonresidential property only, so it is not a duty you owe a residential tenant. The duty that does run in a residential tenancy runs the other way - your tenant must tell you in writing about a contamination release they know of, and faces a penalty of up to $5,000 if they knowingly stay silent, though you cannot treat that silence as a default under the lease.

title: No Certificate of Occupancy Disclosure, but the Date Decides Three Things
bodyText:
You do not have to give a tenant a certificate of occupancy, show one, or disclose when the building got one. No California statute requires it, there is no form, and the certificate itself is a creature of the building standards and your local ordinance rather than of statute.

The date on it matters a great deal all the same, because four separate rules turn on it. Housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous fifteen years is exempt from the Tenant Protection Act's just-cause requirement and from its rent cap, unless it is a mobilehome - and because that is a rolling fifteen years, a building drifts into coverage with time, so recheck it rather than relying on an exemption notice written years ago. A unit with a certificate issued after 1 February 1995 lets you set the initial and all later rents free of local rent control. You may not refuse to rent to a tenant with a waterbed, on the stated insurance and installation conditions, in a structure that got its certificate after 1 January 1973. And in the ten listed counties, a property of sixteen or more units issued a certificate on or after 1 January 2025 must unbundle parking from rent.

So keep the certificate in the property file with its date, because you will need it to answer an exemption question and to defend the exemption notice you serve. And note the one place the certificate is withheld as leverage: a required balcony and walkway inspection, with repairs confirmed, is a condition of the local jurisdiction issuing a final inspection or certificate of occupancy.

title: Submetering gas or electricity to tenants
bodyText: If you take gas or electric service on one master meter and resell it to tenants through submeters, California regulates the rate and the bill, not a pre-lease disclosure. You must charge each tenant the same rate the utility would charge that tenant for service taken directly. You must give each tenant an itemized bill in broadly the same form the utility uses for its own residential customers, showing the opening and closing meter readings and the rates and quantities in every rate block. You must post the current residential rate schedule in a conspicuous place, or post the utility's web address for it and supply a paper copy free on request. Any rebate the utility pays you has to be passed through to each tenant in proportion to what that tenant used in the last billing period. Everything beyond the master meter is yours to maintain and repair. The same rate ceiling and billing form apply where a municipal utility district is the supplier. Watch two limits. For a building permitted on or after 1 July 1982 you generally cannot master-meter at all: each residential unit must be individually metered for electric and gas service, with narrow exceptions. And reselling stays outside utility regulation only while the power goes to you and your own tenants; sell or transmit to anyone else and you risk being treated as a regulated electrical corporation. Separately, if a tenant's own meter serves any area outside their unit, you must disclose that before the tenancy starts or as soon as you learn of it and make a written arrangement about it. Nothing requires a gas or electric cost estimate in the lease, but state the billing method in the lease anyway.

title: Meter conservation charges: no California program
bodyText: California has no meter conservation charge and no on-bill financing programme that lets you recover an energy-efficiency or water-saving improvement through a charge on a tenant's utility bill, so there is no notice you owe a new tenant about one and no rent deduction attached to getting it wrong. Two things apply instead. If you submeter water and bill separately, the bill may carry only four things: the metered volume at allowable rates, a share of the water purveyor's fixed charge, one billing or administrative fee, and a late fee. That administrative fee is capped at the lesser of a set dollar figure, which you may raise each year no faster than the state consumer price index, or a quarter of the volumetric charge. You cannot bolt a conservation or device charge onto that bill. Second, you may not pass through fees the water purveyor or your billing agent charges you - deposits, disconnection, reconnection, your own late payment or any other penalty against you - unless you can document that the penalty was caused mainly by tenants wasting water in breach of state or local water-use rules. For any other utility, the cost of an efficiency improvement is a cost of the property; recover it through rent, subject to whatever rent cap or local ordinance applies, not through a separate meter charge. If you ever do finance an improvement through a charge a tenant pays, put the amount, the basis and the end date in the lease before signing.

title: Capping what you pay for a tenant's utility
bodyText: California has no general statute capping what you may bill a tenant for a utility, but three rules decide whether a flat allowance with tenant-paid overage is open to you at all. If the utility is gas or electricity behind a master meter, it is not: you must charge each tenant the same rate the utility would charge them directly, on an itemised bill showing the meter readings and each rate block, so an allowance-plus-overage figure is the wrong shape. If the utility is water and you submeter and bill separately, it is not: the bill may carry only the metered volume at allowable rates, a share of the purveyor's fixed charge, one capped administrative fee and a late fee. For everything else you pay and recover - trash, sewer billed to you directly, water in a single-family home on your own account - an allowance with the tenant reimbursing the excess is a contract term, and the limits are the ordinary ones. Disclose the method before signing, bill from the provider's actual bill, and keep the figure your own rather than copying a statutory ceiling. Two drafting points matter. Do not pass through penalties the provider charges you. And decide deliberately whether the reimbursement is rent: if it is, nonpayment is a pay-or-quit matter and the deposit covers it; if your lease says it is not, you have narrowed your own remedies. For submetered water the statute already answers that - those charges are not rent.

title: Billing tenants for utilities that are not separately metered
bodyText: California does not make a lease term unenforceable because it bills a tenant for a utility that is not separately metered to their unit. The submetering chapter says so in terms: nothing in it favours or disfavours a ratio utility billing system, the allocation of water and sewer costs by square footage, occupancy or another physical feature of the unit. So allocation is permitted, and because it is permitted it is governed by what you wrote and disclosed rather than by a statute. Three real limits apply. For a building permitted on or after 1 July 1982, each residential unit must be individually metered for electric and gas service, with narrow exceptions, so there is often no master meter to allocate from. For new multiunit construction where the water connection was applied for after 1 January 2018, the water purveyor must require per-unit measurement and, unless the purveyor installs meters, you must install and read submeters - and once a property has to have submeters, you must bill for water under the submetering chapter, which bars allocation for water. And if a tenant's own gas or electric meter serves any area outside their unit, you must disclose that before the tenancy or on discovery and then either reach a written agreement for the tenant to pay that outside use or make another written arrangement, such as becoming the customer of record yourself. Cautious course: state the allocation formula in the lease, keep the provider's bills, and give a tenant the figures on request. For commercial tenants, a separate statute conditions this kind of allocation; nothing equivalent reaches dwellings.

title: Utility disclosures that travel with the lease
bodyText: California requires exactly one utility document to be given with a lease, and only if you submeter water and bill for it separately from rent. Before the lease is executed you must give the tenant, in writing and in at least ten-point type, ten items: that water will be billed separately; an estimate of the monthly bill computed either from the average or median bill for comparable units at the property over any three of the past six months or from average indoor use by a family of four of about 200 gallons a day plus all other charges; the due dates and payment procedure; a mailing address, an email address and a toll-free or local phone number for billing questions, with the hours that number is staffed; the closed list of charges the bill may carry; the tenant's duty to report leaks and your duty to investigate and repair within 21 days; a second set of contact details for reporting leaks; the three items you must supply on request; the write-first-and-ask-for-an-investigation route, including that an unresolved meter dispute can go to the county sealer, with that office's contact details; and a pointer to the submetering chapter. The statute says this may be incorporated into the rental agreement, so a separate attachment is optional. Beyond that, nothing requires you to attach a utility cost history, an average-bill statement or a signed utility addendum. One other written document is mandatory: if a tenant's gas or electric meter serves space outside their unit, the disclosure must be followed by a mutual written agreement or another written arrangement.

title: Getting notice of a tenant's utility shutoff
bodyText: California gives you no right to be copied on a tenant's utility shutoff notice, and no statute lets you sign a separate document with the utility authorising it to tell you that a tenant's service is about to be cut. What exists is a third-party notification service, and it belongs to the tenant, not to you. Every regulated electrical, gas, heat or water corporation, every municipal utility, every municipal utility district and every public utility district must make that service available to residential customers who are 65 or older or who are dependent adults. The customer applies on the utility's own form and must include the designated third party's written consent. Being designated obliges you to nothing, and it does not prevent or delay the shutoff. So for a tenant under 65 who is not a dependent adult, there is no statutory route at all. Practical course: ask the utility whether its tariff offers a broader third-party or landlord notification, since those rules are not in the statutes; and cover it in the lease instead - require the tenant to keep service on and in their own name, to give you a copy of any disconnection or delinquency notice within a short fixed period, and let you pay the arrears and recover what you paid as a lease charge. Do not make the lease authorise you to cut service off yourself. The reverse case is well covered: if you hold the account and fall behind, the utility must warn the occupants and offer them the account.

title: Never interrupt a submetered supply to collect
bodyText: If you submeter water, you may not shut off or otherwise interfere with water service to a dwelling unit for any reason, including nonpayment. That bar is absolute and carries no intent requirement, and it cannot be waived - any purported waiver of anything in the submetering chapter is void. The single exception is practical, not punitive: you or your agent may shut water off to a unit or the property to make repairs, replace equipment or carry out other maintenance. So an unpaid water bill is never a reason to turn a tap off. Your route instead is the lease. Once a water bill has been unpaid for 180 days, or the unpaid amount reaches 200 dollars, you may serve a three-day notice to perform the conditions or covenants or quit - counting three days and excluding Saturdays, Sundays and other judicial holidays - and proceed as an ordinary unlawful detainer. It is not a pay-or-quit notice, because water service charges are not rent. For gas or electricity you submeter behind a master meter, California sets no interruption procedure at all: there is no tariff, no notice period and no reconnection rule for you to follow. Treat that silence as a bar rather than a licence. Cutting a tenant's utility off, whether or not the service is under your control, is unlawful if you do it meaning to end the occupancy, and it exposes you to damages of up to 100 dollars a day with a 250-dollar floor and the tenant's attorney fees.

title: When you hold the utility account and fall behind
bodyText: If the utility account for a tenant's unit is in your name and it goes into arrears, California does not simply let the service be cut. Every regulated electrical, gas, heat or water corporation, every municipal utility, every municipal utility district and every public utility district must make a good-faith effort to warn the occupants in writing before terminating. Where units are individually metered in your name, that is ten days' warning. Where the building is master metered, a utility corporation, municipal utility or utility district must give fifteen days. It posts the notice on the door of each unit or, if that is impracticable, two copies in every accessible common area and at every entrance. The notice must tell occupants what to do to keep or restore service, estimate the monthly cost, name a utility representative to help, and give a legal services phone number. Any other local district that supplies light, heat, water or power, such as a water district, owes the same written warning ten days ahead, master metered or not. In every case the occupants may become customers in their own names without paying a cent of your delinquency, and proof of prompt rent payment stands in for a credit history. A tenant who then pays the utility may deduct what they reasonably paid from the next rent payment, because the rent included the service. For a master-metered building the exposure is worse: if you cause or fail to prevent a shutoff while any unit is occupied, the occupants can sue for restoration costs, actual damages and attorney fees, and so can the utility for the arrears and its own costs and fees, with the judgment recordable against the property. Paying the arrears before termination defeats the utility's claim. Keep the account current, and never rely on a tenant's silence.

title: Utility shutoffs: what the law forbids you to do
bodyText: Cutting off a tenant's utilities is one of the most expensive mistakes a California landlord can make. You may not, meaning to end the occupancy, wilfully cause the interruption or termination of any utility service furnished to the tenant - water, heat, light, electricity, gas, telephone, lift or refrigeration - and it makes no difference whether the service is under your control. Do it and the tenant recovers actual damages plus up to 100 dollars for each day you stay in violation, never less than 250 dollars for each separate cause of action, and the court must award attorney fees to whoever wins. Repeat violations count separately. The tenant can also get an injunction while the case runs, and this remedy sits on top of every other one available. If you submeter water, a second and stricter rule applies: you may not shut water off or interfere with it for any reason, nonpayment included, and that bar cannot be waived. The only exception is a shutoff to make repairs or carry out maintenance. Where the utility itself is the one disconnecting, the rules are its own and they are detailed: at least nineteen days to pay, a ten-day delinquency notice that cannot go out until nineteen days after the bill, a further attempt to reach an adult at the premises, and no cut on a Saturday, Sunday, legal holiday or any day the utility's offices are shut. California has no winter moratorium and no storm-emergency moratorium. If a tenant stops paying, use a notice and the court.

title: A tenant who never transfers the utilities
bodyText: There is no California statute letting you cut off a utility a tenant failed to put in their own name, whether you give them three days' warning or thirty. The opposite is true. Interrupting any utility service furnished to a tenant, meaning to end the occupancy, is unlawful whether or not the service is under your control, and costs you actual damages, up to 100 dollars a day with a 250-dollar floor, and the tenant's attorney fees. For submetered water the bar is absolute and needs no intent at all. So the answer is contractual and administrative, not self-help. Make the transfer an express lease covenant with a date, require proof that the account is open in the tenant's name, and make the cost of service left on your account a lease charge you may recover and apply the deposit to. If you hold the account, give the tenant written notice that you will close it on a stated date, and then close your own account rather than interfering with the tenant's supply - but expect the supplier to warn the occupants first and to offer them the account free of your arrears. One help and one trap. A city utility or municipal utility district may not require that service to later tenants run on your account unless you volunteer, and may not chase you for a previous tenant's unpaid bill. But a public utility district supplying water may require exactly that. Ask which kind of supplier serves the property before you draft.

title: When a tenant's unpaid water or sewer bill reaches you
bodyText: Whether a tenant's unpaid utility bill can land on your property depends entirely on which kind of public supplier serves it, and California's answers contradict each other. A city-owned utility and a municipal utility district may not pursue you or a later tenant for a previous tenant's unpaid residential bill where the tenant opened the account, may not insist that later tenants take service on your account unless you agree to it, and may not refuse a tenant service in their own name because an earlier tenant did not pay. Neither of those protections applies to a master-metered apartment building. A municipal utility district may otherwise require the owner of record to pay for service rendered to a tenant, and once it records a certificate that becomes a lien with the force of a judgment lien, or it may put the arrears on your tax bill after a report, notice and public hearing - but not for electricity. A public utility district may add unpaid charges to the annual assessment on the land, which becomes a lien, though its water-charge lien reaches the property only so far as the person who received the service owns it. And any city, district or sanitation agency that has adopted the right ordinance by a two-thirds vote may collect its sewer and water charges on the tax roll with your general taxes, on an annual report describing each parcel. Practical course: find out who the supplier is and whether tenants hold their own accounts, ask the supplier in writing for its policy on owner liability, and check the tax roll and the recorder before you buy or refinance.

title: Government shutdowns and a tenant's rent
bodyText: California has nothing in its statutes that delays rent, suspends a late fee, bars a termination notice or restricts credit reporting because a tenant is a federal or state worker who went unpaid in a government shutdown, a furlough or a lapse in appropriations. Your ordinary rent, late-fee and notice terms apply, and so do the ordinary limits on them: a late fee has to be a reasonable estimate of what the late payment actually costs you rather than a penalty, and a pay-or-quit notice must count three days excluding Saturdays, Sundays and other judicial holidays. What to do when a tenant tells you a shutdown has interrupted their pay. Decide whether you want the tenancy or the possession, because the choice is yours and the law does not make it for you. If you want to keep the tenant, put any concession in writing and keep it narrow: name the months covered, the amount deferred, the catch-up dates and what happens if a payment is missed, and say expressly that the agreement does not waive any other term or any future breach. A verbal indulgence is the thing most likely to be argued later as a waiver of your right to the rent or as a modification of the tenancy. If you serve a notice anyway, serve it correctly, because a defective notice is worth less than no notice. Servicemembers on active duty have separate federal protections that civilian employees do not.

title: Charging for a service you do not actually supply
bodyText: California has no single statute saying you may not charge for a service you do not provide, but it says it four times in particular settings, and one of them is brand new. From 1 January 2026, if you offer tenants internet through a third party - including a bulk-billing arrangement where the cost rides on the rent - you must let a tenant opt out of paying for it. You may not retaliate for the tenant exercising that right, and if you refuse the opt-out the tenant may simply deduct the cost of the subscription from rent. You may still offer bulk billing; you just cannot make it compulsory. Three older rules point the same way. You may not charge a tenant a fee for serving, posting or delivering any notice - that appears in three separate places in the statutes, so there is no safe version of it. If you submeter water, you may not pass on fees the water purveyor or your billing agent charges you for a deposit, a disconnection, a reconnection, your own late payment or any other penalty against you, unless you can document that the penalty was caused mainly by tenants wasting water in breach of water-use rules. And if a tenant reports a leak or a running fixture and you do not fix it within 21 days, the tenant's metered usage is deemed to be the lesser of actual use and a small statutory figure, dropping to nothing after 180 days unrepaired. The practical rule: charge only for what the tenant actually receives, describe each service in the lease, and credit or stop the charge for any period the service is not available.

title: Getting a building's energy data from the utility
bodyText: California gives you a right to your building's energy data, and in most rental buildings you do not need a tenant's permission to get it. Each utility has to keep at least the most recent twelve complete calendar months of energy usage data for every building it serves. On your written or secure electronic request, as owner, agent or operator, the utility must deliver the building's aggregated energy usage data to you or upload it to your benchmarking account, within four weeks, aggregated monthly. A building counts if it has no residential utility accounts at all, or if it has five or more active accounts of any kind. The threshold that matters for consent is different and lower: where the building has three or more active utility accounts, the utility must deliver aggregated data and that aggregated data is not treated as customer usage information or as confidential, and neither you nor the utility carries liability for its use or disclosure. Below three active accounts, the utility may only hand it over if the accountholder consents in writing or electronically. So for a duplex, or a building where one or two tenants hold the accounts, get the consent - and the natural place for it is the lease. Ask for the data by building and by month, keep the request and the utility's response, and do not ask for a named tenant's individual usage; the statutory right is to the aggregate.

title: A private well serving your rental
bodyText: California has no statute telling a landlord to test a private well or to hand tenants the results. What it has instead is a threshold that turns you into a regulated water system without your doing anything, and a habitability rule that makes an unapproved supply a defect you must fix. Count service connections and people. A system of piped water for human consumption serving at least five but no more than fourteen service connections, and not regularly serving drinking water to more than an average of twenty-five people a day for more than sixty days a year, is a state small water system. At fifteen or more service connections, or an average of at least twenty-five people a day for at least sixty days a year, it is a public water system; if fifteen of those connections or twenty-five of those people are year-round residents, it is a community water system. Those classifications carry their own monitoring, reporting and notification duties, enforced by the state board or your county. So a well serving a single house is usually unregulated, and a well serving a small group of units often is not. Separately, a dwelling is untenantable if it substantially lacks a water supply approved under applicable law capable of producing hot and cold running water. Practical course: find out from the county environmental health department which class your system is in and get that in writing; test at least annually for bacteria and nitrate even where no rule compels it; keep the results; and give them to a tenant who asks.

title: Recycling and organic waste at a rental property
bodyText: If your property is a multifamily residential dwelling of five units or more, California treats it as a business for waste purposes and you must arrange recycling services, so far as a local service provider offers them and they are reasonably available. You satisfy that either by source separating recyclables and subscribing to a basic recycling collection, self-haul or other pickup arrangement, or by subscribing to a mixed-waste processing service that achieves comparable diversion. A property generating four cubic yards or more of commercial solid waste a week has the same duty for organic waste, met by source separating and subscribing to organics collection, recycling or self-hauling the organics, or subscribing to a mixed-waste service that specifically recycles organics. A building of fewer than five units is not a business for the organics chapter. Two things the law gives you. You may require tenants to source separate their recyclable materials, and you may require a tenant to source separate their organic waste - so put both in the lease. And when you hire gardening or landscaping services, your contract with them must require the green waste they generate to be handled in compliance with the organics rules; that is your duty, not the tenant's. What California does not have is a statutory duty to tell tenants where and how to recycle. The customer-facing signage rules reach businesses that give customers access to the premises, not residential tenants. Do it anyway: label every container, show what belongs in each, and give tenants the hauler's instructions, because your local jurisdiction almost certainly requires it and can enforce against you.

title: No Late-Fee Cap, and No Grace Period
bodyText: California sets no maximum late fee and no statutory grace period. There is no percentage ceiling, no dollar ceiling, and no rule that rent is not late until a certain number of days have passed. That sounds permissive and is the opposite. Because no statute fixes the figure, a late charge in a residential lease is a liquidated-damages provision, and California treats those harshly in a dwelling lease: such a provision is void except where the parties agree on an amount presumed to be the damage sustained, and only where it would have been impracticable or extremely difficult to fix the actual damage when the lease was made. So the test is not whether your fee is reasonable in size; it is whether your actual loss from late rent was genuinely hard to calculate when you signed. Costs that are easy to document - a bank charge, staff time, interest - cut against you. Practical course: keep any late charge modest, tie it to a real and documented administrative cost, state when rent is late and when the charge applies, and never pitch it as a deterrent or a penalty. A charge for serving a notice is separately and flatly banned, and interest on unpaid rent is a different mechanism with its own rate. A city with rent stabilisation may cap late fees where the state does not.

title: You Cannot Add a Collection Fee
bodyText: No California statute authorises charging a tenant a collection fee or your costs of collecting rent, and three rules make a lease clause that tries it a poor investment. First, the deposit cannot absorb it: the deposit statute lists four purposes - unpaid rent, damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, cleaning to the move-in level, and failure to restore or return personal property where the lease authorises it - and collection costs are not among them, so do not apply the deposit to them: keeping it for them in bad faith exposes you to up to twice the deposit. Second, a fixed collection charge in the lease is a liquidated-damages provision, void in a dwelling lease unless the actual damage was impracticable or extremely difficult to fix when the lease was made, which collection costs are not. Third, if your lease has a fee-shifting clause, it runs both ways by operation of law whatever it says, and a case you voluntarily dismiss or settle produces no prevailing party and no award at all. What you can recover is what the law gives you: the rent, interest on it, and the costs a judgment carries. If you use a collection agency, its fee is yours to bear unless a judgment awards it. And remember the related flat ban - no fee for serving, posting or delivering any notice.

title: Never Charge for Serving a Notice
bodyText: This one is simple and absolute, and California says it three times. A landlord or the landlord's agent shall not charge a tenant a fee for serving, posting or otherwise delivering any notice. The sentence appears in the unlawful-detainer statute, so it covers the three-day notices to pay or quit, to perform or quit, and to quit; it appears again in the section on ending a periodic tenancy, so it covers the 30-day and 60-day notices; and again in the companion section for the other periodic terminations. There is no exception for a process server's invoice, no exception for a posting-and-mailing charge, and no exception for recovering what you actually paid. So do not put a notice fee in the lease, do not add one to a three-day notice, and do not include one in the amount you state as rent due - a notice that overstates the rent due risks being defective, which costs you the case rather than the fee. If you use a professional server, that cost is yours. Where you can recover something is after judgment, as the costs of the proceeding, which a court awards; and a fee-shifting clause in your lease runs both ways by operation of law.

title: Fixed Damages Figures Are Void Unless the Loss Was Hard to Calculate
bodyText: California reverses the usual rule for dwelling leases, and this single section decides the fate of most of the numbers a landlord would like to put in a lease. In ordinary contracts a liquidated-damages clause is valid unless the party attacking it shows it was unreasonable when made. For a lease of real property used as a dwelling by the tenant or those dependent on them, the rule flips: such a provision is void, except that the parties may agree on an amount presumed to be the damage sustained, and only where, from the nature of the case, it would have been impracticable or extremely difficult to fix the actual damage. The burden is effectively yours, and the test is about calculability at the time of signing, not about whether the figure looks fair. The section applies to leases of real property by its own terms through a companion provision. It also steps aside where another statute expressly prescribes the rule for a particular clause - which is why the returned-payment service charge has its own cap and is not tested this way. So: a late charge, a holdover multiple, a re-letting fee, a lock-change charge, a cleaning schedule, an eviction-cost charge and an alarm-tampering fee are all exposed to this rule. Document the actual cost instead, or charge nothing and claim your real loss.

title: No All-In Rent Pricing Rule for Leases
bodyText: California has an all-in pricing law and it does not reach your lease. The consumer-protection statute that requires an advertised price to include mandatory fees applies to transactions for goods or services, and a lease of real property is neither, so the rule that forces hotels and ticket sellers to show a total price does not force you to advertise rent inclusive of mandatory charges. There is no separate statute requiring a schedule of fees in a rental advertisement, no rule voiding an undisclosed fee, and no cap on fees as a class. What California regulates instead is specific fees, one at a time, and those rules are strict where they exist: the application screening fee is capped and tightly conditioned; a returned-payment charge has its own two-tier cap and three statutory exceptions; nothing may be charged for serving a notice; parking on a qualifying property must be unbundled; and anything collected at the start of the tenancy is security however it is labelled, so it counts against the deposit cap and must be returned. Any fee outside those is tested as a liquidated-damages figure, and in a dwelling lease that test is hostile. Practical course: state every charge in the lease, keep each one tied to a documented cost, and do not treat the absence of an all-in rule as permission to leave fees out of what you quote.

title: Concessions Must Be Written Into the Lease, Separately
bodyText: If you offer a discount, an incentive, a concession or a credit on the rent, California requires the lease to show both numbers. On a property subject to the rent cap, the gross per-month rental rate and any owner-offered discounts, incentives, concessions or credits must be separately listed and identified in the lease or rental agreement, or in any amendment to an existing one. This is not presentation: when the cap is applied, any discount you offered and the tenant accepted is excluded from the calculation, so the lowest gross rental rate over the previous twelve months - the figure your increase is measured against - is the gross rent, not the discounted rent. Getting the paperwork right therefore protects your ability to raise rent later; a lease that shows only the net figure makes the discounted amount look like the rent. There is no statute requiring you to offer a concession, none regulating what you may offer, and none letting you claw a concession back on a breach - a repayment clause would be tested as a liquidated-damages figure, and in a dwelling lease that test is hostile, so a concession is better structured as a reduction in the months it applies to than as a sum repayable on default.

title: Raising the Rent: Two Notice Periods and a Cap
bodyText: California controls rent increases in two independent ways, and you have to satisfy both. The notice rule applies to every periodic tenancy, capped or not. For a residential dwelling let from week to week, month to month or any period less than a month, you may increase the rent by written notice, delivered personally or served by mail. If the increase is 10 per cent or less of the rent charged at any time in the previous twelve months - counting it alone or combined with any other increases in those twelve months - the notice must be delivered at least 30 days before the increase takes effect. If it is more than 10 per cent, the period is 90 days. Service by mail adds the statutory extra days. Where the increase is caused by a recertification of the tenant's income or family composition required by statute or regulation, the 30-day period applies instead. And if any other state or federal law, regulation, recorded regulatory agreement or contract requires longer notice, the longer period governs. Separately, on a covered property the cap limits the amount: no more than 5 per cent plus the change in the cost of living, or 10 per cent, whichever is lower, over any twelve months, and no more than two increases in that period. A notice that is correct on timing can still be void on amount.

title: When Rent Is Due, and What the Lease Must Say About Paying It
bodyText: California's default rule is the opposite of what most landlords assume: absent a usage or a contract to the contrary, rent is payable at the end of the holding where the term does not exceed a year, and for a tenancy by the day, week, month, quarter or year it is payable at the end of each period as it successively becomes due. Rent in advance is therefore a creature of the lease, not of the statute - which is why the lease has to say so, and why a lease silent on timing leaves you collecting in arrears. There is no statutory right to pay rent in instalments, and no rule requiring you to accept partial payment. What California does require is detail about paying. The lease must disclose the name, telephone number and address of the person or entity to whom rent is to be paid; if payment may be made personally, the usual days and hours that person is available; or, at your option, instead the number of an account at a financial institution into which rent may be paid together with that institution's name and street address, provided it is within five miles of the property, or the information needed to set up an electronic funds transfer. The lease must also disclose the form or forms in which rent is to be paid - and separately, you must always accept at least one form that is neither cash nor electronic transfer.

title: No Rent-Receipt Rule - but Your Tenant Can Still Demand a Receipt
bodyText: California's landlord-tenant law says nothing about rent receipts. There is no statute obliging you to issue one, none prescribing what it must contain, none singling out cash payments, and no penalty for refusing. That is unusual - most states in this library have a rule of some kind - and if you stopped at the tenancy statutes you would conclude a tenant has no right to a receipt at all. You would be wrong. A general provision of the Civil Code, enacted in 1872 and sitting far outside the landlord-tenant title, gives a debtor the right to require a written receipt from a creditor for any property delivered in performance of an obligation. A tenant paying rent is a debtor performing an obligation, and money is property, so a tenant who asks for a written receipt is entitled to one. Nothing in that section sets out a form, a deadline or a penalty, so the practical reading is narrow: you owe a receipt when the tenant asks, not automatically. Issue them anyway, and keep copies. A tenant may prove a deposit by any credible evidence including a receipt or a cancelled cheque, the same kinds of proof decide a rent dispute, and a non-payment notice that overstates what is due risks being defective. If you accept cash you have no bank record at all. A rent-stabilised city may require receipts outright.

title: Nothing to Waive on Rent Receipts
bodyText: Some states give a tenant a right to a rent receipt and then forbid the lease from taking it away. California has the first half but not the second. A general provision of the Civil Code does give a debtor the right to require a written receipt, and a tenant paying rent is a debtor - but no statute protects that right by name the way California protects the deposit and entry rights. A lease clause by which the tenant agrees not to ask for receipts is still caught by the general rule for statutory rights, below. It would also be pointless, and it would look bad in front of a judge weighing a rent dispute. Two general rules do bear on it. California voids, as contrary to public policy, any clause by which a tenant agrees to modify or waive the deposit or entry rights, a notice or hearing required by law, procedural rights in litigation, a future cause of action, or your duty of care; and it voids a waiver of any other statutory right unless the lease was presented to the tenant before they took possession. So a receipt waiver is void if the lease reached the tenant only after move-in, unless it repeats the same term from the lease being renewed. A clause drafted broadly enough to waive record-keeping or evidence rights could also catch one of the other limbs. The sensible course is the opposite of a waiver: issue receipts, keep a ledger, and keep the tenant's copy and yours in step.

title: No State Tax on Residential Rent
bodyText: California imposes no state tax on residential rent. There is no gross-receipts tax on rental income as such, no state sales or use tax on a dwelling tenancy, and nothing you must collect from a tenant and remit. Two things are easily confused with one. The first is transient occupancy tax, the levy on short stays in hotels, motels and short-term lets. It is a local tax, imposed by a city or county, and it turns on transient occupancy rather than on renting out a home - so an ordinary residential tenancy is outside it, but a short-term let may well not be, and the details are set locally. State law lets a city or county tax only a stay of 30 days or less, so a stay of more than 30 days can't be taxed this way. The second is business licensing and local gross-receipts taxes: a number of California cities require a landlord to hold a business licence or registration and pay a tax measured on rental receipts, which is a tax on you rather than on the tenant and is not passed through as rent. Neither is a rent tax you collect. Practical course: do not add a line for tax to a residential rent, check the city's rules before taking a short-term booking, and treat a local business tax as a cost of operating, not as a charge to the tenant.

title: No Tax Pass-Through Clause for a Dwelling
bodyText: California has no statute authorising a residential lease to pass through increases in property tax, and none regulating such a clause. Commercial leases do this routinely; a dwelling lease in California cannot rely on any statutory footing for it, and three rules make it a bad idea. A sum the tenant must pay on a contingency, fixed in advance, is exposed to the liquidated-damages rule, under which a figure in a dwelling lease is void unless the actual damage was impracticable or extremely difficult to fix when the lease was made. On a property subject to the rent cap, an increase dressed as a tax pass-through is still an increase in what the tenant pays, so it counts against the 5-per-cent-plus-inflation ceiling and the two-increase limit; calling it a tax recovery does not take it outside the cap. And any change to the rent in a periodic tenancy needs the statutory notice - 30 days up to a 10-per-cent increase, 90 days above that - so a clause purporting to adjust the rent automatically when the tax bill arrives does not dispense with notice. If you want the rent to track your costs, the lawful route is to raise the rent by notice within the cap, not to write a pass-through.

title: No Property-Tax Disclosure to a Tenant
bodyText: California requires no disclosure to a tenant about property taxes, special assessments or a Mello-Roos district. The disclosure obligations that exist in this area run to a buyer, not a renter: a seller of residential property must give notice of a special tax or assessment district, and the natural-hazard and transfer disclosure statements belong to a sale. A tenant has no equivalent right to be told what the property's tax position is, and you owe no statement about it. Two cautions that are easy to miss. First, if you intend to recover a tax increase from the tenant, disclosure is not the obstacle - the obstacle is that no statute authorises the pass-through and the rent cap and notice rules still apply, so see the note on tax pass-throughs. Second, where a property sits in a special assessment district, the assessment may well be the reason your costs are rising; that is a matter for how you set the rent, not something to bill on. Note also that disclosure duties about the property's condition are a different subject entirely and California has many of them, several with prescribed wording and minimum type sizes.

title: No Right to Bill a Government Fee to the Tenant
bodyText: California gives a landlord no statutory right to pass a government fee on to a tenant. There is no provision authorising recovery of a rental-registration fee, an inspection fee, a business-licence fee or a code-enforcement charge, and no mechanism for adding one to the rent. Those costs sit with you. Two consequences follow. A lease clause making the tenant reimburse such a fee has no statutory footing and would be tested as a liquidated-damages figure or simply as an additional charge; and on a property subject to the rent cap, recovering the fee by raising the rent is still a rent increase, subject to the 5-per-cent-plus-inflation ceiling, the two-increase limit and the 30-or-90-day notice. There is one important exception running the other way, in the opposite direction from a reimbursement: where water service is submetered, the statute sets out exactly what you may bill, and a fee or charge the water purveyor imposes on you may be billed through only as that chapter allows. Outside that, treat a government fee as a cost of operating. Local rules may differ in both directions: some cities expressly forbid passing a registration fee to tenants, and a few rent-stabilisation schemes allow a limited pass-through on application.

title: A Fine Against You Is Not a Charge to the Tenant
bodyText: No California statute lets you recover a government fine from a tenant, even where the tenant's conduct caused it. There is no provision for passing on a code-enforcement penalty, a nuisance abatement cost, a false-alarm charge or an administrative citation. If a tenant's conduct exposes you to a penalty, your routes are the ones the law already gives you: the tenant's statutory duties to keep their part of the home clean and sanitary, dispose of rubbish properly, use the fixtures properly and not permit wilful or wanton damage; the tenant's duty to repair deterioration caused by their own want of ordinary care, which you can pursue as damages; the deposit, for damage beyond ordinary wear and tear; and, for serious conduct, the nuisance and unlawful-purpose ground that ends the lease on a three-day notice to quit with no right to cure. What you should not do is write a clause making the tenant liable for any fine you incur. It has no statutory footing, a fixed sum would be tested as a liquidated-damages figure, and a clause broad enough to shift your own regulatory liability may also collide with the rule voiding any waiver of your duty of care. Claim the actual, documented loss instead.

title: No Fee for Disabling an Alarm - but the Duties Are Real
bodyText: California authorises no fee for removing, disabling or tampering with a smoke alarm or a carbon monoxide device, and a fixed charge in the lease for doing so would be tested as a liquidated-damages figure, void in a dwelling lease unless the actual damage was impracticable or extremely difficult to calculate when the lease was made - which a replacement alarm is not. What California does instead is split the duties, and the split is worth knowing. The device has to be operable when the tenant takes possession, and maintaining carbon monoxide devices in a rented dwelling is your duty. You may enter to install, repair, test and maintain them, using the ordinary entry grounds and notice. The tenant's duty is to tell you if they become aware that a device is inoperable or deficient. So if an alarm is disabled and the tenant says nothing, the failure to notify is the breach, not a fee-triggering event. Handle it as you would any other breach: notice to perform, documented replacement cost claimed as actual damages, and the deposit for damage beyond ordinary wear and tear at the end. Keep a record of the devices being operable at move-in, because that is the fact you will need.

title: What You May Not Ask an Applicant
bodyText:
California bans the question, not just the decision. You may not make any written or oral inquiry - on the application form, in an email, or in conversation at a showing - about an applicant's race, colour, religion, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation, marital status, national origin, ancestry, familial status, disability, veteran or military status, or genetic information. The ban covers what you perceive about the person and who you think they are associated with, so asking about a partner's religion or a child's disability is the same violation. You also may not ask about, or require any statement or certification of, immigration or citizenship status. Advertisements, signs and listings may not signal a preference on any of those grounds either, and that holds even for the narrow owner-occupied single-lodger situation that is otherwise outside the discrimination rules.

Two things you may still ask. Income is different: asking how much an applicant earns and where it comes from is expressly not discrimination, though refusing them because of the source is. And you may ask for whatever information or documents you need to verify financial qualifications or to verify identity.

No California statute separately forbids you to keep a record of a protected characteristic, and none requires you to collect one. The safe practice is to leave these fields off the application altogether: a field you never created cannot be used against you, while a note of a protected characteristic in a file is evidence of the inquiry you were not allowed to make. Use one written set of screening criteria and apply it in the same order to every applicant.

title: Housing Vouchers: You Must Consider Them
bodyText:
In California a housing subsidy is a protected source of income, so you may not refuse an applicant, charge them more, or hold the unit out as unavailable because they hold a voucher. That covers federal, state and local public assistance and housing subsidies, Section 8 housing choice vouchers and HUD-VASH veterans' vouchers by name, and money paid either to the tenant or straight to you on their behalf.

Three mechanics catch landlords out. Your income test must be measured against the tenant's own share of the rent, not the full contract rent, wherever there is a government rent subsidy - a three-times-the-rent rule applied to the whole rent is unlawful for a voucher holder. You may not rely on credit history alone: you must offer the applicant the choice of supplying other lawful, verifiable evidence of ability to pay their share, give them a reasonable time to produce it, and actually weigh it. And you must count the combined income of people who will live together on the same basis you would use for a married couple.

You may still ask how much the applicant earns and where it comes from; the question is lawful, the refusal is not. You may verify employment, take references and verify identity. No statute requires your lease to mention vouchers, and there is no small-landlord or owner-occupant exemption.

One warning, because it is the mistake to avoid. A different statute - the one making you accept rent tendered by a third party - ends with a line saying nothing in that paragraph requires you to enter a contract connected with a housing assistance programme. By its own words that line limits only that paragraph. It does not qualify the fair-housing rule above, and it is not permission to turn a voucher down.

title: Renting to Families with Children
bodyText:
Familial status is a protected class in California, so you may not refuse a family with children, steer them to particular units or floors, charge them more, set extra rules for them, or end a tenancy because a child has joined the household. The protection covers an adult who lives with anyone under 18 as parent, legal custodian or designee, a person who is pregnant, and a person in the process of obtaining custody. Age is separately protected: a business cannot discriminate in renting housing on the basis of age, so an adults-only building is unlawful unless it genuinely qualifies as senior housing, and the burden of proving that falls on you.

California statute sets no number of people per bedroom. Occupancy limits come from the state building standards adopted into the California Building Standards Code, from your city or county, and from the federal occupancy guidance that fair-housing agencies apply - not from the Government Code. The practical consequence is that you cannot defend a children-restrictive policy by calling it an occupancy standard. Write your occupancy limit by bedroom count, apply it to adults and children alike, and check it against your local code before you publish it.

No California statute requires your lease to list occupants or to address children, and none lets you cap the number of children as such. You may still select on grounds that have nothing to do with a protected class, and you may enforce noise, supervision and common-area rules so long as they apply to every household. Do not write a rule that only children can break.

title: Screening the People Who Work on Your Property
bodyText:
California does not require you to run a background check on a manager, caretaker or maintenance worker. There is no apartment-employee registration, licence or clearance. What California does instead is regulate how you may screen, and the limits are strict once you have five or more employees.

With five or more employees you may not put a conviction-history question on the application, and you may not inquire into or consider conviction history at all until after you have made a conditional offer. You may never use an arrest that did not lead to conviction, a diversion programme, or a conviction that was sealed, dismissed, expunged, pardoned or met with a certificate of rehabilitation. If a conviction leads you to think again, you must make an individualised assessment of whether it has a direct and adverse relationship with the specific duties of that job, weighing the nature and gravity of the offence, the time since it and the sentence, and the nature of the job. You must then put your preliminary decision in writing, attach the conviction-history report, allow at least five business days for a reply, consider what comes back, and give written notice of any final denial.

You may use a credit report for a job only if the post fits a short list, such as a managerial post or one with regular access to $10,000 or more in cash during the workday. If you do buy one, give the person written notice first, say which permitted basis you are relying on, offer them a copy, and tell them the source if you turn them down. If you order an investigative background report, the written disclosure must stand alone in its own document and you need the person's written authorisation. With five or more employees, keep applications and personnel files for at least four years. A resident manager needs no real estate licence.

title: Evicting for Crime on the Property
bodyText:
