California gives you a fast route and a slow route, and the difference is the cure right. If the tenant maintains or permits a nuisance on the property, or uses the property for an unlawful purpose, the lease is terminated by operation of law and you serve a three-day notice to quit. There is nothing for the tenant to fix: unlike a lease-breach notice, this one does not offer the choice of performing instead. A building used for unlawfully selling, storing, keeping or manufacturing a controlled substance is declared a nuisance by statute, so for drug premises you need not prove a nuisance from scratch - storing or keeping is enough, with no sale needed. If instead you rely on a lease covenant the tenant has broken, you serve a three-day notice to perform or quit, counted excluding Saturdays, Sundays and judicial holidays - though where the broken covenant cannot be performed after the fact, no perform-or-quit notice is needed.

Once a tenant has been in place twelve months you also need a just cause, stated in the notice. Criminal activity qualifies, but only the tenant's own criminal activity on the property, or a criminal threat aimed at you or your agent anywhere. A guest's or a non-tenant occupant's crime is not on that list, which is why a lease covenant that makes the tenant answerable for the people they bring in is worth having.

Four cautions. Get any part of the just-cause procedure wrong and the notice is void. You may not charge a fee for serving the notice. You may not penalise anyone for calling the police or an ambulance, and a lease term that tries to is void. And you may not use the state's sex-offender website to choose tenants. Document the conduct before you serve anything.

title: Registered Offenders: No Landlord Duty, and a Trap
bodyText:
California puts no duty on you to find out whether an applicant is a registered sex offender, to keep one away from a school or park, or to stop two of them sharing a home. Both residency rules exist, but they bind the registrant, not you. It is unlawful for any registrant to live within 2,000 feet of a public or private school or a park where children regularly gather, for as long as they must register. A registrant on parole after a state prison term may additionally not live in a single-family dwelling with another registrant unless the two are related by blood, marriage or adoption - that one lasts only while parole does. Neither is a landlord obligation and neither gives you a right to ask. Cities may add stricter rules, so check locally. You must not use the state's public offender website to decide who may rent from you: that exposes you to damages, a civil penalty and injunctions, so your screening must never query it.

You must give the notice. Every lease of a single-family home, and every leasehold in a residential property of more than four units, must carry the statutory notice telling the tenant that the Department of Justice maintains the public website. Use the prescribed wording, in type no smaller than eight point, unreworded. A unit in a two-, three- or four-unit building falls between the two limbs and is not covered, though including the notice anyway does no harm.

Delivering it is also your shield: once given, you need supply no further information about offender proximity, and the notice gives a registrant no claim against you. It does not wipe out other duties. Serve it, say nothing more about offenders, and answer questions by pointing to the website.

title: What It Costs to Refuse an Assistance Animal
bodyText:
In California, refusing to rent to someone because they use a guide dog, a signal dog or a service dog, or refusing to let such a person keep the dog on the premises, is by statute a denial of equal access to housing. So is refusing because the person depends partly on a spouse's income where the spouse is on the lease.

The money is the point. A person who denies or interferes with those rights is liable for actual damages, an amount the court or jury may set up to three times actual damages, a floor of $1,000 per offence however small the actual loss, and the tenant's legal fees. Interfering includes stopping the dog from doing its job. The same conduct is separately an unlawful practice under the state's fair-housing law, which opens the agency route, a private action with punitive damages, and Attorney General penalties; and because the disability rules also run through the Unruh Civil Rights Act, that statute's own floor of $4,000 can apply. You cannot be made to pay twice under the two damages sections for the same act, but choosing which to use is the tenant's choice, not yours. There is also a criminal statute. Denying a person with a guide, signal or service dog admittance to hotels, lodging places and other places the public is invited is a misdemeanor, with a fine of up to $2,500 (Pen. Code § 365.5(b), (c)). It doesn't name rented homes, and whether it reaches a refusal to rent is a question only case law could settle. The cautious course is to assume it can, and certainly in a leasing office or a short-term let.

You also may not charge an extra fee or an extra deposit for the animal, though the tenant stays liable for damage it does. What you may do is write lease terms that reasonably regulate the animal's presence, so long as they do not interfere with it working. A no-dogs policy does not by itself force you to take a disabled applicant's ordinary pet dog - but the assistance-animal rules override it, and support-animal requests follow the accommodation process instead.

title: Religious Items on the Door
bodyText:
You may not adopt or enforce any restriction that stops a tenant displaying or fixing one or more religious items on the entry door or the entry door frame of the home. A religious item means anything displayed because of sincerely held religious belief, so you do not get to judge whether the object counts. The rule binds you as owner and binds a sublessor; in a condominium it also binds the association, its board and the owner-member, and the association's governing documents cannot override it either.

Five exceptions, and they are the whole of your room to manoeuvre. You may restrict a display that threatens public health or safety, one that stops the door opening or closing, one that breaks any federal, state or local law, one that is obscene or otherwise illegal, and one that - by itself or together with the tenant's other religious items on that door or frame - is larger than 36 by 12 square inches, though you cannot cut it below the size of the door. Anything else is not a lawful restriction, and the statute says even these exceptions operate only so far as the free-exercise guarantees allow.

There is no separate California right to display cultural, ethnic or heritage items as such, and none for flags in a rented home. A cultural display may still be protected indirectly: if the item is religious to the tenant it is covered, if it carries a political message the political sign rules cover it, and refusing it on grounds of the tenant's religion, ancestry or national origin is housing discrimination whatever the item is. Practical course: allow door displays within the size limit, write the size and safety limits into your rules, and say nothing about which faiths or which objects.

title: Canvassers, Candidates and Your Front Door
bodyText:
No California statute gives a candidate, a campaign worker, a petition circulator or a voter registration drive a right to come onto your property or into your building, and none requires you to provide a voter information area or to let anyone canvass the corridors. As far as the statutes go, access to a private residential building is yours to control, and you may keep a no-soliciting rule and refuse entry to the common parts.

Two things cut across that. Your tenants may post political signs - about an election or a legislative vote, an initiative, referendum or recall, or a matter before a public body - in the window or on the door in a multifamily building, and in a single-family home also from the yard, balcony or outside wall; you may restrict a sign only if it is bigger than six square feet, breaks a law, or breaks a lawful common-interest-development document, and you must allow a posting window running from at least 90 days before the vote to at least 15 days after.

Second, a visitor a tenant has actually invited in is not a trespasser. Anyone who comes onto the property at a tenant's invitation, at a reasonable hour or in an emergency, to give information about tenants' rights or to take part in a tenants' association, is protected from any trespass claim, criminal or civil. So the lawful line is between an uninvited caller, whom you may turn away, and an invited one, whom you may not pursue for trespass. Cautious course: apply one written no-soliciting rule to every caller alike, never one that singles out a party, a candidate or a cause, and do not threaten a tenant over who they let in.

title: Foreign Tenants and Foreign Owners: No Restriction
bodyText:
California has no alien land law, no foreign-adversary property ban and no restriction on who may hold or lease real property by reason of nationality, citizenship or country of origin. You are not required to find out whether an applicant is a citizen, a resident or a foreign national, and no lease of yours is void or voidable because of who the tenant is. California goes further than merely being silent: its Constitution guarantees that noncitizens have the same property rights as citizens.

The risk here runs the other way, and it is the only thing a California landlord needs to take from this topic. Asking the question is itself unlawful. You may not inquire into, or require any statement or certification of, the immigration or citizenship status of a tenant, a prospective tenant or an occupant. Refusing someone on grounds of citizenship, immigration status, primary language, national origin or ancestry is housing discrimination, with damages that start at a statutory floor and run to punitive damages and attorney's fees. Disclosing someone's immigration status to pressure them out of the home carries statutory damages measured in multiples of the monthly rent.

What you may still do is verify who you are dealing with and whether they can pay: ask for whatever documents you need to verify identity and financial qualifications, apply the same criteria to everyone, and comply with federal law or a court order if one actually requires something of you. If you operate in another state that does restrict foreign ownership, do not carry that state's application form or lease addendum into California.

title: Veterans: Protection, Not Incentives
bodyText:
California offers a private landlord no payment, tax credit, damage guarantee, risk-mitigation fund or pilot programme for renting to a veteran. If you have come from a state that runs one, there is nothing of that kind to apply for here.

What California does instead is protect. Veteran or military status is a protected class in housing, meaning a member or veteran of the United States Armed Forces, the Armed Forces Reserve, the United States National Guard or the California National Guard. You may not refuse, charge more, offer worse terms, advertise a preference against, or end a tenancy on that basis, and you may not ask about it at the application stage. The protection extends to someone you merely perceive to be a veteran or service member and to someone associated with one, so a question about a spouse's deployment is the same violation.

The HUD-VASH voucher is the practical overlap and the one to get right: it is named in the definition of protected source of income, so refusing a tenant because their rent comes partly from a HUD-VASH voucher breaches the source-of-income rule as well as the military-status rule, and your income test must be measured against the tenant's own share of the rent. Note that a unit let to a voucher holder, HUD-VASH included, is carved out of the unbundled-parking obligation. Separate protections apply to a tenant on active duty, including lease termination on deployment - those are not an incentive to you but you need to know they exist.

title: Staff in Senior Housing: No Work Card
bodyText:
California requires no work card, permit, registration, clearance or certification for people who work in senior or 55-and-over housing. There is no state register of senior-housing staff and no card for a manager, caretaker or maintenance worker to hold. If you run age-restricted rental housing here, your staff obligations are the ordinary employment ones.

What California does regulate closely is the housing itself, because age-restricted housing is an exception to the ban on age discrimination and you carry the burden of proving you qualify. A senior citizen housing development means a development built, substantially rehabilitated or substantially renovated for senior citizens with at least 35 dwelling units. Qualifying residents are 62 or older, or 55 or older in such a development. Beyond that, people who were living with a qualifying resident before that person died, went into hospital or was absent for a long period, or on divorce, can stay on if they were 45 or older or were a spouse, cohabitant or primary source of support, and a disabled child or grandchild who needs to live there also qualifies. Removing a formerly disabled resident takes six months' written notice. For buildings put up from 2001 onwards there is a list of design features - wide doorways and paths, railings, lighting, step-free access, a common room and open space, and easy refuse collection - that creates a presumption the development meets seniors' needs.

Practical course: treat the 35-unit floor and the age thresholds as the gate, keep records proving them, and screen staff under the ordinary employment rules rather than looking for a card that does not exist in California.

title: Renting to Students: The Dormitory Line
bodyText:
California has no licence, registration or certification for private housing let to students, and no lease content it requires you to include. If you rent apartments to students, you are an ordinary residential landlord and the whole of California's landlord-tenant law applies to you unchanged.

The one student-specific rule in California statute is an exemption, and it is narrower than its name suggests. Dormitories owned and operated by an institution of higher education, or by a school running kindergarten through grade twelve, are outside both the statewide just-cause rule and the statewide rent cap. Note all three limbs: it must be a dormitory, and it must be both owned and operated by the institution. A privately owned building let to students, a privately owned building master-leased by a university, and purpose-built student accommodation owned by an investor are none of them within the exemption. So if you run off-campus student apartments, you are subject to the rent cap and to just-cause termination once a tenant passes twelve months, unless another exemption applies (a certificate of occupancy within fifteen years, for example), and the end of an academic year is not by itself a reason to recover possession.

Two other things to know. Fair-housing law lets a postsecondary institution, public or private, reserve housing for male or female students so long as nobody is denied equal access, and reserve separate housing mainly for married students or students with minor dependants - that permission belongs to the institution and not to you. And a joint lease with several students is simply a joint tenancy: get every occupant on the lease and make them jointly and severally liable, because no California statute lets you treat a student household as anything special.

title: Keeping a Tenant's Information Private
bodyText:
California has no single statute requiring a landlord to keep tenant information confidential. Instead it has several targeted duties, two of them absolute.

Where a tenant gives you documentation of abuse or violence - to change the locks, end the tenancy early, or defend an eviction - you may not pass any of it to a third party unless the tenant consents in writing or the law or a court order requires it. There is no business-need exception and none for your insurer or lawyer, though checking with the professional who signed it is not disclosure. Separately, you may not disclose a person's immigration or citizenship status to harass them, retaliate, push them out or get possession; a court that finds you did must order statutory damages of six to twelve times the monthly rent per person, plus legal fees, and the right cannot be waived. Disability and accommodation information is confidential too, under fair-housing rules.

If computerised personal information you hold is taken by someone unauthorised, you must tell every affected California resident, in writing headed "Notice of Data Breach" under five prescribed headings, within 30 calendar days of discovering or being told of the breach. You may take longer only for law enforcement, or to determine the scope and restore the system. If the data belongs to someone else, you must tell them immediately instead. If one breach means notifying more than 500 California residents, you must also send the Attorney General a sample copy of the notice within 15 calendar days.

Where a rent-registration authority asks for a tenant's name, what you supply is confidential in the agency's hands, and it cannot compel more than the name. Otherwise no statute read here sets a consent rule for ordinary tenant information or for a landlord reference. Cautious course: share payment and tenancy information only with written consent, with agents who need it, or when the law requires; and never volunteer abuse, immigration or disability information.

title: Records You Must Keep, Give and Explain
bodyText:
California imposes no rent-ledger duty on a landlord. Nothing requires you to keep a running account, give a tenant a payment history on request, attach one to a nonpayment notice, or answer a records request. Nor did this review find a statute requiring you to retain tenant applications for any period - the four-year retention rule you may have heard of is an employment rule and covers your staff files, not your tenants'.

What California does require is bound up with screening reports, and these duties are easy to miss. If you order an investigative background report on an applicant - the kind that reports on character, general reputation, personal characteristics and mode of living - you must notify the applicant in writing within three days of first requesting it, naming the agency and summarising the applicant's inspection rights, and you must give them a way to tick a box asking for a copy. If you then deny the application, or charge them more than you advertised, because of such a report, you must tell them so and give them the agency's name and address. A credit report has its own rule: you must give the applicant a copy within seven days of getting it, and refund any unused part of the screening fee.

Two reporting points. Screening reports may not include an eviction case the tenant won or that settled, nor most adverse items more than seven years old, nor medical debt - so if a vendor hands you one of those, do not act on it. And if you own five or more units in an assisted housing development, you must offer tenants rent reporting to a credit bureau. Keep an accurate ledger anyway: in a nonpayment case you have to prove what was owed. And if you hold names with Social Security, driver's licence or bank account numbers, you must keep them reasonably secure, and any vendor you share them with must agree by contract to do the same.

title: Unlawful Use Ends the Lease by Itself
bodyText:
If a tenant uses the home for an unlawful purpose, or maintains, commits or permits a nuisance there, California law terminates the lease for you. You do not have to rely on a lease clause and you do not have to give the tenant a chance to put it right: on three days' notice to quit you are entitled to possession. The same limb covers assigning or subletting contrary to the lease and committing waste. Some conduct is deemed a nuisance by name, including using the property for dogfighting or cockfighting, and the deemed list is narrower than it looks - see the separate guidance on nuisance evictions.

This is the strongest termination route California gives a landlord, and the reason to know it is that the alternative is weaker. If you instead treat the conduct as breaking a lease covenant, you must serve a three-day notice to perform or quit, counted excluding Saturdays, Sundays and judicial holidays, and the tenant can save the tenancy by performing - unless the broken covenant cannot be performed after the event.

Three cautions. Once a tenant has been in occupation twelve months you also need a just cause, and unlawful purpose and nuisance are each on the list - but get any part of that procedure wrong and the notice is void, so state the cause in the notice. You may not charge the tenant a fee for serving it. And fair-housing law is not suspended: public-nuisance enforcement is protected only so long as it is non-discriminatory, so a policy that falls hardest on a protected group is still open to challenge. Nothing here reaches transient hotel or motel occupancy. Document the use with dates and evidence before you serve anything, because you will have to prove it.

title: Keeping a Tenant's Abuse Documentation Confidential
bodyText:
Two separate California statutes make what a tenant gives you about abuse or violence confidential, and both work the same way. You may not pass any of it to a third party unless the tenant consents in writing, or the disclosure is required by law or by a court order. One rule covers everything the tenant gives you when ending the tenancy early because of abuse or violence. The other covers everything the tenant gives you when relying on the protection against being evicted or not renewed over it. Between them they reach the tenant's written notice, the restraining or protective order, the police report, the counsellor's or caseworker's statement, and anything else handed over.

There is one thing you are free to do. If the tenant supplies a statement signed by a qualified third party, contacting that third party to check what the statement says is not a disclosure. Verify with the signer and no one else: not the other residents, not a neighbour, not the person named as having caused the abuse, and not a landlord or employer ringing for a reference.

Getting this wrong is expensive. A landlord who breaches the early-termination section, confidentiality included, owes the tenant actual damages plus statutory damages of $100 to $5,000, and those remedies sit on top of every other remedy the law gives. You also may not refuse to rent to someone, or refuse to keep renting to them, just because they once used these rights.

Practical course: keep these papers out of the general tenant file, let only the person who must act on them see them, do not attach them to a notice or a court filing unless the law or a court requires it, and say nothing to other residents who ask.

title: You May Not Evict Over the Abuse Itself
bodyText:
You may not terminate a tenancy, or fail to renew one, because of an act of abuse or violence against your tenant, a member of the tenant's immediate family, or a member of the tenant's household, once the tenant has given you documentation of it. The bar covers non-renewal as well as eviction, so quietly letting a lease run out is not a way round it.

There are exactly two exceptions. The first is where the person who committed the abuse is a tenant in residence of the same unit - someone actually living there with full physical and legal access. The second needs both halves: that person's words or actions must have threatened the physical safety of other tenants, guests, invitees or licensees, and after you serve a three-day notice requiring your tenant not to voluntarily permit or consent to that person's presence on the premises, the tenant must go on permitting it. Note who that notice goes to. It is served on your tenant and asks the tenant to stop letting the person in. Serving it on the perpetrator achieves nothing.

If you get it wrong, your tenant has an affirmative defence in the eviction. Where the perpetrator does not live in the unit, that defence is complete and the cause of action fails. Where the perpetrator does live in the unit, the court takes a different route and can remove that person alone without ending the tenancy.

Two points run your way: your other tenants cannot sue you for complying, and you may still evict on any ground that has nothing to do with the abuse.

title: Changing the Locks After Abuse or Violence
bodyText:
California gives you two lock-change duties, and which one applies turns on one question: does the person who caused the abuse live in the same unit?

If that person is not a tenant of the unit, the tenant may ask you in writing and attach any one of the accepted forms of proof - a protective order, a police report, a counsellor's statement in the statutory form, or any other document that reasonably verifies the abuse, which can be the tenant's own signed statement. You then have 24 hours from the request plus the proof to change the locks at your own expense and hand over a key. The tenant chooses which document to give; you cannot insist on a court order.

If the person is a tenant of the same unit and a court has ordered them out, the trigger is tighter: the tenant gives you a written request with a copy of a court order excluding that person, issued within the last 180 days. Again, 24 hours, your expense, and a key.

Miss the 24 hours and the tenant may change the locks without your permission, whatever the lease says, if the lease was signed on or after 1 January 2011. You must then reimburse the cost within 21 days, provided the tenant used locks of similar or better quality, fitted them properly, told you within 24 hours and gave you a key. Locks here means any exterior lock giving access to the dwelling.

Excluding a co-tenant this way does not release them from rent, and a court can order the same lock change at the end of an eviction.

title: What Documentation You Must Accept, and From Whom
bodyText:
California does not let you set your own evidence standard. Each of the abuse-and-violence protections carries its own list of documents, and the tenant picks from the list.

Four routes recur. A temporary restraining order, emergency protective order or protective order from the family, civil-harassment, criminal or probate-conservatorship courts. A written report by a peace officer acting officially, stating that the tenant, an immediate family member or a household member has filed a report alleging they are a victim. A statement from a qualified third party - a sexual-assault counsellor, a domestic-violence counsellor, a human-trafficking caseworker, a victim-of-violent-crime advocate, or a licensed physician, nurse, psychiatrist, psychologist, clinical social worker, marriage and family therapist or professional clinical counsellor - in the two-part form the statute prints, with the tenant's part and the third party's part. Where a counsellor, caseworker or advocate signs, it must be on their organisation's letterhead. And a catch-all: any other document that reasonably verifies the abuse.

Watch the differences. For the eviction protection, an order or a police report must have been issued or written within the last 180 days. For an early termination, the tenant's notice must reach you within 180 days of the order, the report or the act. For a lock change where the abuser lives in the unit, the court order must be within 180 days. The lock-change list for an outsider has no freshness limit and says in terms that the tenant's own signed statement will do.

Do not demand more, do not ask for the police file, and do not reject a form because you would have preferred another.

title: Where California's Domestic Violence Law Sits, and One Citation to Watch
bodyText:
California's domestic violence law has not moved. It is the Domestic Violence Prevention Act, Division 10 of the Family Code, and the tenancy statutes reach into it rather than defining anything themselves. Domestic violence means abuse against a spouse or former spouse, a cohabitant or former cohabitant, a dating or engagement partner, a co-parent, a child of a party, or anyone related within the second degree. The orders you will actually be shown come from that division: an emergency protective order, a temporary restraining order, a protective order after hearing, and in particular an order excluding a person from a dwelling. The tenancy statutes also accept civil-harassment restraining orders, criminal protective orders, and juvenile or elder-abuse orders.

From 1 January 2027 the definition widens. A 2026 act adds a party subjected to a forced marriage, or an attempted one, to the list of people against whom abuse counts as domestic violence, and adds a definition of forced marriage. Every tenancy protection that borrows the definition - the early-termination right, the eviction bar, both lock-change duties, the screening protections and the ban on penalising calls for help - widens with it automatically on that date. Until then the narrower list applies.

One citation deserves a check before you rely on it. The section protecting a tenant's right to call for help lists the sexual-offence statutes by number, and one of those numbers was renumbered in 2019, while the early-termination section uses the new number. The conduct is the same, so don't read the older list as narrower. If a dispute turns on which sexual offence is covered, take advice rather than reading the older list literally.

title: No Key-Control Rules: It Is All Your Own Policy
bodyText:
No California statute tells you how to run keys. There is no rule requiring a key-control policy at any size of building, no rule about securing or logging master keys, no rule about recovering keys from staff or departing tenants, no duty to rekey between tenancies, and no housing statute requiring background checks on employees or contractors who can get into units. Key control is therefore entirely your own policy, and the only statutory hooks are elsewhere.

Those hooks matter. You must install and maintain an operable dead bolt on each main swinging entry door, window security devices on openable windows, and code-compliant locks on common-area doors in multifamily buildings; a tenant must tell you when one stops working, and you are not liable until you have had notice and a reasonable time. Separately, you may have to change the locks within 24 hours and hand over a key when a tenant gives you abuse documentation or an exclusion order. And holding a key is not a right to use it: entry is confined to the statutory purposes with written notice, and a significant and intentional breach of the entry rules, done to pressure the tenant to leave, is treated as harassment carrying a penalty of up to $2,000 per violation.

What to do: keep master keys locked and logged, issue keys to staff and contractors for a stated job and get them back, rekey or change locks between tenancies as a matter of policy, record every key you issue, and treat an unaccounted-for key as a reason to change the lock. If you screen staff, remember the employment rules on conviction history apply - they are not housing rules, so take advice.

title: Smart Locks: a 2026 Duty Most Landlords Do Not Know They Have
bodyText: California has no landlord-tenant statute about smart locks, keypads or app-based entry - no installation rule, no disclosure duty, no limit on the access logs you keep. What it has instead, from January 1, 2026, is a duty hidden in the Business and Professions Code that applies to whoever runs the account, and if you issue your tenants app logins for a connected lock, that is you. The law calls whoever administers those accounts an account manager, and if you can add or remove a tenant's access yourself that is almost certainly you - a landlord who merely hands over a vendor's app and controls nothing has an argument, but not a safe one. It gives a survivor of domestic violence, stalking, sexual assault or human trafficking the right to send you a device protection request to cut a named person's access to the device or the account. You must let them submit it through secure remote means that are easy to navigate, and you must not demand documentation beyond what the statute lists. Then a clock starts: within two business days you either terminate that person's access and confirm it to the survivor, or tell them clearly how to reset the device to a state that removes all account holders. You may not charge a fee, raise the rate, ask the other account holder to approve it, refuse because the account is in arrears, or tell the person being cut off. Information the survivor gives you is confidential and must be securely destroyed within 90 days. A waiver is void, and the exposure is real: up to $2,500 per device, plus costs and the tenant's attorney's fees.

title: Barring a Non-Tenant From the Property
bodyText:
You can bar someone from your rental property, and California's trespass law gives you more than one route.

The main one: a person who refuses or fails to leave land, buildings or structures you own or lawfully occupy and that are not open to the general public commits a misdemeanour, once asked to leave either by you or your agent, or by a police officer acting at your request. You must make a fresh request to the police each time you want their help, with two exceptions. A single notarised request on the agency's own form can cover a fire-hazard period, or a period while you are away, up to the shorter of a locally set period and twelve months; and a separate notarised request can cover up to twelve months where the property is closed to the public and posted as closed. Either way, tell the agency in writing when you no longer need the help, and know that the request lapses if the property changes hands or the person in lawful possession changes. The request may be filed electronically where the local government accepts that.

A second route is stronger but narrower: once someone has been convicted of a crime committed on your property, a single notice stays in force until you rescind it, for two years after a misdemeanour conviction, five after a felony, and without limit after a violent felony.

Two carve-outs bind you. Lawful labour-union activity and constitutionally protected activity are excluded. And a tenant's own invited visitor is not a trespasser just because you would rather they were not there.

title: The One Inspection California Gives You, and Its Trap
bodyText:
California gives you a single statutory inspection of an occupied home, and it is the tenant's to ask for, not yours to impose: the initial inspection before move-out.

The duty starts with you. Within a reasonable time after either side gives notice to end the tenancy, or before a fixed term runs out, you must tell the tenant in writing that they may request an initial inspection and that they may be present at it. That written notice has to carry the statutory paragraph about reclaiming abandoned personal property. If the tenant does not ask, your duty is discharged.

If the tenant does ask, the inspection happens no earlier than two weeks before the end date, at a mutually convenient time if one can be agreed. Give at least 48 hours' prior written notice of the date and time; the two of you may waive that, but only by both signing a written waiver. Go ahead whether or not the tenant turns up, unless they withdrew the request.

Then the trap. You must give the tenant an itemised statement of the repairs and cleaning you propose to charge the deposit for, reproducing the four statutory grounds for deductions, handed over at the inspection or left in the unit. If the unit was clear enough for you to see what needed doing, you cannot later charge the deposit for anything you failed to list. The tenant then has until the tenancy ends to cure the listed items.

None of this applies where you are ending the tenancy for non-payment, breach or nuisance.

title: Police at the Property: What You Must and Must Not Do
bodyText:
No California statute requires you, as a landlord, to cooperate with law enforcement, to report a crime on your property, to hand over tenant records, or to let officers into a unit or the common areas. But two reporting duties bind you as any person. If you reasonably believe you have seen the murder or rape of a child under 14, or a forcible lewd act on one, you must notify a peace officer; failing to is a misdemeanor punishable by up to six months in jail and a $1,500 fine, and relatives of the victim or offender and anyone who reasonably fears for their own or their family's safety are exempt (Cal. Penal Code § 152.3). And if you know of a death that occurred without medical attendance, after an injury or accident, by suspected suicide, or where a crime is reasonably suspected, as when a tenant is found dead in a unit, you must notify the coroner immediately; not doing so is a misdemeanor (Cal. Health & Safety Code § 102850). Actively concealing an accidental death is a separate crime (Cal. Penal Code § 152). Child-abuse and elder-abuse reporting is mandatory only for listed professions and caretakers; anyone else may report (Cal. Penal Code § 11166(g); Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code §§ 15630(a), 15631(a)). Nor does any statute protect you if you volunteer something you should have kept back. What California regulates is the other direction: how you treat a tenant who calls for help, and what you may reveal.

A lease term that prohibits or limits anyone's right to summon law enforcement or emergency assistance - for a victim of abuse, a victim of any crime, or a person in an emergency - is void. You may not impose or threaten a fee, fine, penalty, termination, non-renewal or worse terms because help was summoned, and that holds even where the caller was not your tenant. The tenant needs no paperwork to show the belief that help was needed, and any waiver is void.

Here is the trap. If you file an eviction within 30 days of anyone summoning help, on a notice treating the call as a lease breach or a nuisance, the tenant is presumed to have made out the defence and the burden shifts to you.

Information a tenant gives you about abuse or violence is confidential, and you may not disclose anyone's immigration status to any agency to pressure a tenant or recover possession.

Cautious course: answer a subpoena, warrant or court order; otherwise get written consent, log each request and what you gave, and admit officers to an occupied unit only on a warrant, the occupant's consent or a genuine emergency.

title: Drug-Free Lease Terms: No Statute, Three Mechanisms
bodyText:
California has no drug-free housing addendum. No statute requires one, authorises one, prescribes its wording or gives you a special remedy for drug activity in a private tenancy. If you want a drug-free term, it is an ordinary lease term and it is worth having, because the statutory routes are narrower than they look.

Three mechanisms exist. First, a tenant who maintains or permits a nuisance on the premises, or uses them for an unlawful purpose, terminates the lease by that act, and you may serve a three-day notice to quit with no right to cure. Second, where the just-cause rules apply, criminal activity by the tenant on the property is at-fault just cause, as is using the premises for an unlawful purpose - but note it must be the tenant's own criminal activity. Third, there is a controlled-substance eviction procedure driven by a city prosecutor, and it operates only in the City of Los Angeles.

Cannabis is the point most often got wrong. State law legalising adult use expressly preserves the ability of a private property owner to prohibit or restrict that conduct on their own property - which means a cannabis ban works only if your lease says so. Put it in writing, and say whether it covers smoking, vaping and cultivation.

One limit binds every such term: you may not enforce it against someone because they are a victim of abuse, violence or crime, or because help was summoned.

title: No Emergency-Contact Rule, but You Must Be Reachable
bodyText:
No California statute requires you to collect an emergency contact from a tenant, and none requires you to give the tenant an after-hours or 24-hour emergency number of your own. What the law does require is identification, and it is lease content. The lease must disclose the name, telephone number and usual street address for personal service of each person authorised to manage the premises, and of the owner or the person authorised to accept service of process and to receive notices and demands; it must also give the name, telephone number and address of whoever rent is paid to. That information has to be kept current, and it binds a successor. A successor owner or manager who has not complied cannot serve a three-day rent notice or evict for rent that fell due during the non-compliance.

So the state makes sure the tenant can reach you. It says nothing about you reaching anyone on the tenant's behalf. If you want an emergency contact, ask for one on the application or in the lease, and be clear about two things. Naming a contact gives that person no right to enter the unit, take possession or remove anything; if the tenant dies or vanishes you deal with the personal representative, and the abandoned-property rules decide the belongings. And the contact's details are personal information about someone who is not your tenant: collect only what you need, keep it with the tenant file and use it only for emergencies.

Good practice: give every tenant a written number to call for fire, flood, gas or a loss of water or power, and keep it current alongside the identification the lease already carries.

title: No Duty to Report an Absence, So Put It in the Lease
bodyText:
California imposes no duty on a tenant to tell you about an extended absence, and no statute requires the lease to contain such a term, sets a threshold number of days, or gives you a remedy if the tenant simply disappears for a month. You also get no statutory right to enter while a tenant is away: being absent is not one of the grounds for entry, and an empty-looking unit is not an abandoned one.

Because nothing forbids it, you may add an absence-notice term, and in California it earns its place for a reason that has nothing to do with inspections. Before you can serve a notice of belief of abandonment you need rent unpaid for at least fourteen consecutive days and a reasonable belief that the tenant has gone. A lease term requiring notice of an absence over a set number of days, and a tenant who said nothing, is evidence going to that belief. The same applies to the entry ground that opens up once a tenant has abandoned or surrendered.

Keep it modest. Pick your own threshold - the law gives you none - require the notice on or before the first day, and limit your remedy to actual damages caused by a deliberate failure to tell you.

Two limits. An absence is never by itself a reason to end a tenancy, and where the just-cause rules apply you still need a ground. And never enforce it against a tenant who is away because of abuse, violence or a crime: that is protected, whatever the lease says.

title: Guests: No Statutory Right, With Four Exceptions
bodyText:
California gives a tenant no statutory right to receive guests. No section says a tenant may have visitors, bars a guest fee, caps overnight stays, or stops you from writing a guest rule into the lease. The one guest-fee rule in the codes applies to mobilehome parks, not to dwellings. So your guest policy is a lease term, and reasonable limits on the length of a stay, on parking and on common-area use are yours to set.

Four things you cannot do with it. First, you may not shut out a tenants'-rights visitor: a person who comes onto residential property at an occupant's invitation, in reasonable hours or an emergency, to give information about tenants' rights or to take part in a tenants' association cannot be treated as a trespasser, and retaliating because a tenant organised is separately unlawful. Second, you may not penalise a tenant because anyone - guest included - summoned police or emergency help for a victim of abuse or crime or a person in an emergency, and a lease term limiting that right is void. Third, you may not hold against an applicant that they or a guest once called for help. Fourth, where a guest is the person causing abuse, the route is the statutory three-day notice asking your tenant not to let them in, not an eviction over the abuse itself.

One point runs your way: relocation benefits after an order to vacate are not payable where the tenant's own guest or invitee caused or substantially contributed to the condition.

title: Every Duty California Puts on a Tenant
bodyText:
California has no single list of tenant duties with its own penalties. What it has is a scatter of obligations, most of which work as a shield for you rather than a sword, and one that bites hard.

The care duties: keep the part of the home you occupy clean and sanitary, dispose of rubbish properly, use the electrical, gas and plumbing fixtures properly and keep them clean, neither damage the place nor let a visitor do so, and use rooms only for what they were designed for. These are drafted as conditions on your repair duty, not as free-standing promises. Your repair obligation falls away only where the tenant is in substantial violation and that violation contributes substantially to the dilapidation or substantially obstructs your repair. Two of them - cleanliness and rubbish - stop applying altogether if you agreed in writing to do them, so bundling cleaning or trash service quietly disables that defence. A separate rule makes the tenant repair deterioration caused by their own want of ordinary care, and a tenant whose own fault caused the condition loses the repair-and-deduct remedy.

The reporting duties: tell you about an inoperable dead bolt or window device, an inoperable smoke alarm, and an inoperable or deficient carbon monoxide device. Until you have notice you are not in breach.

The cooperation duty: cooperate with a bed-bug inspection and give the pest control operator the information it asks for.

And the one with teeth: refusing to allow a lawfully authorised entry is at-fault just cause for eviction.

title: Can the Lease Add a Way to Give Notice?
bodyText:
California has no general rule letting you and your tenant agree on an extra way to give a notice the law requires. There is no provision saying a text message, a tenant portal post or an email counts as notice because the lease says so. Work from three rules instead.

First, where a statute names the method, that method is the method. The three-day notices and the 30-, 60- and 90-day notices each carry their own service rules, and a lease term substituting a different route does not satisfy them. Second, a lease provision by which the tenant gives up a right to a notice required by law is void, so an agreed method can only ever sit alongside the statutory one - never replace it. Third, electronic delivery is possible, but only on terms you do not control: both of you must actually have agreed to transact electronically, that agreement cannot be buried in a paper lease and cannot be made a condition of renting, the tenant can refuse to go on electronically, and an electronic record can never be substituted for an unlawful-detainer notice.

What works: serve by the statutory method every time, and treat any agreed email or text as a courtesy copy that proves the tenant knew. Where the Legislature has allowed an agreed route - emailing the deposit itemisation, electronic delivery of a pesticide notice to an address the tenant gave you - take it in writing and keep the paper route running too.

title: How to Serve a Notice in California
bodyText:
For an unlawful-detainer notice - pay or quit, perform or quit, quit - there are exactly three ways to serve it, in order. Hand it to the tenant. If the tenant is away from both home and work, leave it with someone of suitable age and discretion at either place and mail a copy to the tenant's home. If you cannot find out where the tenant lives or works, or nobody suitable is there, post it conspicuously on the property, hand a copy to anyone living there if you can find one, and mail a copy to the property. Serve a subtenant the same way. Nail-and-mail is the last resort, not the first.

For a notice ending a periodic tenancy you get a fourth option: the same three methods, or a copy by certified or registered mail. A notice changing the terms of a month-to-month tenancy uses the three unlawful-detainer methods.

Mailing costs you time. Where a notice period is fixed by statute, service by mail extends it by five calendar days within California, ten elsewhere in the United States, twelve to the Secretary of State's address-confidentiality programme and twenty outside the country. Build that in.

You may not email, text or post to a portal in place of an unlawful-detainer notice: the electronic-transactions law expressly forbids substituting an electronic record for it. And you may never charge the tenant a fee for serving, posting or delivering any notice. Keep a dated proof of service for every notice you give.

title: Put Every Notice in Writing
bodyText:
California's default is that a contract may be oral unless a statute requires writing - but every notice that matters in a tenancy is one of the exceptions. A notice changing the terms of a periodic tenancy must be in writing. A notice ending a periodic tenancy, from either side, must be in writing. A three-day notice to pay rent or quit, or to perform a covenant or quit, must be in writing. A rent-increase notice must be in writing. A 24-hour notice before entry must normally be in writing, with two narrow exceptions: you may give oral notice, in person or by telephone, to show the unit to buyers, and only if you first told the tenant in writing within the preceding 120 days that the property is for sale; and you and the tenant may agree orally on an entry for agreed repairs or services, fixing the date and approximate time, within one week.

So never rely on a conversation. An oral notice to quit or to change a term is simply no notice, and a court will treat the tenancy as unchanged.

Two points cut the other way. Your tenant can trigger the repair-and-deduct remedy by oral notice, so a telephone complaint starts your clock even though your own notices must be written. And you may rent on an oral agreement, but if you do you must hand the tenant a written statement within fifteen days giving the owner and manager details, where rent is paid and the forms of payment you take. Writing protects you; put it in writing even where the statute does not say so.

title: What Else Must Go in Your Notice to Vacate
bodyText:
A California notice ending a periodic tenancy is not just a date. Every notice you give to end one must also carry, in substantially the statutory form, a paragraph telling the former tenant that state law lets them reclaim abandoned personal property left at the old address, that costs may apply depending on storage and delay, and that acting quickly keeps those costs down. Use the statute's words. Leave the paragraph out and you have handed the tenant an argument that the notice is defective.

A three-day notice to pay rent or quit carries a different load: the amount due, and the name, telephone number and address of the person to whom rent is to be paid, with the usual days and hours that person is available if payment may be made in person - or instead a bank account number with the institution's name and street address, which must be within five miles of the property, or a reference to an electronic transfer procedure already in place.

Where the just-cause rules reach your property, the notice must also state the cause, and a no-fault cause brings its own relocation obligations.

Two things you may not do. You may not charge the tenant any fee for serving, posting or delivering the notice. And California has no provision letting you start work on the unit while a notice runs - the tenancy continues until possession ends, so the unit must stay habitable and you still need proper notice to enter.

title: Changing a Term Other Than Rent
bodyText:
For a tenancy from week to week, month to month or any shorter period, you can change the terms by written notice alone - you do not need the tenant's agreement. For a month-to-month tenancy the change takes effect no sooner than 30 days after notice; for a shorter period, after a period at least as long as the rental period itself. Serve it the way an unlawful-detainer notice is served. The lease may cut the 30 days to seven, but only if you and the tenant agreed that in writing, and then the notice must be given at least seven days before the end of a term and takes effect when that term ends.

The mechanism is powerful. Once served, the notice by itself makes the new terms part of the lease if the tenant stays on after it takes effect. You do not need a signature or a new lease.

Three limits. Rent is not covered - a rent increase has its own notice tiers and its own two service methods, and any change that increases what the tenant pays should be treated as a rent increase. Where a statute, regulation, recorded regulatory agreement or contract sets a longer notice period, use it, and check your local ordinance too. And you cannot use this route to end a tenancy or to add a term the law forbids: a change the law would void in a lease is just as void in a notice.

A smoking ban for a tenant already in place is subject to the same rules for changing terms: in a periodic tenancy it needs this notice, and a fixed-term lease cannot be changed by notice before the term ends.

title: Giving the Tenant a Copy of the Lease
bodyText:
You must give the tenant a copy of the rental agreement within fifteen days of the tenant signing it. Once in every calendar year after that, if the tenant asks, you must give another copy within fifteen days. If you do not have the agreement or a copy, you must instead hand over a written statement saying so, together with the owner and manager details, where and to whom rent is paid and the forms of payment you accept. If the tenancy is oral, the same written statement is due within fifteen days of the agreement. A new owner or manager has fifteen days from taking over to comply.

Failing to give the copy is not, by itself, a defence to enforcing the lease. The consequences are different and sharper. A successor owner or manager who has not complied cannot serve a three-day notice for rent, or evict for nonpayment, for rent that accrued while out of compliance - though the tenant still owes it. Whoever signed the agreement on the owner's behalf without complying becomes the owner's agent for service of process, for performing the owner's obligations and for receiving rent in cash, by check, by money order or in any form you have accepted before. And the tenant may serve you by registered or certified mail at the address where rent is paid.

If a licensed broker or property manager gets the tenant's signature, that licensee must also deliver a copy as soon as reasonably practicable. Deliver at signing and log the date.

title: What a California Lease Must Contain
bodyText:
California has no single section listing what a lease must say, and nothing requires the start and end dates on the first page. The requirements are scattered, and four of them put text inside the lease document itself.

First, the agreement must disclose the name, telephone number and usual street address for service of each person authorised to manage the property and each owner or person authorised to act for the owner; to whom and where rent is paid, with the usual days and hours if paid in person, or a bank account with an institution within five miles, or the details for electronic transfer; and the forms of payment you accept.

Second, where the rent-cap and just-cause rules apply, the statutory notice must appear in the lease, in an addendum, or in a separate notice the tenant signs, in at least 12-point type. If the property is exempt, the exemption statement belongs in the rental agreement itself.

Third, if you have banned smoking anywhere on the property, every lease signed with a new tenant must include a provision specifying where smoking is prohibited.

Fourth, a tenant's undertaking to repair or maintain the unit only works if it is part of the consideration for the rental - so write it into the lease, not a side letter.

Fill every blank, use the statute's exact words where it dictates them, and remember that a lease negotiated in one of five languages must be translated in full before signing.

title: No Statute Makes the Tenant Initial Anything
bodyText:
No California statute requires a tenant to initial any part of a residential lease. There is no provision saying a particular clause is unenforceable unless initialled, and none requiring a separate signature next to a term. The two Civil Code sections that do demand a separately signed or initialled provision are about contracts to buy and sell real property, not leases, and the third is an arbitration provision in a purchase contract.

One formatting rule in the leasing law comes close, and it is about placement rather than initials: if the lease automatically renews or extends when the tenant stays on or fails to give notice, that provision must appear in the body of the lease in at least eight-point boldface, and a recital that the lease contains such a provision must appear in at least eight-point boldface immediately before the place where the tenant signs. Get that wrong and the renewal term is voidable by whoever did not prepare the lease - which is the tenant.

Initial anyway. Have the tenant initial each page, and separately initial any term that is unusual or that limits their rights: a fee, an optional addendum, a pet or smoking rule, a prescribed statutory notice. Initials are not a cure for an unlawful term - a void term stays void - but they are good evidence the tenant saw the page, and they close off the argument that something was buried. Keep the signed original and give the tenant a copy.

title: You May Treat Month-to-Month Differently
bodyText:
California has no parity rule between lease types. No statute forbids terms that are more burdensome for a month-to-month tenant than for a fixed-term one, or the reverse, and nothing caps the difference in rent between the two. So you may charge a month-to-month premium, offer a discount for a twelve-month commitment, or make a term, a fee or a pet rule available on one footing and not the other.

What you cannot do is use lease type as a proxy. Fair housing still applies to the whole bargain, so a difference that falls on families with children, on voucher holders, or on any other protected group is a fair-housing problem whatever label you put on it. And several local ordinances regulate rent and just cause in ways that may constrain the gap - those are not resolved here and you need to check your city.

Note also that California's own protections mostly do not turn on lease type. The just-cause and rent-cap rules key off how long the tenant has lived there, not whether the lease is fixed or periodic. The deposit cap does not vary with the term. Two places do turn on it: the rules for changing terms and for ending a tenancy by notice apply only to periodic tenancies, and the duty to translate a lease negotiated in one of five languages applies only where the term is longer than one month - so a pure month-to-month tenancy escapes it.

title: Type Size: No Rule for the Whole Lease, Several for Parts
bodyText:
California sets no minimum type size for a residential lease as a whole, and nothing makes a small-print lease inadmissible in evidence. But it sets floors for particular passages, and the penalties for missing them are substantive rather than evidentiary - which is worse.

Two matter most. An automatic renewal or extension provision must appear in the body of the lease in at least eight-point boldface, with a recital that the lease contains such a provision in at least eight-point boldface immediately before the signature line; miss either and the renewal term is voidable by the tenant, and the fallback is a month-to-month renewal on the old terms. And where the rent-cap and just-cause rules apply, the statutory notice must be in no less than 12-point type; failure to comply with any part of that section makes the termination notice void.

Other floors sit in the disclosures you deliver with the lease - the bed-bug notice and the water submeter disclosure at 10-point, the flood-hazard disclosure at 8-point.

Practical approach: do not try to meet each floor separately. Set the whole lease and every attached disclosure in 12-point or larger, and put the automatic-renewal text and its recital in boldface at the places the statute names. That satisfies every floor at once and removes the argument that a term was unreadable. Keep a copy showing the type size you actually used.

title: Plain Language: California Asks for Translation, Not Simplicity
bodyText:
Nothing in the sections we read sets a readability standard for a California lease. There is no reading-grade test, no requirement to divide and caption the lease by sections, no dollar threshold below which a stricter form applies, and no official who must approve your form. A long, dense lease is not unlawful for being long and dense.

What California requires instead is language access, and it bites hard. If you negotiate the tenancy primarily in Spanish, Chinese, Tagalog, Vietnamese or Korean - orally or in writing, whatever the tenant's stated preference - and the term is longer than one month, you must give the tenant, before signing, a translation of the lease in that language covering every term and condition, plus a notice in that language at the time and place of signing. The English text still governs, but the tenant can rescind the lease if you did not comply, and any waiver of the duty is void. The exception is narrow: the tenant negotiated through their own adult interpreter, fluent in both languages and not supplied by you.

Two other levers reach an incomprehensible lease without any readability statute. A term can be struck as unconscionable, and whole categories of lease term are simply void by statute. So the practical standard is: write short sentences, use the statute's own words where it dictates them, and translate in full where those five languages are in play.

title: No Front-Page List of the Terms Against the Tenant
bodyText:
Some states make a landlord print, near the front of the lease, a statement listing every term that restricts the tenant or waives a tenant right, sometimes with an option to have the form pre-approved by the attorney general and an exclusion for high-value contracts. Nothing we found in California does any of that. There is no statement of consumer restrictions, no schedule of waivers, no pre-approval route and no dollar threshold.

California's answer to the same worry is blunter: instead of making you list the terms that go against the tenant, it makes many of them void. A lease provision by which the tenant gives up the deposit or entry protections, the right to sue you later, a notice or hearing required by law, procedural rights in litigation, or your duty of care is void as against public policy. Other statutory-right waivers are void unless the lease was presented before the tenant took possession. And any waiver of the habitability rules is void as to any condition that makes the unit untenantable.

So a front-page list would not save a bad term. Two front-of-lease obligations you do have, though, are real: where the rent-cap and just-cause rules apply, the prescribed notice must be in the lease, an addendum or a signed notice, in at least 12-point type; and an automatic-renewal provision needs a boldface recital immediately above the signature line. Put both where the tenant cannot miss them.

title: When a Lease Has to Be in Writing
bodyText:
A lease for longer than one year is invalid unless it, or a note or memorandum of it, is in writing and signed by the party you want to hold to it. If an agent signed for that party, the agent's authority must itself be in writing and signed by the party. The same rule catches any agreement that by its terms cannot be performed within a year of being made, and any agreement employing a broker or agent to lease real estate for longer than a year for a commission. Separately, an estate in real property other than an estate at will or a term not exceeding one year can be transferred only by a signed written instrument.

A lease of a year or less may be oral. That is the general contract rule in California: contracts may be oral unless a statute says otherwise. But an oral tenancy still triggers your duty to hand the tenant a written statement of the owner, manager and rent-payment details within fifteen days.

Two traps. A text message or instant message - anything of an ephemeral nature not designed to be retained - cannot by itself make a contract to convey real property without a conforming written confirmation. And writing is not the end of it: a lease for a term exceeding one year is void against a later good-faith purchaser or mortgagee who records first, unless you record the lease. If the term runs past a year, record a memorandum of it.

title: How Long a Lease California Allows
bodyText:
California caps the length of a lease by the kind of land, not by the kind of tenant. A lease or grant of any town or city lot reserving rent or service of any kind is invalid if it provides for a period over 99 years. A lease or grant of land for agricultural or horticultural purposes reserving rent or service is invalid beyond 51 years. For an ordinary urban or suburban rental, 99 years is the ceiling, and nothing in these rules touches a normal one-year or month-to-month tenancy.

Formalities are lighter than in several other states. There is no seal requirement - California abolished every distinction between sealed and unsealed instruments - and no statute requires the owner to sign personally or to grant a written power of attorney beyond the ordinary rule that an agent signing a lease over a year needs written authority.

One formality does catch owners out. If the property is community property of a married couple, both spouses must join in signing any instrument leasing it for longer than one year, personally or through a duly authorised agent. A lease signed by the spouse who holds record title alone is presumed valid in favour of a lessee who took in good faith without knowing of the marriage, and an action to avoid it must be brought within one year of the instrument being recorded. Do not rely on either: get both signatures on any lease over a year, and check title before you sign.

title: Code Editions Move; Your Lease Cannot Freeze Them
bodyText:
California does not freeze a building standard at a fixed edition, and no statute lets a lease fix one either. The state's standards must impose substantially the same requirements as the most recent editions of seven named model codes, and if the state has not adopted a new edition by regulation, the newest edition counts as adopted one year after it is published. Local amendments take effect 180 days after the state code is published. So the edition that governs your building can change during a tenancy, and a lease clause saying the code "as it existed at signing" applies does nothing - the obligation is statutory, and waivers of the habitability rules are void as to any condition that makes a unit untenantable.

Two things do protect existing buildings. Construction standards are not applied backwards to a building already approved or built, though maintenance, use and change-of-occupancy standards are. And on alteration and repair, the rules must permit you to replace, keep and extend the original materials and go on using the original methods of construction, so long as the building complies with the published standards or an approved local alternative and does not become or stay substandard.

One timing point worth knowing: from 1 October 2025 to 1 June 2031 a city or county generally cannot make its own changes to the residential standards, with narrow exceptions including home hardening and emergency standards. Check the current edition with your building department before any work, and keep the permit records showing which edition your building was built to.

title: No Truth-in-Renting Handbook to Hand Out
bodyText:
California has no truth-in-renting law. There is no state handbook or rights-and-responsibilities guide you must give a tenant, no agency-published statement of tenant rights to attach to the lease, and no statute that voids a lease term just because it misstates the law or attaches a penalty for printing a misleading one. If you have seen a "tenant rights handbook" for California, it is guidance, not a delivery duty.

What California does instead is stronger in one direction and weaker in another. Stronger: rather than requiring you to tell the tenant their rights, it voids the terms that take them away. A provision by which the tenant waives the deposit or entry protections, a future cause of action, a notice or hearing required by law, procedural rights in litigation, or your duty of care is void as against public policy, and any waiver of the habitability rules is void as to a condition making the unit untenantable. A misleading clause is therefore unenforceable without anyone having to prove it misled.

Weaker: there is no single notice that tells the tenant the rules. The closest thing is the rent-cap and just-cause notice, which must be in the lease, an addendum or a signed notice in at least 12-point type where those rules apply.

Practical course: do not print terms the law voids - they gain you nothing and invite a challenge - and deliver each specific disclosure California does require.

title: When a Tenant May Walk Away Early Without Your Agreement
bodyText:
California gives a tenant several statutory routes out of a lease that you cannot bargain away, so treat an early departure as a legal question rather than a breach you can assume.

Four routes matter most. First, if you do not, within a reasonable time after the tenant asks, put and keep the tenant in quiet possession, put the home into good condition, or repair it, the tenant may end the lease. Second, if a condition that makes the home unfit is not repaired within a reasonable time after notice, the tenant may move out and is discharged from rent from the day of vacating - but only twice in any twelve months, and not where the tenant or a household member caused the condition. Third, a tenant, or a household member, who is a victim of abuse, violence or a crime may end the tenancy on the statutory notice with qualifying documentation, and the law caps what you can collect. Fourth, a servicemember called to qualifying duty has federal and state rights to terminate.

There are narrower ones too: if you let one room as a dwelling to more than one household, every tenant in the building stops owing you rent while that double letting continues; and if your lease renews automatically unless the tenant gives notice, the renewal term is voidable by the tenant unless it is set out in the bold, repeated form the statute demands.

Two things California does not give the tenant: a general right to cancel for a change of mind or job, and a right to cancel because you misrepresented something, which is governed by ordinary contract and fraud law instead. If you want a buy-out, it has to be an agreed lease term.

title: Fire, Flood and Quake: You Get No Termination Right of Your Own
bodyText:
California gives the tenant a casualty exit and gives you none. If the home is destroyed, the tenancy ends by itself - no notice, no election, nothing to serve. If it is damaged but not destroyed, the tenant may end the lease where the destroyed part was the greater part or was what induced the tenant to rent; you are left with the repair duty and, where the just-cause rules apply, with a statutory ground or nothing.

So do not write a clause saying you may terminate after a flood, fire, earthquake or storm and rely on it. Nothing authorises it, a waiver of the tenant's unfitness rights is void, and where the just-cause rules apply a notice that does not match a listed ground is void outright. A clause of that kind is worth little and may cost you the notice.

What to do instead, in order. Decide honestly whether the home is destroyed or merely damaged, and record it with photographs and a contractor's assessment on the day. If it is destroyed, the tenancy is over and your job is the deposit accounting and the return of rent paid for time you cannot deliver. If it is damaged, repair it, and if the tenant cannot live there meanwhile, say in writing that rent is not running for that period rather than waiting to be asked. If you intend to demolish rather than repair, that is a separate route with its own written notice and its own penalties for getting it wrong. And check your local ordinance first: several cities add relocation payments and their own just-cause grounds after a disaster.

title: Illness, Incapacity and Moving Into Care
bodyText:
California has no general rule letting a tenant end a lease because of illness, infirmity or a move into assisted living, and none letting you end one for those reasons either. A tenant who becomes too unwell to stay is, in principle, still bound by the lease, and the family will often ask you to release them. You are free to agree, and a short written surrender agreement settling the move-out date, the rent to that date and the deposit is almost always the better outcome than an argument you will win slowly.

Two narrow rules do exist. Where the tenancy runs at the pleasure of either party - an ordinary month-to-month - it ends on notice to the other party of a party's death or incapacity to contract. So if a month-to-month tenant loses legal capacity and you are given notice of it, the tenancy ends on that notice; a fixed-term lease is not ended by incapacity at all. And if you operate a nursing or convalescent home on a month-to-month basis, the tenancy ends on the patient's death, rent stops that day, and any advance rent must go back to the estate within two weeks; you cannot contract out of that.

Two cautions. Illness and disability are protected characteristics, so never use a tenant's condition as a reason to end or refuse to renew a tenancy, and handle a request to be released, to transfer units or to have a live-in aide as a reasonable-accommodation request. And if your city has a rent or just-cause ordinance, senior and disabled tenants often have extra protection there.

title: When a Tenant Dies
bodyText:
A tenant's death does not end a fixed-term lease in California. It ends a month-to-month tenancy only when notice of the death is given to the other side, and then it ends on that notice. So on a fixed term the estate stays liable for the rent for the balance of the term, subject to your duty to credit what you could reasonably have avoided; on a month-to-month, work from the date notice reached you and prorate.

Do four things, in this order. Make sure the home is secure and document its condition, but do not clear it out: the belongings are the estate's, not yours. Find out who is handling the estate - an executor, an administrator, or for a small estate a relative acting on a sworn affidavit - and deal in writing with that person only, because paying a deposit to the wrong relative does not discharge you. Follow the ordinary left-behind-property procedure for anything in the unit, writing to the person you reasonably believe owns it as well as to the tenant's address. And account for the deposit to the estate on the usual timetable, treating the estate as the tenant.

Two special cases. If a surviving co-tenant or a lawful occupant remains, the tenancy continues as to them and this is not a vacancy. If you run a nursing or convalescent home on a monthly basis, the hiring ends on the patient's death, rent stops that day and advance rent goes back to the estate within two weeks.

California does not make you collect a contact person, and does not give one any authority. Ask for one anyway.

title: Tenancies at Will, and Why You Probably Do Not Have One
bodyText:
California recognises a tenancy at will and gives it its own exit: the landlord ends it by written notice, served the same way as any notice to quit, allowing not less than 30 days, with the period stated in the notice. But you will rarely be in that position, because the law pushes an open-ended letting into a periodic tenancy instead.

If you let a home or lodgings without agreeing a term, the term is presumed to be whatever period you use to reckon the rent - rent set monthly means a monthly tenancy - and if nothing was agreed about either length or rent, the tenancy is presumed monthly. If a tenant stays on after a term ends and you accept rent, you are presumed to have renewed on the same terms for the same period, capped at one month where rent is monthly and at one year in any case. So accepting a payment after the term expires is a decision, not a formality: it renews.

The practical consequences are three. Work out which kind of tenancy you have before you draft a notice, because the periodic-tenancy notice rules, not the 30-day at-will rule, will usually be the ones that bind you, and they are longer for a tenant of a year or more. If your lease gives you a right of re-entry, the ordinary three-day notice applies to it - except where the letting had no agreed term and you ended it under the month-to-month route instead. And where the just-cause rules apply, no notice of any kind works without a stated ground.

title: No Seasonal or Vacation Tenancy Category
bodyText:
California has no seasonal tenancy. There is no summer-let category, no resort or vacation-rental tenancy with shorter notices, and no rule that a letting for part of the year escapes the residential landlord-tenant statutes. If you rent a dwelling for three months over a season, you have an ordinary fixed-term residential tenancy and every duty that goes with it: habitability, the deposit cap and accounting, entry limits, the notice rules, and the demolition and other pre-signing disclosures.

The only line California draws is between a tenancy and genuine transient occupancy. A guest in a hotel, motel or residence club whose stay is subject to the local transient occupancy tax is not a person who hires, and the residential chapter does not reach them.
