That exclusion is about the nature of the establishment and the tax, not about the season or the length of the stay, and it cannot be manufactured: in a residential hotel you may not make an occupant move out or check out and re-register before 30 days' occupancy in order to keep them transient, and doing so carries a penalty and the tenant's legal fees.

So plan a short season let as a tenancy. Use a fixed term with real start and end dates, keep the deposit inside the cap, and remember that a tenant who stays on and pays after the end date is presumed to have renewed. If you are running something closer to a hotel, check your city's short-term-rental ordinance and its transient occupancy tax before you rely on the exclusion.

title: Possession, Money, or Both: Choosing Your Remedy
bodyText:
In California the possession case and the money case are different cases, and the order you bring them in decides what you can collect.

The eviction action gets you possession, the rent found due where the case is for non-payment, and up to $600 on top if the detainer was malicious. It does not get you the rest of the term. Nothing in the abandonment and damages sections affects the eviction statutes, and bringing an eviction does not cost you a separate action for the larger damages - but you cannot recover twice for a loss already decided on the merits.

Two mechanics are worth knowing. If the tenant hands back possession before trial, or before judgment where there is no trial, the eviction becomes an ordinary civil action; to claim damages beyond what the eviction could award, you must first amend the complaint and serve it like a fresh summons and complaint. And once you take possession under an eviction judgment, the option of keeping the lease alive and suing for rent as it falls due is gone, unless the tenant gets relief from forfeiture.

For the money itself, small claims is open to a landlord but it is narrow: an individual may claim up to $12,500, a company or other entity only up to $6,250, and nobody may file more than two claims over $2,500 anywhere in the state in a calendar year. Above that, or if you want the balance of the term, you are in the regular court.

One trap: if the tenant prepaid more than a month and asks in writing for notice, you must report the re-letting within 30 days.

title: What You Can and Cannot Contract Out Of After a Casualty
bodyText:
The short answer: the tenant's unfitness rights are off limits, the mitigation credit is off limits, and almost everything else about casualty is a drafting question with one real opportunity in it.

You cannot take a waiver of the tenant's repair rights for any condition that makes the home unfit to live in; such an agreement is void. There is one exception, and it is useful: you and the tenant may agree that the tenant will improve, repair or maintain all or stated parts of the home as part of what the tenant gives for the tenancy. It has to be part of the rent bargain, not a bare duty added on.

You cannot contract out of the credit for rent you could reasonably have avoided. When a tenant breaches and leaves, your damages are reduced by the loss the tenant proves you could reasonably have avoided, and no clause changes that. Two related points work in your favour: your efforts to re-rent do not waive your damages claim, and the balance of the term after judgment is recoverable only if your lease says so - so put that recital in. But if you re-rent before judgment instead, your recovery on that route is subject to any limits your own lease sets, so do not cap yourself by accident.

As for the destruction rule itself, no statute says it may be waived. Treat it as unwaivable in a dwelling lease unless you presented the lease before the tenant took possession, and even then do not rely on it. Also check whether a renewal clause has to be in bold type to bind the tenant.

title: If the Property Is Taken for Public Use
bodyText:
California's constitution allows private property to be taken or damaged for a public use only when just compensation, set by a jury unless that is waived, has first been paid to the owner or into court; the Legislature may let the condemnor take possession earlier by depositing the probable compensation in court. State and local government may not take an owner-occupied residence in order to hand it to a private person, subject to listed public-health and crime-prevention exceptions.

For your tenancy, start from two ordinary rules. A hiring ends when the thing hired is destroyed, and when a hiring ends early the tenant pays the proportion of the rent for the use actually had, unless that use was merely nominal and of no benefit. So a total taking that ends the tenancy also ends the rent, and you prorate to the date possession goes.

The Eminent Domain Law then sets the lease rules. If all the leased property is taken, the lease ends. If part is taken, the lease ends for that part and its share of the rent stops, and either you or the tenant may ask the court to end the whole lease if an essential part is taken or the rest no longer suits the lease's purpose. The lease ends when the condemnor takes title or is authorised to take possession, whichever is first, not when a notice arrives, so don't tell a tenant their lease is over before then. The tenant keeps any right to compensation for the leasehold. All of this gives way to what your lease itself says about a taking, so a condemnation clause is worth having.

Practically: get the condemnor's notice and timetable in writing, tell the tenant at once in writing what is happening and who to pay, keep paying attention to the just-cause rules if you serve any notice, and take advice on apportionment before you agree any division of the award. Relocation payments may also be due to the tenant.

title: Foreclosure: What Happens to Your Tenant, and to You
bodyText:
If the lender forecloses, your tenant does not simply lose their home. A month-to-month tenant must be given 90 days' written notice to quit before being removed. A tenant on a fixed-term lease entered into before title transferred at the sale keeps possession to the end of the term, and all the rights and obligations under the lease survive the foreclosure - unless the buyer will live there as a primary residence, or the tenant is the borrower or the borrower's child, spouse or parent, or the lease was not at arm's length, or the rent is substantially below market without a subsidy. The buyer carries the burden of proving the lease is not protected, and 90 days' notice is still required. None of this displaces a local just-cause ordinance.

The older rule still sits behind that: after a sale on execution, a judicial foreclosure or a trustee's sale, a holdover occupier can be removed on three days' notice, but a residential tenant gets notice at least as long as the rental period, capped at 30 days. Treat 90 days as the operative figure for a residential tenancy.

Two things catch landlords and buyers out. A sale of a one-to-four-unit home is not final for 15 days, extended to 45 if a tenant in occupation signals an intent to bid, because a qualifying tenant has a statutory chance to buy. And a new owner or manager must give the tenant the statutory ownership and rent-payment details within 15 days, and until it does it cannot serve a three-day rent notice or evict for rent that accrued during the gap.

title: Converting or Withdrawing Rental Housing
bodyText:
California protects your right to stop being a landlord, and then regulates how you do it. No public body may force you to offer, or keep offering, residential property for rent - the narrow exception being certain older residential-hotel rooms in the largest cities. But in a city with rent control, the ordinance may require you to give the city notice of your intention to withdraw, under penalty of perjury, listing the units, the tenants and the rents, and to record a memorandum of it. Where it does, withdrawal takes effect 120 days after that notice reaches the city.

The long stop matters: a tenant who is at least 62 or disabled and has lived there a year before your notice may extend their tenancy to a full year from the notice, provided they tell you in writing within 60 days. You then have 30 days to tell the city of the claim, and 90 days from your original notice to tell the city and the tenants of any other tenancy you elect to extend. During an extension the tenancy continues on the same terms and neither side is released from the lease.

Two limits. Going out of business does not override local land-use control over converting housing to condominiums or to non-residential use, or over demolition; and if a tenant is sued, they may defend by showing you did not comply.

Separately, if you are applying for a demolition permit you owe written notice to current and prospective tenants, with real money consequences for failing. And converting to condominiums brings its own notices. Each tenant must get written notice of intention to convert at least 60 days before the tentative map is filed, and 180 days' written notice before a tenancy ends because of the conversion. Rent and your repair duties carry on through those 180 days. Each tenant also gets an exclusive right to buy their unit on the public terms or better, for at least 90 days from the public report. If the lease was negotiated in Spanish, Chinese, Tagalog, Vietnamese or Korean, every conversion notice must be in that language. Miss a notice and the city can't approve the final map.

title: No Cold-Weather Notice Rule, and No Winter Eviction Bar
bodyText:
California has nothing on cold weather. There is no rule requiring a tenant to warn you before vacating in winter so the pipes can be drained, no rule requiring you to keep the heat on in an empty unit, and no seasonal moratorium stopping you from ending a tenancy or evicting between set dates. Whatever month it is, the ordinary notice rules and, where they apply, the just-cause rules are the whole story.

That means two practical things. First, if freezing matters in your location - the mountains, the high desert, the far north of the state - you have to put it in the lease yourself, because no statute supplies it. A short term works: require the tenant to tell you in writing before an absence of more than a set number of days, to keep the heat at a stated minimum in freezing weather while they are away, and to report a leak or a loss of heat at once. Pick your own figures; the law gives you none. Keep the remedy to actual damages caused by a deliberate failure.

Second, do not let that clause do more work than it can. You cannot charge a fee for serving any notice. You cannot make an absence a ground for ending the tenancy. You cannot use it against a tenant who is away because of abuse, violence or a crime. And you still owe a working heater: that duty is yours whatever the lease says, and a failed heating system in January is a habitability problem, not a tenant problem.

title: Telling Your Tenant About a Proceeding Against the Property
bodyText:
California puts no general duty on you to tell a tenant that the property is in trouble. There is no statute requiring you to disclose a pending foreclosure, a tax default, a lawsuit, a receivership or a code-enforcement case, and the one pre-lease foreclosure disclosure that used to exist was repealed years ago.

In several of those situations the news reaches the tenant without you. When a notice of sale is posted in a foreclosure, the lender's side must post and mail a prescribed notice to the resident telling them what a new owner may and may not do. When an enforcement agency orders a building vacated because conditions endanger health and safety, the agency itself notifies the tenant of their entitlement to relocation money - and you are the one who has to pay it, on a short clock tied to the vacate date. And the duty actually runs the other way for court papers: a tenant who receives notice of a proceeding to recover the property must tell you at once, hand over the written notice, and is liable to you for the damage caused by not doing so.

Where you do owe a notice, it is specific, not general. Applying for a demolition permit triggers a written notice to current and prospective tenants with penalties attached. Withdrawing the building from the rental market triggers the Ellis Act machinery where your city has adopted it. And a new owner or manager must give the ownership and rent-payment details within 15 days.

The cautious course: tell the tenant in writing, early, about anything that will affect their possession or where rent goes. Silence is not a defence to a misrepresentation claim.

title: How Long You Have to Sue for Rent and Damages
bodyText:
Work from the writing. An action on a contract, obligation or liability founded on a written instrument must be brought within four years, so a signed lease gives you four years from the breach to sue for unpaid rent, damage beyond the deposit, or the balance of the term. If the tenancy was oral, you are down to two years. The same four-year clock covers a book account, an account stated and a balance on a mutual, open and current account whose items are in writing - useful where you ran a ledger rather than suing on the lease itself.

Two hard edges. Once the four years have run you must not sue, start an arbitration or begin any other proceeding to collect the debt; and the period can be extended only by an acknowledgment or promise in writing, signed by the tenant. A part payment counts only on a promissory note, and no payment revives a claim once it is barred. So a tenant's token payment on rent doesn't reset the clock.

Separate from all this is the eviction clock, which is much shorter and catches landlords out: a three-day notice to pay rent or quit may be served only within one year after that rent became due. Older arrears are still a debt you can sue for, but they cannot found the notice.

Practically: diary four years from the end of the tenancy for a written lease, sue for everything in one action rather than in instalments, and do not let an arrears ledger drift past a year before you serve a notice.

title: When a Tenant Files for Bankruptcy
bodyText:
A bankruptcy filing is governed by federal law, and federal law is where your answer comes from. Two consequences matter.

First, do not write a clause making bankruptcy, insolvency or an assignment for creditors an event of default, and do not act on one if your form already has it. A term that ends the lease or forfeits the tenancy merely because the tenant filed is the classic unenforceable ipso facto clause under federal bankruptcy law. California adds nothing to save it and has no statute of its own making a tenant's bankruptcy a ground for anything.

Second, know the one California rule in this area, because it is unusually favourable and easy to miss. A writ of possession issued on an eviction judgment must be enforced without delay even though you have received notice that the tenant has filed a bankruptcy - except as to collecting money. So a judgment for possession already in hand does not simply evaporate when a petition is filed. The exception is important: anything aimed at the money, including the rent judgment, is a different matter, and the mobile-home and manufactured-housing situations are carved out.

Practically: if a tenant tells you they have filed, stop all collection activity at once and take advice before serving any notice or filing anything; do not change the locks; keep accounting for the deposit in the ordinary way; and treat rent falling due after the filing as a separate question from the arrears. Where you already hold a possession judgment, proceed on it only with advice, because the federal stay rules are detailed and the penalties for getting them wrong fall on you.

title: Confession of Judgment Is Abolished, Not Merely Unavailable
bodyText: Do not put a confession-of-judgment clause, a cognovit note, or any term by which the tenant agrees in advance that judgment may be entered against them, in a California lease. Since January 1, 2023 a judgment by confession is unenforceable and may not be entered in any superior court. That is a flat abolition, not a set of conditions you could satisfy: the statute does not distinguish consumer from commercial, residential from business, or represented from unrepresented, and the chapter that once set out how to take such a judgment - the acknowledgement, the attorney's certificate, the statement of indebtedness - has been repealed down to this single sentence. Only judgments obtained or entered before that date are untouched. Three consequences for your lease. A clause purporting to authorise one buys you nothing, because no court may enter the judgment. It is also affirmative evidence of overreach in front of a judge weighing the rest of your lease, and California separately voids any term by which a tenant waives procedural rights in litigation or a notice or hearing required by law. And it will not shortcut an eviction in any event: possession of a dwelling comes only through an unlawful detainer, with its own notice, service and judgment requirements, and a stipulated judgment negotiated after a dispute has arisen is an entirely different thing from a confession signed at the outset.

title: No Prescribed Parking-Rules Notice, but New Large Buildings Must Unbundle
bodyText: California does not make you deliver parking or towing rules to a tenant before signing, does not dictate a heading or type size for them, does not limit how you change them mid-term, does not limit the vehicle information you may ask for, and does not tie a parking permit to the lease term. Your parking rules are an ordinary lease term, so change them the way you change any other term of a periodic tenancy: written notice of a change of terms, and no change at all during a fixed term without the tenant's agreement. Two real constraints apply instead. First, if the building got its certificate of occupancy on or after January 1, 2025, has 16 or more units and sits in Alameda, Fresno, Los Angeles, Riverside, Sacramento, San Bernardino, San Joaquin, Santa Clara, Shasta or Ventura County, off-street parking must be priced and papered separately from rent, in an addendum or its own agreement, for the life of the property, with tenants getting first refusal of the spaces; several affordable and voucher properties are excluded. Non-payment of that parking charge can never support an eviction, though you may revoke the space after the 45th day. Second, the towing rules are signage and authorisation rules, not lease rules: a clause saying you may tow earns you nothing unless the statutory sign is up at every entrance. Check your city's own parking ordinance as well.

title: Pet Deposits, Pet Rent and the One-Month Cap
bodyText: California has no pet-specific deposit or fee cap, and that is the point: every up-front pet charge falls inside the ordinary security deposit limit instead. A pet deposit, a pet fee, a pet cleaning charge, anything you collect at the start of the tenancy by any name, counts as security. So the pet money plus the ordinary deposit together cannot exceed one month's rent, or two months' rent if you are a natural person, or an LLC whose members are all natural persons, who owns no more than two rental properties with no more than four units between them, and the tenant is not a service member. You may not call any of it non-refundable, and a lease that does is unlawful on its face. Monthly pet rent is a different animal: it is rent, not security, and no statute caps the starting figure, so set it as you like and collect it monthly rather than up front. Because it is rent, adding or raising it during a tenancy is treated as a rent increase, subject to the rent cap and the notice rules where they apply. Never charge a pet deposit, pet rent, extra security, insurance or any other fee for an assistance animal, and apply no breed, size or weight limit to one. Never require a tenant to have an animal declawed or devocalized, never advertise in a way that discourages applicants whose animal is not, and never make occupancy turn on it: a prosecutor can seek $1,000 per advertisement or per animal.

title: No State Pet Fact Sheet, but a Pet-Policy Duty Starts April 1, 2027
bodyText: California publishes no pets-and-eviction fact sheet and does not make you hand a tenant any pet pamphlet with the lease. Nothing changes about that today. What does change is bigger, so plan for it now: from April 1, 2027 your written pet policy or pet addendum becomes a disclosure you owe every applicant. From that date you must have the policy in writing, give a written copy with every rental application (electronically if the application is electronic), leave a space on the application for the applicant to acknowledge receiving it, and provide a link or other electronic access to it on the property's website, in digital advertising you control, and in what you send to rental search engines where the platform supports a link. A policy that bans pets outright still counts as a pet policy and must be published the same way; if you set no pet rules at all, the policy must say so. The policy has to describe, in plain language, the rights, responsibilities and requirements of pet-owning tenants. You may amend it for future applicants only, and must honour the version in force when the application was handed over. If you charged an application fee without disclosing the policy and the applicant therefore drops out or becomes ineligible, you must refund the fee within seven business days of a written request. None of this forces you to allow pets.

title: You Cannot Write Yourself In To Care For a Tenant's Animal
bodyText: California gives you no right to enter a dwelling to feed, water, care for or remove a tenant's animal, and unlike most states you cannot fix that with a lease clause. The entry grounds are a closed list - emergency, necessary or agreed repairs and services, showing the unit, a deposit inspection, abandonment or surrender, a court order, water submetering, and a balcony inspection - and any lease provision by which the tenant waives or modifies those entry rights is void as against public policy. So the advance-consent clause that works in other states does not work here: do not ship one, and do not rely on an emergency-contact nomination as if it were entry authority. Three routes remain. If an animal is genuinely in distress, that is an emergency and you may enter without notice on that footing alone, so document what you saw and what you did. Otherwise call animal control, a humane society officer or a peace officer: an officer must take possession of a stray or abandoned animal and provide care, and must seize immediately where prompt action is needed to protect the animal or others, with the cost becoming a lien on the animal. If the tenancy has ended and the unit is vacated, the abandoned-property procedure does not apply to animals at all; they go to the animal authorities instead. Ask tenants for a caretaker's name as useful information, not as permission.

title: California Does Give You a Lien on an Apartment Tenant's Property
bodyText: California is unusual: keepers of furnished and unfurnished apartment houses, apartments, cottages and bungalow courts have a statutory lien on a tenant's baggage and other property of value on the premises, for rent, accommodation, services, meals, extras requested and money advanced, plus the cost of enforcing the lien. Hotel, motel, inn, boarding house and lodging house keepers have a parallel lien. Do not get excited. The lien is enforceable only after final judgment in an action you bring for those charges, so it is a collection tool, not a self-help tool, and it never licenses changing locks or holding belongings hostage. While the case is pending you can take possession of the property only on a court order, granted after a motion on ten days' written notice to the tenant, only if you show by affidavit that the property is about to be destroyed, substantially devalued or removed, and only after filing an undertaking with sureties the court approves. The order lets you enter peaceably - with a key or passkey or through an unlocked door, between sunrise and sunset - and you then owe the duties of a paid custodian. Anything exempt from enforcement of a money judgment is outside the lien entirely, which strips out most household goods. If the judgment is unpaid 30 days after it becomes final you may sell at public auction after published and mailed notice. For property simply left behind after a tenancy, use the abandoned-property procedure instead.

title: Which Appliances You Can Leave Out of the Lease
bodyText: California has no rule presuming that an appliance standing in the unit is yours unless the lease says otherwise, so list what you supply and the list governs. But two appliances cannot be excluded at all. For any lease entered into, amended or extended on or after January 1, 2026 you must supply a working stove that can safely generate heat for cooking and a working refrigerator that can safely store food; both are habitability characteristics now, and an appliance under a manufacturer or government recall is not safe, which you must put right within 30 days of notice of the recall. There is one narrow opt-out and only for the refrigerator: if the tenant asks to bring their own, the lease must carry the statutory acknowledgment word for word and give the tenant a 30-day written-notice route back to one you supply, you may not make the tenancy conditional on it, and you are then off the hook for maintaining their unit. There is no equivalent opt-out for the stove. Four property types are exempt from both: permanent supportive housing, single-room occupancy units, residential hotel units, and units in facilities with shared or communal kitchens, including assisted living. Everything else - dishwasher, washer, dryer, microwave, air conditioner - is yours to include or leave out, but once you list it you have promised to maintain it.

title: Carpet Cleaning Is Not a Charge You Can Make Automatic
bodyText: A lease term requiring the tenant to pay for professional carpet cleaning at move-out, or a standing carpet-cleaning deduction, is unenforceable in California. You may charge for professional carpet or other professional cleaning only where it is reasonably necessary to return the unit to the condition it was in when the tenancy began, leaving out ordinary wear and tear - so the charge has to be justified unit by unit, not by policy. You may never charge for ordinary wear and tear or its effects, for conditions that pre-dated the tenancy, or for the cumulative effects of wear across one or more tenancies, so a carpet worn thin by ten years of ordinary use is your cost, not the tenant's. Work by a contractor, by you, or by your employee is limited to a reasonable amount necessary to restore the unit. California sets no carpet age or useful-life table and no ten-year carpet rule, and no statute lets you unlock a move-out charge by having the carpets professionally cleaned before move-in - that condition exists in other states, not here. Practical course: photograph the carpets at move-in and again at move-out, offer the pre-move-out inspection, and if you deduct, send the invoice and the photographs with the itemised statement. A tenant cannot waive any of this in the lease, and a bad-faith retention exposes you to twice the deposit on top of actual damages.

title: Home Businesses: One Carve-Out You Cannot Write Around
bodyText: California gives tenants no general right to run a business from a rented home, so a residential-use-only clause does the work for ordinary cases - consulting, remote work, a craft sold online - subject to your city's zoning, which is where any real limit lives. There is one exception, and it is absolute. A licensed family child care home cannot be restricted at all: every provision in a written instrument that purports to restrict the leasing of property for use as a family daycare home is void, and so is every restriction on using or occupying the property that way. Restriction there means a restriction imposed orally, in writing or by conduct, and it includes an outright prohibition. You also may not refuse to rent to someone because they are a family daycare provider. So read your own residential-use-only and no-commercial-use clauses as already carrying that exception, whether or not they say so, and never enforce one against a licensed provider. What survives is everything about noise, lease violations and nuisance, which the statute expressly leaves alone, plus your right to require an increased security deposit once a daycare home starts operating, and your written consent for the expanded capacities. Food businesses may have their own carve-outs: cottage food operations and microenterprise home kitchen operations sit in chapters this review could not reach, so take advice before enforcing a lease term against one.

title: A Tenant May Run a Licensed Child Care Home, and You Cannot Say No
bodyText: A tenant who holds a licence may operate a family child care home in your rental and no lease term can stop it. Any provision restricting the leasing of the property for that use is void, as is any restriction on using or occupying it that way, and restriction covers something imposed orally, in writing or by conduct, prohibition included. You may not refuse to rent to someone because they are a family daycare provider, whether the property is a detached house, a townhouse, a unit inside a dwelling or a unit in a multifamily building where the zoning allows residential use. The use counts as residential and as a use by right for every local ordinance, and it is not a change of occupancy for building code purposes. What you keep: a prospective provider living in a rental must give you 30 days' written notice before starting, you may require an increased security deposit once operation starts or once you learn of it - more than you ask of other tenants, but still within the statutory deposit limit - and the expanded capacities need your written consent, up to eight children in a small home and up to fourteen in a large one. The provider must carry liability insurance of at least $100,000 per occurrence and $300,000 aggregate, or a $300,000 bond, or keep signed parent affidavits instead; if insurance or a bond is carried, ask in writing to be named an additional insured. Noise, nuisance and ordinary lease enforcement are untouched.

title: No Hunting or Fishing Rights Come With a California Lease
bodyText: California gives a tenant of land no hunting or fishing rights, and no statute reverses that if the owner stays silent. Nothing passes with the tenancy, so if a tenant wants to hunt or fish on land you let, that has to be written into the lease or a separate licence, and you should say expressly that no hunting, shooting or fishing right is granted if you do not want one implied. The point that matters in practice runs the other way. The trespass statute lets permission come from the owner, the owner's agent, or the person in lawful possession - and a tenant in possession is that person. So your tenant can lawfully give a third party written permission to enter cultivated or fenced land, or posted unenclosed land, even though you did not consent. The same is true of the request to leave that triggers a trespass, the written permission to build a fire on posted land, and the consent needed to drive a vehicle on land not open to the public. If you want to keep control of who comes onto the land, reserve it in the lease: take the shooting and fishing rights to yourself, require your written consent before the tenant admits anyone for those purposes, and say who may post the signs. Also note that a tenant's own hunting on your enclosed land can create liability if an animal belonging to someone else is killed or injured.

title: Cannabis: You May Ban It, and Your Smoking Policy Already Does Half the Work
bodyText: Adults 21 and over may lawfully possess up to 28.5 grams of cannabis, up to eight grams of concentrate, and up to six living plants, and may smoke or ingest it. None of that binds you. Proposition 64 expressly left private property owners free to prohibit or restrict any of the conduct it permits on their own property, so you may ban cultivation, ban smoking and vaping, and even ban possession outright in the lease. Two mechanics are worth knowing. First, the permission to smoke cannabis is withheld anywhere tobacco smoking is prohibited, and smoking there includes vaping and heated devices - so a no-smoking policy adopted under the landlord smoking statute removes the cannabis permission in the same areas without you writing a word about cannabis. If you adopt one, the lease must specify where smoking is prohibited, and changing an existing tenancy is a change of terms needing written notice. Second, the rule stopping cities from banning indoor home cultivation is a limit on local government, not on you. California gives medical-cannabis patients no housing protection, and no statute shields a cardholder from a lease term - but the law on whether a disability accommodation can ever compel it is unsettled, so take a written medical request through your accommodation process instead of refusing on the clause. Cannabis is still federally illegal, which matters if your property is federally assisted.

title: No California Rule on Firearms in a Rental
bodyText: California says nothing about firearms in a residential lease. No statute bars you from restricting firearms, no statute makes such a restriction unenforceable against someone with a carry licence, no statute protects a tenant's possession against the lease, and there is no parking-lot rule protecting a firearm locked in a tenant's vehicle - the employer parking-lot statutes that exist in other states have no California counterpart. So a firearms term is an ordinary lease term: you may include one, leave it out, or deal with firearms only through the general rules on nuisance, disturbance and unlawful activity, which already reach reckless storage, threats and any discharge. If you do want a restriction, three cautions. Draft it as a requirement to comply with state and federal law plus specific storage obligations, rather than a flat ban, because a flat ban is hard to enforce and invites a fight you do not need. Keep it out of the disability and accommodation space. And remember your general rules already give you a ground to act on actual danger, which is what you usually care about. Check your city and county too: local firearm ordinances are common in California and are not resolved here. Where a tenant is the subject of a restraining order, the firearm relinquishment rules in that order operate independently of your lease.

title: A Lease Clause Banning Solar Is Probably Void
bodyText: California has no statute that creates a tenant's right to install a portable solar panel by name - but it has a far blunter provision that very likely reaches your lease. Any covenant, restriction or condition in a contract or other instrument affecting any interest in real property that effectively prohibits or restricts the installation or use of a solar energy system is void and unenforceable. A lease is a contract affecting an interest in real property, and the statutory definition of a solar energy system is wide: any solar collector or device whose primary purpose is collecting, storing and distributing solar energy for electricity or heating, designed to serve one utility retail customer on the property, together with racking, mounting, awnings, canopies and patio covers, on the ground or on a building. A tenant's balcony or plug-in panel serving their own unit fits that description. What survives is reasonable restriction, not prohibition: a restriction is reasonable only if it does not significantly increase cost or decrease efficiency, and for photovoltaic systems 'significantly' means more than $1,000 over the system's cost as proposed or a drop of more than 10 per cent in efficiency. No California case has applied this to a residential tenancy, so treat it as a real risk rather than a settled rule. Practical course: do not write a flat ban. Require written notice, a licensed installer, compliance with permits and codes, no penetration of the roof or structure without consent, removal and restoration at the end, and proof of liability cover.

title: Running an EV Charger: You Are Not a Utility, but You Are a Reseller
bodyText: Operating or offering electric-vehicle charging at your property does not make you a public utility. The statute says so twice over: a facility supplying electricity to the public only to charge light-duty plug-in electric vehicles is not a public utility for that reason alone, and an electrical corporation does not include someone distributing electricity through private property solely for their own use or their tenants' use and not for sale to others. So you need no certificate and no rate approval. What you do have is a resale problem. If your building takes service on a master meter and you bill tenants for electricity through submeters, you must charge each user the same rate the utility would have charged them directly, pass through any rebate in proportion to use, give an itemised bill in the utility's own form with opening and closing meter readings, post the current residential rate schedule or a link to it, and maintain and repair the submeter equipment yourself. Complaints go to the Public Utilities Commission, which may involve your county sealer. California has a detailed statute for billing tenants for water through submeters and no equivalent for electricity, so the master-meter rules are what you have. A meter you use to measure something you charge for is a commercial device under the weights-and-measures law, and your county may charge you an annual registration fee for it. Until 2029 the device fee is capped at $3 per apartment for an electric submeter you own, and at $26 for most other commercial measuring devices, plus a location fee. Whether a charger counts, and the testing rules, sit in regulations this review couldn't read, so ask your county sealer before you meter and bill per kilowatt-hour.

title: EV Chargers at Move-Out: The Statute Leaves It to Your Agreement
bodyText: California makes you approve a qualifying tenant request for a charging station at the tenant's own allotted space, but it says almost nothing about what happens to the equipment when the tenancy ends. What it does say helps you: the written agreement the tenant must consent to has to cover your requirements for installation, use, maintenance and removal of the station and of its infrastructure, and the tenant must pay, as part of rent, the cost of electricity used and the cost of damage, maintenance, repair, removal and replacement. So removal is yours to specify, and its cost is the tenant's, provided you wrote it down before any work started. No statute says who owns the station at move-out, whether the tenant may take it away, whether you must buy it, or whether the space must be restored. Watch the insurance: the tenant's liability cover only has to run until the station is removed or the tenant gives up possession, so if you let the equipment stay you inherit the risk the next day. Do not treat removal as an ordinary deposit deduction: you may claim the deposit only for the statutory purposes, you must photograph the unit before and after, and you must itemise. What to do: before you approve anything, sign an addendum that says whether the station and conduit stay or come out, who pays, by when, to what condition, and who insures it afterwards.

title: EV Chargers in Shared Parking: No Tenant Right, but an Owner Right in an HOA
bodyText: Your statutory duty to approve a tenant's charging station runs only to a parking space allotted to that tenant. If your parking is shared, unassigned or first-come, no tenant can make you put a charger in it, and you are never obliged to provide an extra space to fit one. If a charger does have the effect of giving the tenant a reserved space, you may charge monthly rent for that space. The duty also drops away entirely where chargers already serve tenants at ten per cent or more of the designated spaces, where parking is not part of the lease, or where the property has fewer than five parking spaces. The picture flips if you own a condominium or a home in a planned development, because there the right is yours as an owner against the association: a governing document that effectively prohibits or unreasonably restricts a charger in your unit or your designated space is void, the association must process your application like an architectural request and must deny it in writing within sixty days or it is deemed approved, and if your own space will not work the association must license you space in the common area. In exchange you take on installation and electricity costs, a licensed contractor, a certificate of insurance within fourteen days, and restoration after removal. That right does not pass to your tenant. What to do: decide in the lease whether shared-area charging is allowed at all, and if it is, name the space, the reservation charge, who maintains the equipment and who pays for damage.

title: Renting Out a Condo or HOA Home: What the Association Cannot Do to You
bodyText: If you rent out a condominium, townhouse or a house in a planned development, the association's governing documents bind you as owner, but California limits hard what they may do to your right to rent. A rental ban cannot be applied to you at all unless it was already in effect on the day you took title. On top of that, any governing-document provision that prohibits, has the effect of prohibiting, or unreasonably restricts renting is void, and no development may cap rentals below twenty-five per cent of its separate interests; it may set a higher percentage, and it may still ban rentals of thirty days or less. An accessory dwelling unit does not count as a separate interest, and a unit the owner lives in is not counted as rented, so neither consumes the development's rental allowance. You may also rent out part of your own owner-occupied unit for more than thirty days whatever the documents say. Before the tenancy starts you must give the association proof of when you took title plus your prospective tenant's name and contact details. Every year you must also tell the association in writing whether the unit is rented out, how it should send you notices, and who can act for you while you're away. If you don't, its notices go to the last mailing address you gave it or, failing that, to the unit, where your tenant will get them. If the association willfully breaks these rules it owes you actual damages and a civil penalty of up to one thousand dollars. What the association keeps is real: conduct, parking and guest-access rules still bind your tenant. What to do: get the current governing documents, send the title and tenant information before move-in, and treat a sub-twenty-five-per-cent rental cap as unenforceable rather than quietly complying.

title: No Duty to Disclose the Association's Rules to Your Tenant
bodyText: California does not make you give your tenant the association's declaration, bylaws, rules, budget or financial statements, and it does not require your lease to describe what the association must do, to state that you know the common-interest development law, or to go to the board for review or filing. There is no California equivalent of the condominium-lease recitals some jurisdictions require. What you do owe runs the other way, to the association rather than the tenant: before you rent you must give it proof of when you took title plus your prospective tenant's name and contact information. Every year you must also tell the association in writing whether the unit is rented out, how it should send you notices, and who can act for you while you're away. If you don't, its notices go to the last mailing address you gave it or, failing that, to the unit, where your tenant will get them. That gap is a practical risk, not a relief. The association's conduct, parking, noise and guest-access rules will govern how your tenant lives there, and the association will come to you, the owner, when they are broken. You cannot enforce against a tenant a rule they were never shown. So attach the current rules and regulations to the lease as a named addendum, have the tenant sign for them, keep a dated copy, and send any later amendment the same way. Say in the lease who pays a fine the association levies for your tenant's conduct. Where a city has its own condominium or rental ordinance, check it for the address. What to do: treat the rules addendum as standard practice even though no statute requires it.

title: Accessory Dwelling Units: Two Protections You Can Rely On, and a Rent-Cap Trap
bodyText: California protects ADU rentals in two ways that are settled. If the property sits in a common interest development, a governing-document provision that effectively prohibits or unreasonably restricts building or using an ADU or junior ADU on a single-family lot is void, so long as the unit meets the Government Code's ADU articles; only reasonable restrictions survive, and a restriction is unreasonable if it makes an ADU unreasonably expensive, effectively impossible, or impossible to build at all. Separately, an association may not prohibit or unreasonably restrict renting an ADU or junior ADU, and for the twenty-five-per-cent rental cap an ADU is not counted as a separate interest while a unit the owner occupies is not counted as rented, so your ADU tenancy does not eat the development's rental allowance. Now the trap. If you live in the house and rent out no more than two units or bedrooms, including an ADU, just cause does not apply to those tenancies — but there is no matching exemption from the rent cap, and the owner-occupied two-unit exemption from both rules is expressly unavailable where either unit is an ADU. A newly built ADU is outside the rent cap for fifteen years from its certificate of occupancy, and after that the cap bites. An ADU is also rarely sellable separately from the house, so the separately-alienable exemption will usually not be open to you. Two Government Code rules matter before you let. An ADU approved through the state's by-right route must be let for more than 30 days, and a local ADU ordinance may require the same of other ADUs. A junior ADU must be let for more than 30 days, and if it shares a bathroom with the house, the owner must live in the house or the junior unit, so you can't let both while living elsewhere. What to do: get the local ADU ordinance before you build, and diary the fifteen-year date.

title: No State Limit on Renting a House in a Single-Family Zone
bodyText: No California statute stops you renting out a house in a single-family zone, and none makes your own occupancy of the lot a condition of renting it. The state pushes the other way: it limits what associations may do to restrict renting, and it strips local rent control from a home that can be sold separately from any other dwelling unit. Where owner occupancy does appear in the statutes it works as an exemption in your favour, not a limit. If you live in the house and rent out no more than two units or bedrooms, including an accessory dwelling unit, just cause does not apply to those tenancies. If you lived in one of two units in a single structure as your principal residence when the tenancy began, still do, and neither is an accessory dwelling unit, both the rent cap and just cause drop away. Renting a single room to one lodger in the house you occupy has its own termination route and is the only carve-out in the fair housing definition. Two cautions. If your lot or unit came from the state's two-unit development or urban lot split schemes, a unit created under them may only be let for more than 30 days. An urban lot split also needs the applicant's sworn statement that they intend to live in one of the units for three years, and neither scheme can be used where it would demolish or alter housing a tenant has lived in during the last three years. Get the approval conditions from the city before you sign a lease. And the real constraint here is local: short-term-rental caps, occupancy limits, boarding-house definitions and rental registration all sit in city and county ordinances. What to do: check the zoning and rental ordinance for the specific address, and keep written proof of your own occupancy if you are relying on an owner-occupied exemption.

title: Renting Out a House: the One Disclosure That Turns on It Being a House
bodyText: Letting a single-family house or a condominium in California triggers one disclosure that depends on the property being a house rather than an apartment, and it is not about how many people may live there. It is the Tenant Protection Act exemption statement. If the unit can be sold separately from any other dwelling unit, and you are not a real estate investment trust, a corporation, a limited liability company with any corporate member, or mobilehome-park management, you may claim exemption from the rent cap and from just cause — but only if the tenant has the statutory statement word for word, and for any tenancy that commenced or renewed on or after 1 July 2020 it must be in the rental agreement itself, not in a side letter. Leave it out and the exemption is simply not available: your house falls under both the rent cap and just cause. Adding the statement to a new or renewed agreement also counts as a similar provision for the refusal-to-renew ground. There is no type-size rule and no first-page rule for that exemption statement. The companion notice for covered properties does carry one — not less than twelve-point type — so set the exemption statement in twelve-point type too and put it where a tenant will actually read it. California prescribes no statement about permitted occupancy or how many people a house may hold; that is a building-code and local matter. What to do: use the prescribed wording unaltered, in the agreement, and re-test the exemption if ownership changes.

title: No State Landlord Register, but Check the City Before the First Tenancy
bodyText: California has no statewide landlord register and no state rental licence. Two general state filings can still apply. If you regularly rent for profit under a fictitious business name (for an individual, a name without your surname; for a company, a name other than its registered one), you must file a fictitious business name statement with the county clerk within 40 days of starting, publish it, and until then you cannot maintain a lawsuit, an eviction included, on business done under that name (Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §§ 17900(b), 17910(a), 17915, 17917(a), 17918). And an out-of-state company transacting intrastate business here must qualify with the Secretary of State before it can sue (Cal. Corp. Code §§ 2105(a), 17708.07(a); see `edu-confirmed-absences-outside-title-ca`). The obligations are local: many cities require a business licence or business tax certificate to rent out residential property, and the rent-controlled cities run rent registries on top of that. Those are ordinances, so you must check the city and the county for the specific address; this library does not resolve them. Two state rules shape that local layer and are worth knowing before you set a rent. First, where a local ordinance or charter controls rents and requires rents to be registered, the local agency must establish and certify permissible rent levels and, on your request or the tenant's, must issue a certificate of the permissible rent level within five business days; it may charge a reasonable fee for it; the figure binds the agency absent fraud unless appealed, and you may ask for a certificate for a vacant unit that already has a base rent. Second, if you have made a good-faith attempt to comply and cured a deficiency after notice from the agency, the only remedies against you are restitution to the tenant and the registration or filing fees — no penalty or other sanction — and annual rent adjustments denied during the lapse are restored going forward. Charging above a certified ceiling is a different and worse problem: refund on demand, and treble damages if wilful. If you lease or collect rent for someone else for compensation you need a broker licence, with trust-fund duties an owner does not have. What to do: get the licence and registration position in writing from the city first, and request a rent certificate before setting a rent in a registration city.

title: You Never Have to Record a Lease, but a Long One Is Worth Recording
bodyText: California imposes no duty to record or register a residential lease, and an unrecorded lease is fully valid between you and your tenant and against anyone who has notice of it. There is a priority rule that matters the moment you sell or refinance. A conveyance of an estate for years — which a lease is — other than a lease for a term not exceeding one year is void against a later buyer or lender who takes in good faith, for value, and records first, and against a judgment affecting title recorded before notice of the action. A lease of a year or less sits outside that rule entirely, so nothing is gained by recording it. So if you have a long lease, an option, or a below-market term that must survive a sale, record it in the county where the property sits; recording gives constructive notice of its contents to everyone who deals with the land afterwards, and the definition of a conveyance for these purposes reaches every written instrument creating or affecting an interest in real property. Landlords commonly record a short memorandum instead of the whole lease, to keep the rent and the tenant's details off the public record; no California statute requires or forbids that, and we found no provision on a memorandum of lease at all, so have a lawyer draft one. Keep separate from all of this the rent registration some rent-controlled cities require: that is a local filing about rent levels, not a recording of your lease. What to do: record anything over a year that must bind a future owner; otherwise do nothing.

title: Rental Inspections: No State Programme, and Your Lease Cannot Let the Inspector In
bodyText: California runs no statewide periodic inspection programme for ordinary rental dwellings, and no statute lets a term in your lease stand in for the tenant's consent when a housing inspector wants access. Enforcement sits with the local housing or building department, or the health department where there is none, and its officers may enter and inspect any building or premises whenever necessary to secure compliance with, or prevent a violation of, the State Housing Law. That is the inspector's own authority, not yours. Your right to enter is a closed statutory list: an emergency, necessary or agreed repairs and services, showing the unit, the move-out initial inspection under the deposit statute, abandonment or surrender, a court order, the water-submetering chapter, and compliance with the exterior elevated element inspection law. Letting a code inspector in is not on the list, so coordinate the visit with the tenant and give your own written notice for any entry you do make. The one inspection you must actually buy is structural: in any building with three or more multifamily units, balconies, decks, porches, stairways and walkways with load-bearing components had to be inspected by 1 January 2026 and every six years after that, by a qualified independent professional you hire, with a written report within forty-five days. A tenant's refusal to allow an entry the statutes authorise is at-fault just cause for termination. Many cities do run proactive rental inspection programmes with fees and certificates; the State Housing Law lets them charge for enforcement. What to do: diary the six-year inspection, never rely on a lease clause for an inspector, and check the city's programme for the address.

title: Skipping the Move-Out Inspection Offer Has No Fine, but It Still Costs You
bodyText: California gives you one inspection-notice duty and attaches no fine of its own to missing it. Within a reasonable time after either side gives notice to end the tenancy, or before a fixed term ends, you must tell the tenant in writing that they may request an initial inspection and may be present at it. If the tenant does not request one, your duties under that part of the statute are discharged — but only if you made the offer. The exposure runs through the deposit instead, and it is sharp. If an inspection does happen and the tenant's belongings were not blocking your view, you may not deduct for any repair or cleaning that was not named in the itemised statement you handed over or left in the unit. A bad-faith claim on, or retention of, the deposit exposes you to statutory damages of up to twice the deposit on top of actual damages, the court may award them whether or not the tenant asked, and you carry the burden of showing your amounts were reasonable. A bad-faith failure on the itemisation and documentation duties costs you the right to claim any of the deposit at all. The duty does not apply where the tenancy ended on a three-day notice for nonpayment, waste, nuisance or unlawful use. What to do: put the written offer into your standard termination pack, give forty-eight hours' written notice of the inspection date, photograph before and after, and itemise everything you intend to deduct.

title: No Duty to Disclose a Code Order, and Three Reasons to Disclose Anyway
bodyText: California puts no duty on you to tell a prospective or current tenant that the unit is under a code-enforcement notice, an abatement order or an order to vacate. The notice duty sits with the enforcement agency: tenants must be given copies of the violation notice, the agency's order after inspection, its decision to repair or demolish, and any building or demolition permit — and the agency, not you, delivers them to each affected unit, by posting on the property plus first-class mail to each unit or posting on each unit. The order must itself tell the tenant you cannot retaliate. Silence is still a bad plan, because a live order costs you three ways. Once an inspector has told you in writing to abate or repair and thirty-five days have passed without good cause, you may not demand or collect rent, raise it, or serve a three-day notice to pay or quit, and you owe actual damages plus between one hundred and five thousand dollars, with attorney's fees. If the order requires the unit vacated, you owe the tenant relocation benefits, payable within ten days of the order being mailed and posted or at least twenty days before the vacate date, whichever is later. And a home that could otherwise be freely repriced on a vacancy loses that right while it carries serious unabated violations. One disclosure you genuinely owe: if you apply for a demolition permit you must give written notice to current tenants before applying, and to a prospective tenant before taking any fee or signing. What to do: disclose a live order in writing, and abate before you re-let.

title: You Cannot Turn Down a Voucher Because of the Programme Inspection
bodyText: No California statute lets you refuse a tenancy, or end one, because a subsidy programme will inspect the unit, and none makes a tenant's refusal to admit the programme inspector a ground for an expedited eviction the way some states do. The rule that actually governs runs the other way. Source of income is a protected class in California, and it is defined to include federal, state and local public assistance and housing subsidies, naming Section 8 vouchers and the HUD Veterans Affairs Supportive Housing voucher by name. Discrimination is defined broadly: refusing to rent or lease, refusing to negotiate, any other denial or withholding of housing, providing inferior terms, conditions, privileges, facilities or services, and cancelling or terminating a rental agreement. So declining a voucher applicant because of the housing authority's inspection, or because you do not want the programme's paperwork, is a fair housing problem rather than a screening criterion. The only relevant carve-out is refusing to rent a room to a single roomer or boarder in your own owner-occupied house, and even then the advertising rules still bind you. What you keep is your ordinary, consistently applied standards, including a sensible test of the tenant's own share of the rent. If an inspection finds a defect, treat it as a repair question: the unit has to meet California's habitability standards whether or not a subsidy pays the rent, and the rent-demand bar bites on an unabated code order either way. What to do: build the inspection into your turnaround schedule, and keep your written criteria uniform.

title: Out-of-State Owners: Entities Must Qualify, and a Strict Lease Disclosure
bodyText: California does not require an out-of-state individual owner to appoint an in-state agent, to employ a California broker, or to file anything before suing a tenant; a nonresident may hold a California broker licence on the same terms as a resident. An out-of-state company is different. A foreign LLC or corporation transacting intrastate business here must register or qualify with the Secretary of State, naming a California agent for service of process, and until it does it may not maintain an action, an unlawful detainer included, though it may defend one (Cal. Corp. Code §§ 17708.02(a)(4), 17708.07(a), (b), 2105(a), 2203(c)). Transacting intrastate business means repeated and successive transactions here (Cal. Corp. Code §§ 191(a), 17708.03(a)); whether letting a property qualifies is a case-law question, so qualify before you file (see `edu-confirmed-absences-outside-title-ca`). An unregistered foreign LLC is deemed to have appointed the Secretary of State as its agent for service of process, and an unqualified foreign corporation is deemed to consent to California jurisdiction, for claims arising from that business (Cal. Corp. Code §§ 17708.07(d), 2203(a)). And anyone renting under a fictitious business name cannot sue on that business until the statement is filed and published (Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §§ 17910, 17918). What California requires instead applies to every residential landlord wherever they live, and it is strict and lease-based. The lease itself must disclose the name, telephone number and usual street address at which personal service may be effected for each person authorised to manage the premises and for an owner or someone authorised to act for the owner for service of process and for receiving notices and demands; plus the name, telephone number and address of whoever rent is paid to, the days and hours for personal payment, and the forms rent may take. Keep it current. It binds a successor owner or manager, who must comply within fifteen days of taking over and may not serve a nonpayment notice or evict for rent that accrued while out of compliance. If you sign the lease for an owner and this is not done, you are deemed the owner's agent for service of process, for performing the owner's obligations, and for receiving rent in cash or any form previously accepted. Giving an address where nobody can be served backfires twice: anything the tenant mails there is conclusively deemed received on the date posted, and the tenant may serve court papers by registered or certified mail to the rent-payment address. Disclosing a manager does not shield an undisclosed owner. What to do: give a real California street address with a person behind it.

title: Six Portfolio Tests, and No General Small-Landlord Exemption
bodyText: California has no general small-landlord concept. Fair housing covers every landlord whatever the size of the portfolio, and the only carve-out is refusing to rent a room to a single roomer or boarder in your own owner-occupied house. Six separate tests do real work, each attached to one duty, and you have to check the one in front of you. The security deposit cap is one month's rent, but two months' if you are a natural person, or a limited liability company whose members are all natural persons, and you own no more than two residential rental properties that together hold no more than four dwelling units offered for rent — and the larger deposit is unavailable against a service member, who you also may not refuse for that reason. The electric vehicle charging duty drops away where the property has fewer than five parking spaces, where chargers already serve tenants at ten per cent or more of designated spaces, or where parking is not part of the lease. Just cause does not apply to a single-family owner-occupied residence where you rent no more than two units or bedrooms, including an accessory dwelling unit. Both the rent cap and just cause fall away for two units in one structure where you occupied one as your principal residence when the tenancy began and still do, and neither is an accessory dwelling unit. Both also fall away for a separately alienable home where you are not a real estate investment trust, a corporation, a corporate-member LLC or mobilehome-park management — and only if the prescribed statement is in the lease. Note that two of these have two limbs that must both be met. What to do: count and document the units before relying on any of them.

title: No Government Approval Needed to Make a California Lease Valid
bodyText: California has no communal or native land tenure and no statute that makes a residential lease wait on a government officer's signature to be valid. There is no California equivalent of the territorial schemes where a lease of family or communal land is only provisional until a governor approves it, where rent cannot be charged and possession cannot be given before approval, and where the lease must then be deposited and registered. Nothing in California's statutes conditions the validity of a dwelling lease on approval by a commission, a land board or a state officer, and nothing suspends rent or possession pending one. Your lease is effective when the parties sign it. Two things to keep separate from that. Land held in trust for a federally recognised tribe, and allotted land, are governed by federal and tribal law rather than by the California landlord-tenant statutes; if the address is on a reservation or on trust or allotment land, the state rules may not apply at all, a lease there may well need federal approval, and you should take specialist advice rather than using a standard California lease. And where a public agency owns the land and leases it out, any approval requirement comes from that agency's own authority and its contracting rules, not from a lease-approval statute. What to do: for an ordinary California dwelling, nothing — do not add an approval condition to the lease; for anything on tribal trust or allotted land, get advice before you sign.

title: No California Statute Makes You Carry Landlord Insurance
bodyText:
Nothing in California's statutes requires a residential landlord to carry liability or property insurance, to register a policy with any agency, or to tell a tenant whether the building is insured. The only places the codes tie insurance to a rental dwelling run the other way: they say when a tenant may be required to insure something. So insuring is a commercial decision here, not a legal duty - and the exposures California does create are large.

You owe a duty of care imposed by law, and a lease term by which the tenant gives up the right to have you perform it, or gives up the right to sue you later, is void. You cannot paper over an uninsured loss. If the building is declared substandard you can be ordered to pay the tenant's moving, storage and replacement costs. The deposit, rent-cap, just-cause and retaliation statutes each carry their own damages on top.

What to do: carry landlord liability and property cover sized to the building, because no statute sets a figure for you. If a management company collects your rent, have yourself and the company each named on the other's policy. Check your own city: several rental registration and inspection schemes ask for proof of insurance, and state law does not displace them. Check any loan or association condition, which can be stricter than anything the state requires. And start the renewal conversation with your broker early, because replacement cover in fire-exposed areas takes time to arrange.

title: Renter’s Insurance: No Rules, With Three Narrow Exceptions
bodyText:
California does not require renter's insurance, does not forbid you from requiring it, does not cap what you may require, and nowhere makes you tell a tenant in writing that your policy will not cover their belongings. There is no force-placed-insurance machinery and no admin fee the law allows you to add. If you want renter's insurance, the lease is the only place it comes from, and the lease then sets the amount, the proof and the deadline.

Three narrow places do deal with insurance, and two of them are a real requirement you may impose. A tenant who wants a waterbed or other liquid-filled bedding in a building that got its certificate of occupancy after 1972 must hand you a valid waterbed policy or certificate before installing it, from a carrier licensed in California with a Best's rating of B or higher, covering property damage with loss of use, kept in force until the bedding leaves, and you may ask for evidence at any time; the carrier must warn you ten days before cancelling or non-renewing. You may also take an extra half month's rent as deposit and charge a reasonable administration fee. An e-bike or e-scooter that is not on the listed safety standards still qualifies to be charged in the unit if the tenant insures it for storage there. A tenant installing a charging station must insure it.

What to do: if you require renter's insurance, put the amount, the proof and the renewal proof in the lease, and never state a figure as though a statute set it.

title: When a Tenant’s Insurer Pays - or Refuses
bodyText:
California has almost nothing on how a claim against a tenant's insurance is handled between you and the tenant. No statute makes you a beneficiary of the tenant's policy, lets you claim on it directly, requires you to be named on it, bars you from suing the tenant once the insurer pays, or regulates what either of you must do when a claim is filed. One rule exists, and it protects the tenant's claim from you: where the tenant carries the waterbed policy the law lets you insist on, your failure to use your own inspection and enforcement rights under that section is not a ground for the insurer to deny the claim. Read that as a warning about every other kind of cover too, because an insurer will look for a reason to refuse.

So the lease does the work. What to do: say in the lease that your insurance does not cover the tenant's belongings and that the tenant is responsible for insuring them. Where you require a policy, require that you be named as an additional insured and that the tenant give you a certificate, and ask for a replacement certificate each year. Do not agree to look only to insurance for a loss the tenant caused, and do not sign a waiver of subrogation you have not had reviewed. Keep dated photographs and your own repair invoices: a claim you cannot document is a claim you will not be paid for, whoever is insuring it.

title: Arbitration in a California Lease: One Narrow Statutory Door
bodyText:
California has a general arbitration act: a written agreement to arbitrate a present or future controversy is valid, enforceable and irrevocable except on grounds that would let any contract be revoked. Nothing in the tenancy statutes bans a residential lease arbitration clause. But only one tenancy statute actually invites one, and it is narrow: if your written agreement sets out the habitability sections themselves, it may provide that any dispute about a condition said to make the premises untenantable goes to arbitration on either party's application, with the arbitrator splitting the cost. That is a repair dispute, not a rent dispute and not an eviction.

Treat everything wider than that as unsettled and expensive to test; for that reason this library does not offer an arbitration clause for California. A lease cannot take away the tenant's procedural rights in litigation, the tenant's right to a notice or hearing the law requires, or the tenant's right to sue you later, so a clause that sweeps in eviction, deposits or entry is at risk of being void in part. Eviction has its own statutory court, county and timetable, and arbitration does not get you possession.

What to do: if you want arbitration, limit it to habitability and money disputes, keep possession actions expressly in court, do not waive a jury for anything else, split the costs as the statute contemplates, and have the clause drafted by a California lawyer. California's real-estate arbitration format rules reach a lease with an option to purchase, not an ordinary lease. If your lease includes an option to buy, title the arbitration clause "ARBITRATION OF DISPUTES" and set it in at least 8-point bold type, or capitals if typed. Follow it with the statute's initialled notice, word for word. The clause can't limit claims for bodily injury or wrongful death.

title: No Statute Makes You Try to Settle First
bodyText:
California has no landlord-tenant statute that requires, permits or forbids an informal dispute-resolution step before court. There is no mandatory mediation for residential tenancies, no meet-and-confer rule, no good-faith-effort requirement and no state programme you must use. If you want a conversation before a filing, the lease has to create it, and the lease must not turn it into a precondition, because a tenant cannot be made to give up a notice the law requires or procedural rights in litigation.

What California gives you instead is a cheap, fast forum rather than a pre-filing ritual. The small claims court exists to resolve minor disputes quickly: its hearings are informal by statute, the judge may question witnesses and investigate the dispute, lawyers do not appear for the parties at the hearing, and every county must run a free small claims advisory service that will help either side prepare a filing and understand the procedure. A natural-person landlord may claim up to twelve thousand five hundred dollars there; a company or other entity is limited to six thousand two hundred and fifty. Unpaid rent after the tenant has gone, deposit disputes and damage claims all fit.

What to do: use the optional informal-resolution clause if you want the step, send the notice it describes by a method you can prove, and keep the small claims route in view - for most money disputes with a former tenant it is faster than anything you could build into the lease.

title: Which Consumer Law Reaches a California Landlord
bodyText:
California has three consumer statutes a landlord is likely to meet, and only one of them reaches you.

The Consumers Legal Remedies Act and the Consumer Contract Awareness Act are both built around the sale or lease of goods or services. Goods there means personal property and services means work and labour, so a residential tenancy - the hiring of real property - falls outside both. That matters in two directions. You do not get caught by their remedies, but you also do not get their safe harbours, and the rule many landlords have heard about, that a signed contract may not be handed back with blank spaces still to be filled in, is not the rule that governs your lease.

The unfair competition law is different and it does reach you. It makes any unlawful, unfair or fraudulent business act or practice, and any untrue or misleading advertising, actionable. Its reach is the sting: breaking any other statute in the course of running your rental business becomes an unfair competition claim on its own. A tenant who has actually lost money or property can sue for an injunction and to get that money back; the Attorney General, a district attorney or a large city attorney can sue for civil penalties of up to two thousand five hundred dollars for each violation; and the clock runs four years, longer than most tenancy limitation periods. The false-advertising statute it borrows from also stands on its own: a statement you know, or should know, is untrue or misleading, made to the public to dispose of real property, is a misdemeanor carrying up to six months in jail or a $2,500 fine. It doesn't name leases, so whether it reaches a rental listing is for case law; assume it does.

What to do: give every tenant a complete, filled-in copy of the signed lease within fifteen days anyway, advertise rent and fees accurately, and treat any repeated practice across your portfolio as carrying penalty exposure per unit and per tenant.

title: No Penalty for Printing a Void Term - But Plenty for Using One
bodyText:
California has no provision that fines you, or gives the tenant damages, simply because your lease contains a term the law makes void. There is no equivalent of the knowing-use penalty some states attach to a prohibited lease clause. The void term is just void: the court strikes it and the rest of the lease stands.

Do not take comfort from that. California attaches its money to conduct rather than to drafting, and the amounts are real. Cutting utilities, changing locks, removing doors or windows, or removing the tenant's belongings to force a tenant out exposes you to actual damages plus up to one hundred dollars a day, never less than two hundred fifty dollars for each separate violation, and the winning side's attorney's fees. Theft, extortion, threats or a significant and intentional entry violation aimed at making a tenant leave brings a civil penalty of up to two thousand dollars for each violation, recoverable in small claims court. Retaliating against a tenant who has asserted a repair right gives actual damages plus one hundred to two thousand dollars for each retaliatory act where you acted with fraud, oppression or malice, and the court must award fees to whichever side wins if either asks at the outset. Claiming or keeping a deposit in bad faith exposes you to twice the deposit on top of actual damages, and you carry the burden of proving your deductions were reasonable. Disclosing a tenant's immigration status to an agency to harass, retaliate or force them out brings six to twelve months' rent for each person disclosed. Threatening to disclose it to make them leave is one of the two-thousand-dollar acts.

What to do: strike void terms from your template anyway. A clause you cannot enforce still invites a tenant to argue the whole lease was unfair, and attempting to act on one is what turns a dead clause into a damages claim.

title: Homestead Waivers in a Lease: Nothing to Waive, and No Power to Do It
bodyText:
A homestead waiver does not belong in a California residential lease, and a landlord who copies one in from another state's form gets nothing.

California's homestead exemption is part of the rules on enforcing money judgments, not part of landlord-tenant law.
