It attaches to the principal dwelling in which the judgment debtor or the debtor's spouse lived when the creditor's lien attached and has lived continuously since. Nothing in the tenancy statutes mentions it, and nothing anywhere says a lease may deal with it.

Two things make a lease waiver a bad idea even before you reach the exemption rules themselves. First, a lease provision by which the tenant waives a statutory right is void unless the lease was handed to the tenant before the tenant took possession, and it is void outright if it gives up a notice or hearing the law requires or the tenant's procedural rights in litigation - and exemption claims are made by a procedure in the enforcement of judgments. Second, in practice the exemption shields a debtor's equity in a dwelling, and a tenant who rents from you has none; a waiver aimed at a renter is most likely empty rather than effective.

What to do: take the homestead clause out of your template. If you hold a money judgment against a former tenant, work the exemption rules through the judgment-enforcement procedure with a collection lawyer rather than through the lease, and do not assume your lease has removed any protection.

title: Liens for Work Your Tenant Orders
bodyText:
If your tenant hires a contractor and does not pay, the contractor can look at your building. California's mechanics lien law sits in the Civil Code in a long chapter on works of improvement, and it is the law that decides whose interest a lien attaches to and what an owner can do about work ordered by someone else. Your interest is subject to a lien for work you didn't contract for if the work was done with your knowledge, unless you give a notice of nonresponsibility. That notice must be signed and verified by you, and you must both post it and record it within 10 days of learning of the work. A no-liens clause in your lease doesn't bind the contractor, because an owner can't by contract impair another claimant's lien rights.

What is clear is the shape of the risk. The exposure follows from your knowledge of the work, not from your signature on the contract. And if your lease requires the tenant to make the improvement, whether a notice of nonresponsibility still protects you is a question only case law could settle, so get advice before you agree to that. Nothing in the landlord-tenant statutes gives you a lien defence, and no statute requires or blesses a no-liens lease clause here.

What to do: require your written consent before any work beyond ordinary cleaning and decoration, and give it only for a scope you have seen. Make the tenant tell you the contractor's name, licence number and start date before work begins, and require the tenant to give the contractor written notice that the work is the tenant's and not yours. Keep a copy of everything. When you learn of tenant work, post and record a notice of nonresponsibility within 10 days, and ask a California construction lawyer first if the lease requires the work.

title: A Lease Renewal Can Release Your Guarantor
bodyText:
California has no statute about lease guaranties as such. There is no requirement that a guaranty state a maximum amount or an end date, no rule that a guaranty must be written on or refer to the lease, and no cap on what you may ask a guarantor to put up at the start of a tenancy. The general law of suretyship fills the gap, and one of its rules is the trap.

A surety is released, so far as not indemnified by the principal, if the creditor alters the original obligation in any respect without the surety's consent, or impairs or suspends the creditor's rights against the principal. A guarantor is a surety for this purpose. So renewing the lease, raising the rent, agreeing a repayment plan, or letting the tenancy roll on month to month on changed terms can each release a guarantor who signed for the original term and was never asked about the change.

Three practical consequences. First, get the guarantor's consent to future changes in writing at the start, in the guaranty itself, rather than chasing a signature at each renewal. Second, a guaranty that reaches future renewals may be revocable: a continuing guaranty can be revoked by the guarantor as to future transactions, unless there is continuing consideration the guarantor doesn't renounce. Whether a lease guaranty is one, and whether the tenancy is that consideration, only case law can settle, so take a fresh guaranty at each renewal. Third, watch the small claims limits if the guarantor is who you want to sue: against a guarantor who charges nothing for guaranteeing, the small claims demand cannot exceed three thousand one hundred and twenty-five dollars, far below the ordinary limits, so a larger claim against a parent or a friend who co-signed must go to the regular court.

What to do: use the optional guaranty clause, give the guarantor a copy of the lease when they sign, and keep their consent paperwork with the lease.

title: Letting Property You Do Not Own Outright
bodyText:
California has no usufruct. The civil-law idea of a holder who may use and take the fruits of land that belongs to someone else does not exist in any California code, so no rule tells you what happens to a lease granted by one. What California has instead is the common-law life estate, and the rules are short and useful.

Someone who holds a life estate may use the land as a fee owner would, except that they must do nothing that injures the inheritance. If a holder of a life estate, or of an estate for years, grants more than they lawfully could, the grant does not forfeit their own estate: it simply passes whatever they could lawfully pass, and no more. Read those two together and the practical answer appears. A lease from a life tenant is good while the life estate lasts and no longer, and the people holding the remainder may sue over injury to the inheritance even though a life or term estate stands in the way, and even if they have since parted with their interest.

What to do: before you sign, find out what estate your landlord holds, or what estate you hold if you are the one letting. Check the recorded deed, any trust or probate order, and whether a trustee, executor, conservator or attorney-in-fact is signing. Where the term is longer than the interest is secure, either keep the term short or get the remainder holders to sign too. And remember that whoever signs on the owner's behalf must disclose in the lease who the owner is and who may be served with notices.

title: Special Districts and Special Taxes: Nothing Goes in a Lease
bodyText:
No California statute makes you tell a tenant that the property sits in a special district, that it carries a Mello-Roos special tax or an assessment-bond lien, or that a district provides its water, sewer, fire or lighting. There is no district statement for a lease, no prescribed wording, and nothing you must initial.

California puts that disclosure on sellers instead. A seller of single-family residential property whose land carries a continuing Mello-Roos lien, a fixed-lien assessment collected in instalments to secure 1915 Act bonds, or a contractual assessment, must make a good-faith effort to get the district's own disclosure notice and deliver it to the buyer. Watch the boundary, because it is not where landlords assume. That disclosure article covers a sale, an exchange, a real property sales contract, a lease with an option to purchase, any other option to purchase, and a ground lease coupled with improvements. An ordinary residential tenancy is outside it - but a lease-option or a rent-to-own arrangement is inside, and a waiver of the article's requirements is void. If you offer your tenant an option to buy, you have stepped into the seller's disclosure regime and the district notice is one of the things you owe.

What to do: leave district language out of an ordinary lease. If you are letting with an option to purchase, treat the transaction as a sale for disclosure purposes and get the notices before signing. Where a special tax is simply part of your costs, remember you cannot pass it to the tenant as an extra charge unless the lease provides for it and the rent rules allow it.

title: What a California Tenant Cannot Agree to Give Up
bodyText:
California has no single section listing the tenancy rights that cannot be waived. It does it twice over instead, and a landlord drafting a lease has to read both layers.

The general layer voids any lease provision by which the tenant agrees to modify or waive the security deposit or entry rules, the right to sue you later, the right to a notice or hearing the law requires, procedural rights in litigation about the tenancy, or the right to have you perform a duty of care imposed by law. It then goes further: a provision waiving any other statutory right is void unless the lease was handed to the tenant before the tenant took possession, with a carve-out for a renewal carrying the same provision forward. Both rules apply to leases executed from 1976.

The section-by-section layer adds its own voiding clause to most of the modern statutes: habitability, retaliation, automatic renewal type size, just cause, the rent cap, immigration-status disclosure, the right to summon emergency help, rent payment methods, translation of a negotiated lease, and water submetering. In those places the waiver is void however the lease was presented and whenever it was signed.

What to do: never use the lease to change a figure, a deadline or a procedure a statute fixes. Where you want a term the statute leaves to agreement - tenant-performed maintenance, a forfeiture clause, a smoking policy - draft it as the statute allows rather than as a waiver. And present the whole lease before move-in, every time: a lease first presented after the tenant has the keys loses every statutory-right modification in it, unless the modification repeats one in the lease being renewed.

title: Smoke From the Next Unit: You Cannot Waive the Claim Away
bodyText:
California has no statute about smoke drifting from one dwelling into another. Nothing makes drift a nuisance by name, nothing makes you responsible for it, and nothing lets a lease settle it in advance. What California gives you is the power to ban smoking, and what it takes away is the clause you were hoping to rely on if you do not.

A waiver will not work. A lease cannot make a tenant give up the right to sue you later, and it cannot make a tenant give up the right to have you perform a duty of care the law imposes to prevent personal injury or damage to belongings. A clause saying the tenant accepts smoke from other units, or releases you from any claim about it, runs straight into both and is void. Worse, the clause can hurt you twice: a court reading a void release may take it as evidence you knew drift was a problem in the building.

The useful route is the policy, not the waiver. You may prohibit smoking of cigarettes and other tobacco products anywhere on the property, and if you do, the lease has to say which areas are covered. Imposing the ban on a tenant already in place is subject to the rules for changing lease terms - proper written notice in a month-to-month tenancy, and no change by notice during a fixed term - and your own city may already regulate smoking in multi-unit housing more strictly than the state. If anyone works for you in the building, the state's smoke-free workplace law also applies. It bars an employer from knowingly permitting tobacco smoking at a place of employment or in an enclosed space, such as a lobby, elevator, stairwell or covered parking, though not inside a private residence. Whether that reaches every enclosed common area of a rental building is a question only case law could settle, so treat the enclosed common areas where staff work as smoke-free and post "No smoking" signs at the entrances.

What to do: decide the smoking policy and write it into the lease with the areas named; do not promise a smoke-free building you cannot deliver; and never promise one you have not designated, because a promise you break is a claim a waiver cannot stop.

title: The Tenant Cannot Agree to Shorter Notice for Showings
bodyText:
California does set an entry-notice period, so unlike some states there is something here to waive - and the answer is that the tenant cannot waive it. Any lease provision by which the tenant agrees to modify or waive rights or remedies under the entry statute is void. There is no separate-signed-addendum route, no shortened period the parties may agree in advance, and no at-the-door waiver you can paper in the lease.

Two things do work, and neither is a waiver. First, no notice at all is required if the tenant is present and consents at the time of entry - that is a decision the tenant makes then, not a promise made at signing. Second, for showings to buyers only, you may give the notice orally, in person or by telephone, provided you first told the tenant in writing within the previous 120 days that the property is for sale and that you or your agent may contact them orally about it; the oral notice still has to state the date, approximate time and purpose, and you must leave written evidence of the entry inside the unit. Twenty-four hours is presumed reasonable either way, and a notice mailed at least six days ahead is presumed reasonable too.

What to do: for showings to prospective tenants, give the written notice. For showings to buyers, send the 120-day written letter the moment you list the property, then use the oral route - and leave the entry note inside every time, because that is the step landlords forget and the one a tenant can prove you missed.

title: Entry for Regular Services: The Lease Cannot Create It
bodyText:
A clause reserving no-notice entry on a fixed schedule for filter changes, pest treatment or meter reading does not work in California, however conspicuously it is written. Entry is limited to the purposes the statute lists, and although supplying necessary or agreed services is one of them, the written-notice rule still applies: reasonable written notice stating the date, approximate time and purpose, during normal business hours, with twenty-four hours presumed reasonable. A lease provision modifying or waiving the entry rules is void, so the tenant cannot agree in advance to drop the notice.

Two routes are open. The statute lets you and the tenant agree orally to an entry to make agreed repairs or supply agreed services, provided the agreement fixes the date and approximate time and the entry happens within a week; that is an agreement made at the time, not a standing lease term, and apart from an emergency or the tenant being present and consenting at the time of entry, it is the only way to enter for services without written notice. Separately, where you submeter water, the statute gives you entry to install, repair or replace a submeter, to investigate abnormally high usage, and to read a submeter - and for reading, notice must be in writing only, so the oral route is closed.

Pest control works differently again: if you have a contract for periodic pest control service, each new tenant gets a copy of the company's notice, and a pesticide application you make yourself has its own advance-notice rules.

What to do: publish the service schedule in the lease as information, then serve the statutory notice for each visit. Door-hanger notices satisfy the statute if left where a reasonable person would find them.

title: When a Subsidised Unit Fails Inspection, Who Loses the Rent
bodyText:
If you let to a tenant whose rent is partly paid by a housing authority, nothing in California law tells you what happens to the rent when the unit fails an inspection. That question is answered by the federal voucher rules and by the contract you sign with the housing authority, not by the Civil Code. Under those federal rules you must keep the unit up to the programme's housing quality standards; a life-threatening defect has to be put right within 24 hours of notice and anything else within 30 days unless the authority allows longer. Miss the deadline and the authority stops paying its share, and a long enough stoppage ends your contract altogether.

The trap is what you must not do next. The missing subsidy is not the tenant's debt. The tenant owes only the tenant's own share, and the authority's failure to pay is not a breach by the tenant, so do not bill the shortfall to the tenant, do not serve a pay-or-quit notice for it, and do not end the tenancy over it. Read the housing authority's contract and its tenancy addendum before you sign: those terms override anything in your own lease that says otherwise.

California adds one rule of its own, and it runs the other way. If you end or decline to renew a rent-limiting agreement with a government agency, the tenants who benefited from it get at least 90 days' written notice, and for those 90 days they still owe only the share the agreement calculated.

For a tenant with no subsidy there is no proration statute at all. A rent reduction for an unfit unit comes from the habitability rules instead.

title: Late Fees on a Subsidised Tenancy
bodyText:
California has no late-fee rule for subsidised tenancies, and no late-fee cap for any tenancy. That does not make a late fee safe. Three things decide what you may charge a voucher tenant.

First, the fee can only attach to the tenant's own share of the rent. The housing authority's payment is not the tenant's obligation, so a tenant who pays their share on time is not late, however late the authority is. Work out your fee on the tenant portion and nothing else, and never add a charge because the authority's cheque has not arrived.

Second, your contract with the housing authority governs. Federal programme rules bar you from collecting anything from the tenant beyond the tenant rent the authority has set, and the tenancy addendum you must attach to the lease overrides your own late-fee clause where the two conflict. Check the addendum before you sign, and if it caps or bars late fees, that is your answer.

Third, California's general rule on fixed charges applies with full force: a figure written into a lease as damages is void unless it was impracticable to work out your actual loss and the figure is a reasonable estimate of it. Set your fee from what a late payment really costs you - staff time, bank charges, the cost of serving a notice - record how you got there, and keep it modest. The one late-fee schedule the Legislature has written for a residential tenancy sits in the submetered-water chapter and is in single-digit dollars; treat it as a warning about scale, not as your authority.

title: No State Guide to Hand a Tenant
bodyText:
There is no California rights-and-responsibilities guide you have to give a tenant - not before signing, not at renewal, and there is no acknowledgment for the tenant to sign. No state agency publishes a guide a landlord must deliver, and nothing in the codes penalises you for not handing one over. If you have seen a California tenants' guide, it is published as public information, not as a document the law puts in your hands.

One government publication does sit in the statutes, and it is worth knowing about rather than acting on. Residential landlords are told to give prospective tenants a consumer booklet about the health risks of mould, developed and distributed by the state department - but the duty does not start until six months after the department approves a booklet, and that approval has not happened. The same is true of the mould disclosure duty itself. So nothing is owed today, and you should keep an eye on it rather than build a process around it.

What California does instead of a guide is specific: a list of individual disclosures tied to particular facts about your property, plus a prescribed notice about rent increases and just-cause termination that goes in the lease itself. That is where your attention belongs. Work through the disclosure checklist for the address, give the tenant a signed copy of the lease with every disclosure attached, and keep proof of delivery. A general guide you are not required to give adds nothing; a disclosure you forget can void a termination notice or cost you damages.

title: The Only Statement of Tenant Rights You Must Give
bodyText:
No California agency publishes a statement of tenant rights that you must attach to a lease, and nothing requires a state form to be the first page, nothing requires the tenant to sign or initial each page, and no statute stops you from suing a tenant because you did not deliver one. So the shape this requirement takes in other states does not exist here.

California has one prescribed statement about tenant rights instead, and it matters far more than a general handout would. Where the rent-increase cap and the just-cause termination rules apply to your property, a notice in the statute's own words - telling the tenant that the law limits rent increases and that after 12 months of occupancy you must give a reason to end the tenancy - has to reach the tenant. You may put it in the lease, in an addendum, or in a separate written notice the tenant signs and gets a copy of. It must be in at least 12-point type, and if the tenancy was negotiated mainly in Spanish, Chinese, Tagalog, Vietnamese or Korean, the translation duty applies to it as well.

Treat it as compulsory even when you think you are exempt, unless you are certain. Failing to comply with any part of the just-cause section makes your written termination notice void - not merely defective - so a missing notice can cost you an entire eviction. If the property is exempt, the exemption statement belongs in the rental agreement itself. Use the statutory wording, keep a signed copy, and repeat it on renewal.

title: Tenants Who Organise: What You May Not Do
bodyText:
California gives tenants no affirmative right to organise - no right to a meeting room, no right to hold a tenants' meeting in a common area, no right to post or hand out literature in your building, and no statute telling you to recognise or deal with a tenants' association. Your common areas stay yours to manage, and a reasonable rule about soliciting, posting and using shared space is lawful.

What the law gives tenants instead is protection, and it is strong. You may not raise the rent, cut services, push a tenant out, bring a possession action, or threaten any of those things in order to retaliate against a tenant who has lawfully organised or taken part in a tenants' association, an organisation that advocates tenants' rights, or who has peaceably exercised any legal right. Unlike the ordinary retaliation rule, this one has no 180-day window and no once-a-year limit - it applies whenever retaliation is the purpose. The tenant bears the burden of producing evidence that your purpose was retaliatory, but if they make the case you face actual damages, $100 to $2,000 per act where there was fraud, oppression or malice, and the prevailing party's attorney's fees in a retaliatory eviction damages action if either side asks for them at the outset. Threatening to report a tenant or anyone connected with them to immigration authorities counts as retaliation in its own right. Any waiver of these protections in your lease is void.

There is also a trespass immunity you cannot override: a person invited in by an occupant, during reasonable hours or in an emergency, to give information about tenants' rights or to take part in a tenants' association is not a trespasser. So do not threaten such a visitor with trespass, and if you need to act for a lawful reason, state that reason in writing at the time.

title: Running the Tenancy Through an Online Portal
bodyText:
California has no statute about tenant portals. Nothing bans one, nothing licenses one, and nothing regulates a portal fee. But three rules together mean you cannot make the portal the only way to deal with you.

Rent first. You must let the tenant pay rent and the deposit by at least one method that is neither cash nor electronic transfer - in practice a cheque or money order - and you may not charge a fee for paying by cheque. Cash-only is allowed only for up to three months after a bounced or stopped cheque, with written notice and a copy of the dishonoured instrument attached. A waiver of any of this is void. You may offer the portal and encourage it; you may not require it.

Signatures and consent next. An electronic signature is as good as ink, but the agreement to do business electronically cannot be buried in a paper lease and cannot be made a condition of the tenancy - it has to be a separate, optional agreement, and that rule cannot be contracted around. A tenant who agrees to transact electronically may later refuse to do so, and that right cannot be contracted around either. If your portal stops a tenant printing or saving a document, that document is not enforceable against them.

Notices last, and this is the hard stop. A notice served the statutory way to end a tenancy or demand rent cannot be replaced by an electronic record. Serve those on paper, however good your portal is. Keep a paper path for payment, for signatures and for notices, and treat the portal as a convenience you offer.

title: Housing an Employee: No Disclosure Duty, but a Separate Eviction Route
bodyText:
California puts no special paperwork on a landlord who houses an employee. There is no signed disclosure of the conditions of occupancy, no statement of what happens when the job ends, and no duty to offer the worker a tenancy once you dismiss them. Nor is there any filing with a government office for a sponsored or guest worker, and no statute makes an employer answerable for a worker's rent or utilities.

What California does give you is a distinct removal route. The eviction statute reaches a person who took occupancy as a servant, employee, agent or licensee, and lets you treat them as holding over once the employment or agency has lawfully ended or the agreed occupancy period has run out. The just-cause rules recognise the same ground, so an employee's failure to leave after the job ends is a stated cause for termination where those rules apply. You still have to end the relationship lawfully first, and if what you really created was a tenancy at will you must serve the ordinary notice before relying on this route.

Two cautions. Write down, when the arrangement starts, whether the person occupies as part of the job or as a tenant paying rent, because that single point decides which route you have later. And if you house five or more employees in connection with their work, whether or not they pay rent, the Employee Housing Act may apply to the accommodation itself. So may some rural housing used by five or more farm workers. Housing within the Act needs an annual permit to operate. The rules about charging rent or crediting lodging against wages sit in the wage orders, not in the landlord-tenant law. Get advice before you set a rent for an employee.

title: Military and Airport Zones: One Lease Disclosure, and It Is Not About Noise
bodyText:
California requires no military noise or accident-zone disclosure in a lease. There is no notice to give because the property sits under a flight path, inside an air installation's noise contour or accident potential zone, or within a set distance of a named base, and no tenant right to walk away within 30 days of learning about it. The airport-in-the-vicinity notice you may have seen belongs to property sales and subdivision sales, not to renting.

One military-related disclosure does bind you, and it is about explosives rather than noise. If you actually know of a former federal or state military ordnance location within one mile of the dwelling - an area a government agency has identified as once used for military training that may still hold live munitions - you must give a prospective tenant written notice of that knowledge before the rental agreement is signed. For a tenancy that was already running when the rule came in, the notice was due as soon as practicable. The duty turns on your actual knowledge: nothing obliges you to investigate, but once you know, you must tell, and you cannot unknow it for the next tenant.

Practical course. Check whether the address is near a former ordnance area and record what you find, because the answer travels with the property. Put the notice in the lease or in a signed addendum so delivery is provable. And if you are near a base or an airport and expect noise complaints, say so in the lease voluntarily - it is not required, but a tenant who was told is a tenant who does not claim surprise.

title: No Shoreline or Beach Access Disclosure
bodyText:
California requires no shoreline disclosure in a residential lease. Nothing makes you tell a tenant that the property adjoins a beach, that the public has a right of access across it, where the tide line runs, that an accessway or easement crosses the land, or that erosion or sea-level rise may affect the site. There is no prescribed form and no acknowledgment, and no chapter anywhere in the California codes is about a shoreline disclosure to an occupant.

That does not mean coastal property is unregulated - it means the regulation runs between the owner and the state, not between you and your tenant. Public access along the coast is secured by coastal planning and permit law and by recorded accessway and easement documents. Those obligations bind the land whoever occupies it, so if a public accessway crosses your property your tenant cannot lawfully block it and neither can you.

Two practical points follow. First, read the title documents for the address before you let. A recorded public access easement, a deed restriction or a coastal permit condition is a term your tenant will run into, and a tenant who finds strangers crossing the garden after they move in will say you should have told them. Put the facts in the lease voluntarily and the complaint disappears. Second, if you are letting a property anywhere a tenant could be surprised - public steps through the lot, a seasonal flood route, a bluff - describe it in writing and have the tenant sign. Nothing requires it, and it costs you nothing but a paragraph.

Separately, check whether the city or county has its own coastal or short-term-let rules for the address; this library does not resolve local ordinances.

title: Terms California Lets You Add, and the Two That Earn Their Place
bodyText:
California has no list of optional lease terms. The Civil Code works the other way round: it implies duties into every tenancy and voids the terms that take a tenant's rights away, and what is left over is yours to negotiate. So the useful question is not what you are allowed to add but which additions actually change your position.

Two do, and both are easy to miss. First, a forfeiture clause. In a written lease for a term longer than a year, if your rent notice did not declare a forfeiture and the lease has no forfeiture clause, the court must hold the writ of possession for five days after judgment so the tenant can pay everything due and stay. Put a forfeiture clause in and that mandatory stay does not apply. Second, tenant-performed maintenance. An agreement that the tenant will improve, repair or maintain the dwelling is void as a habitability waiver unless it is part of the consideration for the rental - so it has to be written into the lease itself, visibly tied to the rent, not recorded in a side letter.

There is also a timing rule that costs nothing to obey. A clause by which the tenant gives up a statutory right is void unless the lease was put in front of the tenant before they took possession - so present the whole lease, with every addendum, before handover, and never paper it afterwards. Some rights cannot be given up at all whatever you do.

Everything else - guests, pets, parking, smoking, rules, absences, interest on arrears - is ordinary contract drafting. Add what serves you, and check each term against the void list.

title: Every Disclosure a California Lease Has to Carry
bodyText:
California has no single section listing what you must disclose. The duties are scattered, most are triggered by a fact about your property, and three of them put text inside the lease document itself. Work through this list for the specific address before you let.

Always: the name, telephone number and street address for service of the manager and of the owner or the owner's authorised person; where and how rent is paid and which forms of payment you accept; the rent-cap and just-cause notice in the statute's own words, in at least 12-point type, or the exemption statement if the property is exempt; general bed bug information before a new tenancy; and - for a single-family rental, or a leasehold of a building with more than four units - the registered-offender database notice in at least 8-point type.

If the fact applies: a former military ordnance area within a mile that you know about; a demolition permit you have applied for; the pest control company's notice where you have a service contract, and the pesticide notice before each application; a shared gas or electric meter serving anything outside the unit; the water submeter billing disclosure; flood-hazard and methamphetamine or fentanyl contamination notices; mould where you know of it; asbestos; the federal lead-based paint disclosure for pre-1978 housing; a Proposition 65 warning; the areas where you have banned smoking.

Three traps. Give the tenant a signed copy of everything and keep proof of delivery. If the tenancy was negotiated mainly in Spanish, Chinese, Tagalog, Vietnamese or Korean, translate the whole lease before signing. And if you grant an option to purchase, you become a seller: the full transfer and natural-hazard disclosure statements fall due before the contract is made.

title: House Rules: No Statute, So the Lease Is Everything
bodyText:
California has no house-rules statute for ordinary rental housing. No section says a rule must be reasonable, serve the convenience, safety or welfare of tenants, apply fairly to everyone, or be explicit enough to follow. None requires rules to be posted or given to the tenant, and none says a rule adopted later binds the tenant on notice. The conditions you may have read about belong to other states, and the one place California does legislate on park rules is the mobilehome law, which does not reach a dwelling.

So a house rule binds your tenant only because the lease says it does. Write the rules, attach them, and say in the lease that they are part of it and that breaking one is a breach of a material term - that is what gives you the three-day perform-or-quit route and, where the just-cause rules apply, a stated cause.

Changing rules mid-tenancy is where landlords come unstuck. In a periodic tenancy a change to the terms needs the statutory notice, so if a new rule really changes the bargain - charging for something that was free, taking away parking or storage - treat it as a change of terms and serve that notice. In a fixed-term lease you can change rules during the term only if the lease reserved the power. Never use a rule to cut a tenant's statutory rights or to shift your repair duty; those provisions are void. And never change rules or cut a service in response to a complaint, a repair request or tenant organising - that is retaliation, with damages.

title: Habitability and Building Rules California Does Not Have
bodyText:
California's habitability law is strong, so the gaps are easy to miss. This is the list of things the state does not require, each worked out in its own row.

Nothing requires a habitability statement in the lease, and nothing regulates a written promise to repair made before signing - no completion date, no remedy if you miss it. There is no rent escrow or pay-into-court route for a tenant, and so no exemption to notify. You may not name the contractor a tenant must use, and you have no right to end a tenancy because a repair turns out to be expensive. A lease term requiring repair requests in writing does not bind the tenant.

On the building side: no defective drywall disclosure, no sprinkler disclosure and no retrofit duty for an existing dwelling, no child fall-prevention window guards, no steam radiator covers, no state lead notice beyond the federal one, no lead-safe certificate for a building, no radon disclosure, no certificate-of-occupancy disclosure, and no tenant right to a portable cooling device - though that last one changes in 2027, so watch it. There is no joint move-in inventory requirement, no general right of periodic inspection, and no right to fix a tenant's breach and bill it.

One point stays open: we found no water-heater temperature duty in the statutes, but the plumbing code is a regulation this library has not read, so set the thermostat to the manufacturer's recommendation and record it.

What fills every gap is the implied duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in, which the lease cannot waive.

title: Other Rules California Does Not Have
bodyText:
California regulates renting heavily, which makes the blank spaces worth knowing. Each of these is worked out in its own row.

Money: no late-fee cap and no grace period; no collection fee; no all-in or mandatory-fee pricing rule for leases; no tenancy statute requires a rent receipt, even for cash - but a general obligations provision does give a tenant the right to require one on request, so this is not a clean absence and is indexed under the rent-receipt row rather than here; no state tax on residential rent and no tax pass-through or property-tax disclosure; no right to bill a government fee or a fine against you to the tenant; no cap on holdover charges and no statutory holdover rate; no deposit-alternative or fee-in-lieu statute; no faster deposit route on request; no landlord-held utility deposit; no duty to pay deposit interest.

Process: no possession bond and no confessed judgment; no lease-designated party to accept eviction papers; no express ban on charging eviction costs to the tenant; no winter eviction bar and no cold-weather notice.

Paperwork: no truth-in-renting handbook; no statute making the tenant initial anything; no front-page list of the terms against the tenant; no rule making you treat month-to-month the same as a fixed term.

People and property: no emergency-contact rule; no tenant duty to report an extended absence; no tenant right to receive guests; no key-control or master-key rules; no statutory drug-free addendum; no firearms rule; no seasonal-tenancy category; no termination right of your own after fire, flood or quake; no restriction on foreign tenants or owners; no veteran incentives; no work card for senior-housing staff.

In each gap the answer is the lease plus the general law, and each row gives the cautious course.

title: Three Points Checked Across All of California Law
bodyText:
Three questions whose answer, if it existed, would sit outside the landlord-tenant chapters. We looked across the whole of California's statute law for each.

Squatters and unwanted occupants. There is no fast route outside the courts - no sheriff removal on a sworn complaint, no police removal of a transient occupant on your affidavit, no same-day hearing. Anyone in possession, however they got there, comes out by unlawful detainer and a writ, and taking the property back yourself is forcible entry. The single exception is narrow: if you live in the home and have one lodger, you may end the arrangement by written notice and the lodger's right to stay ends by operation of law.

Cash rent receipts. No tenancy statute requires a receipt for rent, in cash or otherwise. But the general law of obligations, which sits outside the tenancy chapters, gives a debtor a right to a written receipt from a creditor on performance - that section has now been read, and it answers the question: a tenant who asks you for a written rent receipt is entitled to one. Give a written receipt for every cash payment regardless. It costs nothing and it is your evidence too.

Registration before you can win a possession case. There is no statewide landlord register or rental licence, and nothing makes registration a precondition to judgment. Two things outside the tenancy law can still stop a company landlord in its tracks: a corporation whose powers are suspended for unpaid tax, and an out-of-state entity that has not qualified to do business here. Check your entity's standing with the Secretary of State and the tax authority before you file, not after. A third reaches any landlord, company or not: if you rent under a fictitious business name, you cannot maintain an action on business done under that name until the fictitious business name statement has been filed and published (Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §§ 17910, 17918).

title: Smoke-Free Rules in California
bodyText: California lets you ban smoking anywhere on your property, including inside units. If you do, every lease signed on or after January 1, 2012 with a tenant new to the unit must say where on the property smoking is banned. The library's smoking clause names the whole property, so using it meets that rule. A tobacco ban also covers cannabis, because state law does not allow smoking cannabis where tobacco smoking is banned, and for both, smoking includes vaping. Going smoke-free during an existing tenancy is a change of terms. For a lease made before 2012, the ban needs written notice served as Civ. Code § 827 requires. For a later lease, you must follow the federal, state and local rules for changing an existing lease's terms. Local smoking ordinances still apply.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: California follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (Cal. Com. Code § 3311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (Cal. Com. Code § 1308(b)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. California also has an older statute saying that accepting a check marked payment in full on a disputed or unliquidated claim is not an accord and satisfaction if you protest by striking out or deleting the notation, or if you accepted it inadvertently or without knowing of the notation (Cal. Civ. Code § 1526). The two statutes conflict and which one controls is case law this library has not reviewed, so don't rely on striking the notation. Separately, a tenant may pay, without condition, the amount they concede is due, leaving you every remedy for the balance (Cal. Civ. Code § 1525). The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: California's landlord-tenant statutes impose no general duty of good faith of the kind in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (the Civil Code's residential hiring sections (§§ 1940-1954) searched); good faith appears only in specific rules. Courts in many states read a covenant of good faith and fair dealing into every contract, a lease included; whether and how California's courts do is case law this library has not reviewed, so act as if the duty applies. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.
